# Every change in 0.5.0

The complete list of what [0.5.0](../CHANGELOG.md) brought, from v0.4.1. The changelog's
0.5.0 section has the highlights.

## Added

- **Say a vault key's value is no 2FA seed.** A secret fill refuses a value that looks like a seed,
  and some real values look like one, such as a 16-letter app password. In a vault's tab, a key's
  menu has *Mark as no 2FA seed…*, and a marked key then fills as a plain value on the same notice
  and grants as any key. A chat can't make the mark, a new value takes it away, and an `otpauth`
  address is refused whatever the mark says (#5237).
- **Install from a terminal.** `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/purlis/purlis/main/install.sh | sh`
  installs the latest stable release on macOS (Apple silicon) or Linux (x86_64), and
  `PURLIS_CHANNEL=dev` installs the dev build. On macOS it avoids the first-launch refusal an
  ad-hoc signed app downloaded in a browser meets. When `gh` is signed in, it checks each
  download's build provenance first and installs nothing that fails.
- **A sandbox block that names no socket or service lets you choose it.** When the sandbox
  refused a local socket and nothing said which (a build runner that started Docker, a
  background command read back later), the Notice said there was no socket to allow and offered
  only *Start without the sandbox*. It now also offers *Choose the socket…*: a list of the
  sockets purlis finds on this machine (Docker's, Podman's, your SSH agent's, a database's) and
  a box to type a path. The socket you choose is checked as one the sandbox named is, with the
  same warning for a container engine's, and then offers *Allow once*, *Allow for this chat*
  and *Always allow*. Only you can
  choose, in the window; nothing a chat printed fills the list or the box.
- **A blocked local socket or system service can be allowed.** When a sandboxed chat is refused
  Docker's socket, a database's, an SSH agent's, or macOS's certificate check that Go tools such
  as `gh` and `glab` use, its Notice names it, says plainly what allowing it means (a container
  engine's socket is about the same as no sandbox), and offers **Allow once**, **Allow for this
  chat** or **Always allow** for this project on this machine, or **Keep blocked**. Nothing is
  allowed by default. What you allow is listed in Settings with Remove, and kept only on your
  machine, never in the project's committed file. A project can declare the sockets and services
  it expects with `[sandbox].expects`, which changes only what the Notice says. An
  administrator's policy can forbid all of it with `"socket-grants": false` (ADR 0093).
- **A branch folder has one live writer.** The first chat that commits, updates or pushes in a
  branch folder through purlis claims it. When a second live chat tries `purlis worktree commit`,
  `update` or `push` there, purlis refuses and names the chat that holds the folder. The holder
  hands it over with `purlis worktree done` or `abandon`, or the person does. A claim whose
  chat has ended is released. When purlis can't tell whether the holder is still running, for
  example while it restores after a restart, it refuses. A task started in a folder another
  chat holds is warned that its writes there will be refused (#3901).
- **`purlis worktree update` and `purlis worktree push`.** From inside a branch folder, `update`
  fetches and rebases it onto the branch it was cut from (or `--base <branch>`), stopping on a
  conflict with the files named, then `--continue` or `--abort`; `push` pushes the folder's own
  branch, with `--force-with-lease` right after an update. In a sandboxed chat the app runs
  them, as it runs `purlis worktree commit` (qw387).
- **A branch cut for a chat that never started says so.** A writing chat's branch is cut just
  before its chat starts. If purlis is killed or crashes in between, the folder and the branch
  stay behind. The explorer now marks such a branch `unclaimed`, with how long ago it was cut.
  purlis never removes it on its own: start a chat in it, or remove its folder from its menu.
  Branches and worktrees made with plain git are never marked (#835).
- **A branch's own folder can be copied, revealed and opened in a shell.** A branch's row in the
  explorer, and its *Files* row, have *Copy absolute path*, *Reveal* and *Open a shell tab here*,
  as a folder inside it has; the palette lists them for each branch of the focused workspace.
  A branch folder that is itself a link is refused, never followed (#1143).
- **A chat can ask to move a recorded browser login to another site** (#4996). When it names a
  different site for a login already in the project's settings, purlis shows the site recorded
  now and the one proposed, and asks: Allow once, Allow for this chat, Always replace, or Keep the
  recorded site. Always replaces the login's line, showing it first; nothing changes until you
  choose.
- **A browser login is a persona's tool.** `[sandbox.personas.<persona>] tools = { shop-login =
  { vault, browser = "https://…/login", user, key } }` lets a sandboxed chat log a browser in:
  it runs `shop-login -s=<session>`, and purlis opens the declared page in a browser of its own,
  fills the login from the vault only on that page's site, and leaves the logged-in session for
  the chat to load. The chat never sees the login and cannot send it to another page, host or
  program. It waits for the same Allow as the persona's hosts and tools, and needs Playwright's
  `playwright-cli` installed (#1407).
- **A browser site can be allowed for everyone in the project.** A browser's site ask offers
  Allow for everyone in this project beside this chat and this project on this machine. The site
  is kept in the project's settings (`[sandbox] browser-sites`), for browsers alone: chats'
  commands still ask for that host. A site a teammate adds is shown to you once in a Notice, and
  reaches your browsers only after that. Each is a row of its own in Granted, and removing it
  ends the browsers it reached (#2443).
- **A browser's chip names its page, and its rows say who drives.** A browser view's chip says
  where its page is and on which device (`localhost:5173 on this Mac`), and follows each
  navigation the agent or you make. It names the page's origin alone, never a path or a title.
  A chat's browser row and its thumbnail say when you are driving it, and when purlis is
  signing in to a page in it (#2300).
- **A browser you open goes where you type.** New browser in the palette opens a browser in a tab
  of its own, with an address field above its page. It reaches the project's sites and the
  services on this machine you allowed for the project, and asks once before going to a site new
  to the project. Only http and https addresses go (#2176).
- **A chat always knows its open tasks.** While it has any, every turn begins with a short
  roster: each task's number, name and state. A task it was told had stopped on the person is
  announced once when it is back at work. A dispatch under the exact name of one of its tasks
  that is still open is refused, naming that task's number and state and saying to wait on it,
  tell it more or cancel it (#3788).
- **A browser login a persona doesn't declare asks once, and the chat waits** (#4595). When a chat
  logs its browser in with vault credentials, purlis shows one notice with the site large and
  editable, and the vault and key names. It offers Allow once, Allow for this chat, Always allow
  and Keep blocked. Always allow adds the one line to the project's settings and allows it on
  this machine; the other two write nothing.
- **A chat closes its own finished task.** `purlis dispatch close <chat>` closes a task the chat
  dispatched once it has reported: its finished row goes, and a task kept open after its report
  is ended. Its report stays in the Dispatches tab. A task still working, in a turn, or one you
  typed in is not closed this way (#1981).
- **A chat can fill a 2FA code from a seed in your vault.** `browser_fill_secret` with `code`
  names the key that holds the seed (an `otpauth://totp/` address or the base32 secret); you
  allow it for one site, once or for the chat, on the same notice as any secret, and purlis works
  the current code out as it fills. Only the code reaches the page; the seed never leaves the vault's side.
- **A chat can put a vault secret into a field of its browser, with your yes.**
  `browser_fill_secret` names a field from the page, a vault and a key; you see the key, its
  vault, the exact site, the page and the field's label on one notice, and choose Allow once or
  Keep blocked. purlis fills it only into a one-line field whose own frame is on that site at the
  moment of filling, and the value never reaches the chat (#5115, spec #5100).
- **A chat knows who asked for it and where else its persona is working.** A chat purlis
  started is told at its start which chat asked for it, which other tasks that chat asked for,
  and every other chat running as the same persona in the project, each with its workspace,
  name, state and start time. When that changes, its next turn is told in one line, and a turn
  is told nothing when nothing changed. `purlis persona where` and the `persona_where` tool
  show the same picture at any time, and a Claude Code chat runs the tool without asking.
  purlis answers from its own record of the open chats, so it works in a sandboxed chat; a
  chat can only ask about itself, and it learns names and states, never another chat's brief
  or transcript (#1450).
- **A sandboxed chat may run a server.** When a server a Codex or opencode chat starts is
  refused its port (`npm run dev` on 5173), its Notice offers **Allow only for this chat** or
  **Allow for me on this machine**. The server then runs on a socket of the chat's own, never on
  a TCP port of this Mac. purlis's front door answers on `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`, checks each
  request's address, and keeps your browser's cookies from the server.
  - The chat's browser opens the server with no second ask, and so can your own browser.
  - A page the server sends runs in your browser as a site of this Mac. It can read your other
    local apps' cookies that are not HttpOnly, send requests to those apps as you, and send
    what it reads to the internet. Open it in the chat's own browser unless you trust it.
  - `purlis listen <port> -- <command>` starts a server there, for example
    `purlis listen 5173 -- npm run dev`, and Vite, Next.js and other Node servers run unchanged.
  - A port below 1024, or one something on this Mac already listens on, is never offered.
  - The grant is listed in Settings' Network page with Remove.
  - A Claude Code chat's sandbox cannot be given one port to serve on, so its Notice says so and
    offers Start without the sandbox (#2019).
- **A chat on a harness that can take no skills is told so when it starts** (Skill studio
  preview, #3585). A chat on a harness the project declares, with no skill format purlis can hand
  skills by and no MCP servers, shows one line on its tab at its first start. The line says that
  skills are not supported there, in the words the Skill studio uses. A chat on any other harness
  shows nothing.
- **A chat on a pool that opts in to minting gets its GitHub token from the cluster**, so `gh` works
  with the desktop closed and nobody is asked about each run. The token covers only the repos on both
  the Pool and the Claim, stays in the runner's memory, and is revoked as the chat ends. A refused mint
  goes to the desktop and the person's Ask. Pools that do not opt in are unchanged (#4207).
- **A chat can propose a change to purlis's own configuration, and you apply it.** When a
  sandboxed chat edits the project's manifest, a persona's `mcp.json` or `persona.md`, or a
  skill's files, the change is shown on its tab and in the Inbox, the file as it is and as the
  change would make it, with **Apply** and **Dismiss**. Apply writes exactly that, as you, only
  while the file is still what the chat read; it rides your next save, and is recorded. The chat
  is told applied, dismissed or stale on its next turn. Claude Code chats propose with their own
  edits; other harnesses run `purlis propose <file> --from <draft>` (#1975).
- **A chat starting on a cluster pool says where its runner has got to.** While it waits, the Start
  dialog says it is waiting for room in the cluster, downloading the runner image, starting your
  runner, or that your runner was resting and is coming back. Where the cluster gives a reason for
  a long wait, the dialog shows it.
- **A chat started without the sandbox can use its persona's browser logins.** `browser_login`
  performs the login for it as for a sandboxed chat: a login its persona declares, allowed on this
  machine, from a vault its persona may use (#2560).
- **A chat's Activity: one timeline of what it and its tasks said to each other.** A chat
  tab's menu and the palette have _Activity_, which opens a read-only tab listing every task
  the chat dispatched and the tasks under those, oldest first: each brief, follow-up, progress
  note, question, answer and report, with its time and who said it to whom. The name of the
  chat that said a line opens that chat. What a chat said is shown as text and never as markup,
  and a long line is clipped until you ask for all of it. A file that the reports of two tasks
  working in the same folder both name is marked on each. The tab follows the work while it is open. To make this possible a
  dispatch's record on this machine now keeps the text of the messages the two chats sent
  through purlis: the first 500 of a task, for 30 days after the task ended. After that each
  message keeps its line and its time, and its words are gone. Nothing of either chat's
  conversation is kept (#1495).
- **A chat's browser asks before it goes to a site new to the project.** A link a page offers
  loads, so public sites are readable; an address the agent writes for a new site, a form it
  submits there, or its typing on a page or frame of one, asks you first. A chat's sites wait as
  one ask, with Allow for this chat, Always allow in this project on this machine, and Keep
  blocked. An Allow is a **browser site**, for the browser alone: the chat's own commands still
  ask for that host. Browser sites are listed apart in the Granted list, and removing one ends
  the browsers it reached. On the open web nothing asks (#2018).
- **A chat's browser on its tab and in the Chats list.** Each browser a chat drives is drawn
  live, as a small picture, beside the chat's tab, and listed under the chat in the Chats list;
  either opens it in a tab of its own, which names the device it runs on above the page.
  Closing that tab closes only the view: the browser ends with its chat. Settings › You ›
  Chats list › *Open a chat's browser beside it* opens each new one beside its chat (#2024).
- **A chat's browser says what an action changed, and what is out of view.** Every browser tool
  that acts on a page takes `changes`, and then answers the lines of the page new or gone since
  it was last read, so the agent need not take a whole snapshot after each step; and a snapshot
  or a find marks an element the page lays out beyond what it shows `(out of view)` (#2137).
- **A chat's browser timeline.** What a chat's agent did in its browsers, with the screenshots
  its browser tools returned, opens in a tab of its own from the palette or a browser's row
  menu: *Browser timeline of <chat>*. Where you or purlis drove the browser it says so, and keeps
  no screenshot. It holds nothing typed and no address of a signed-in browser, stays on this device within
  a bound (its newest 200 moments and 24 screenshots, and 96 MiB of screenshots per project), no
  chat can read it, and it goes when the chat closes (#2017).
- **A chat's `gh` can act as your organisation's own GitHub App** (#2053). Declare it on a
  persona's tools as `gh = { vault = "…", mint = "github-app", app = "<client id>", key = "…" }`,
  with the App's private key in that vault. Each run of `gh` then gets a short-lived installation
  token in `GH_TOKEN`, limited to the GitHub repos of the clones in the chat's workspace that
  purlis cloned or you saved from the window (save a clone you made yourself once). The key
  itself is never handed to anything: `secret exec`, `get` and `cp`, other tools and the Vaults
  tab's reveal all refuse it. A runner chat gets the token its desktop mints. For GitLab, declare
  `glab` with a project or group access token, as any tool is.
- **A Claude Code chat's Network view says where an administrator's settings open local
  ports.** Where managed Claude Code settings turn local binding on, which outranks purlis's
  setting, or cannot be read, the chat's Network view says so and names the file, as doctor's
  `sandbox local ports` row does (#1699).
- **The skill run chip on a chat's tab shows the tokens the run has spent so far**, where the chat's program reports usage (#2872).
- **A Claude Code chat may run a server on macOS.** When a server a Claude Code chat starts is
  refused its port, its Notice offers **Allow only for this chat** or **Allow for me on this
  machine**, as a Codex or opencode chat's does. Start the server with
  `purlis listen 5173 -- npm run dev`: it is reached through purlis's front door on
  `http://127.0.0.1:5173`, with the same checks, and Claude Code's own sandbox settings stay as
  they were (#3316).
  - It works for Node servers such as Vite, Next.js and Express. Another kind of server cannot be
    given one port in a Claude Code chat: start it without the sandbox, or in a Codex or opencode
    chat.
  - Removing the grant in Settings' Network page stops the server being reached at once.
- **A Claude Code chat can be allowed a service on this Mac.** Its Notice now offers **Allow
  only for this chat** or **Allow for me on this machine** instead of only Start without the
  sandbox. Its commands reach the port through the chat's proxy by the name
  `this-mac.internal:<port>` (curl, and any client that uses the proxy), or by
  `kubernetes.docker.internal` or `host.docker.internal`, and only while the port is allowed.
  Removing the grant stops new connections at once; one already open ends when the chat
  restarts. For kubectl, **Point kubectl at it…** lists your kubeconfig's contexts and gives the
  chat its own copy of one whose cluster is on this Mac, credentials included, which the chat
  can read; its server is named `https://this-mac.internal:<port>` with the certificate still
  checked. A context elsewhere is listed with why. Your own kubeconfig is never changed (qw384b).
- **Move here brings back a repository the chat cloned on the runner.** It is made here with its
  branch, its commits and its uncommitted work, and what came in it that a tool here runs or
  reads is named on the chat's tab, as for any clone. A runner from an earlier purlis still
  leaves such a repository there, and Move here's row says so (#3811).
- **A cluster Pool can opt in to minting GitHub App tokens in the cluster** (#4204). A cluster admin
  sets `spec.forge` on a Pool (the App's key Secret, an allow-list of repos and `mintInCluster`) and
  names the Secret in the chart's `forge.keySecretNames`, the only Secret the operator may read. A
  desktop records the opt-in as it adds the pool. Nothing is minted yet.
- **Run a workspace's chats in your team's cluster.** The add pool dialog has a Kind: Cluster
  takes your kubeconfig's context and the name of a Pool of purlis's cluster operator, shows the
  cluster operator's key for you to check against the one your cluster's admin gives you, then
  claims a runner there as you, pairs it and keeps it. A workspace set to run on that pool runs
  its chats on that runner. Before every link purlis checks that the Pool still names the key you
  checked and that the operator still vouches for the runner it paired with; either changed is
  refused and asked about, as a Docker runner's changed key is. purlis runs your own `kubectl`,
  found where its installers put it. The pool keeps its own copy of the context, taken when it
  was added; to pick up a changed kubeconfig, add the pool again (#3292).
- **A cluster pool's `deleteSuspendedAfter`, `noticeBeforeDelete` and `maxAge` now act.** A kept
  Claim suspended for being idle for 30 days is deleted with its volume, after a seven-day notice on
  the Claim. A `stopped` Claim or Pool is never deleted. A runner past its 14 days starts on the
  pool's current image the next time it is idle; a chat is never ended for it (#3981, #3982).
- **A cluster Claim says when its runner is stuck**, and the operator removes what deleted Claims
  left behind (#3739).
- **`purlis profile sign-in <profile> --pool <pool>` on a cluster pool.** The command now signs a
  profile in on the runner of a cluster pool you marked *This is my own*, while the cluster vouches
  for its claim, the same way the row in Settings › Pools does. An unmarked pool, or one not
  vouched for at that moment, is refused in words and nothing runs there (#4164).
- **A cluster runner forgets what is no longer chosen.** Showing a marked cluster pool's profiles,
  or a chat's start there, has its runner forget the profiles no longer chosen for it, and removing
  a profile on this Mac has it forget that one too (#4183).
- **Your profiles on a cluster pool's runner.** A cluster pool you marked *This is my own* now
  lists its profiles on its row in Settings › Pools, as a Docker pool does: Add a profile…,
  Remove, and Sign in, which runs the harness's own login on the runner over your own
  `kubectl exec`. Nothing of this Mac's sign-in goes there. A profile goes to the runner, and
  signs in there, only while the pool is marked and the cluster vouches for its claim at that
  moment. On a kept claim a sign-in outlives the pod; on a fresh claim the row says it lasts only
  for that claim. The pool's chosen profiles are kept as `profiles` in its record, spelled as a
  Docker pool's (#3819).
- **A cluster pool you mark as your own can run its persona's tools and browser logins.** Turn on
  This is my own on its row in Settings, under Pools. It starts off, only you can turn it on, and
  its words say who else can read what the runner holds. Each time a value or a token is about to
  go, the cluster must vouch for the runner, then and again after you allow it. If it does not
  answer, nothing is sent. A pool you have not marked is refused in words that say how to mark
  it (#4071).
- **A cluster pool keeps its own warm count, and names its times.** A `Pool` takes
  `warmReplicas` (0 unless set, 20 at most). The cluster operator keeps that many runners warm
  for each person who has a fresh claim on the pool, in their own namespace and counted in their
  quota, and brings a warm pool scaled by hand back to that count. A `Pool` also takes
  `idleAfter` (30m), `deleteSuspendedAfter` (720h), `noticeBeforeDelete` (168h) and `maxAge`
  (336h). The cluster refuses any other spelling and a notice that comes after the deletion. The
  operator does not act on the four times yet (#3737).
- **A cluster pool's idle runners suspend after its `idleAfter`** (30 minutes unless the pool says
  otherwise). A runner with no chat, no browser and no project held by its desktop stops and its
  pod ends; a kept runner's volume stays. Its Claim says `Idle`, and the next chat you start there
  runs a kept runner again; a fresh runner comes back with a new key, so its Claim is made again. It takes a runner image with this version of purlis; an older image never
  suspends (#3980).
- **A chat on a harness your project declares gets what its declaration says.** It is started
  with the variables its `env` namespace reaches in your environment, each judged on its own, so
  a prefix never passes one named like a credential. Shift+Enter in its pane sends its
  `[terminal] newline`. A curation prompt, the first task and *Start a chat here* type into it
  by its `[terminal] ready_to_type` and `paste_drawn_whole`, as they do for a built-in harness,
  and only on one line: purlis cannot tell that it takes a longer paste whole (#967, #1013).
- **You control which options a declared tool runs with.** A persona's tool takes `args`, a list
  of patterns for whole arguments (`args = ["get", "describe", "pods", "--namespace=*"]`); a
  chat's run of the tool goes ahead only where every argument matches one, and an option only
  where a pattern spells one. A pattern holds no place, so `"*"` lets in any command's verb.
  `args` is part of the tool's Allow, so changing it asks again (#3421).
- **A project can say which harness profiles a persona's tasks run on.** `[dispatch.profiles]`
  in the project's committed file lists them per persona (`devops = ["work"]`). A chat
  dispatched to that persona, as a task or a handoff or by your own "Ask a persona" from a tab,
  then starts on one of the listed profiles or not at all, whoever chose the profile: the
  asking chat with `--profile`, the persona's own definition, or the asking chat's own
  profile. The refusal names the profiles the project lists and says what can be done about
  it. A persona with no list of its own is held to the list of the persona it extends; one
  with none at all is dispatched to on any profile the project offers, as before. A list only
  narrows: a listed profile is still one the project offers and this machine approved, and one
  that starts its harness with the permission prompts off is still refused for any chat
  another chat starts (#1509).
- **A dispatch refused while you were away is shown when you are back.** A chat running with
  its permission prompts off dispatches only under a grant that already stands, as before, and
  is refused at once where there is none. That refusal is now kept, and the hand in the title
  bar lists it: "steward wanted devops while you were away", how many times and when, with
  three answers. **Allow from now on** makes the grant for you on this machine for that one
  pair, for work in the workspace the refused task would have worked in, so the next run
  works; it starts nothing. **Never for this pair** is your never for it.
  **Dismiss** puts the item away, and it stays away while the chat asks on: it is shown again
  only if the pair is refused a week or more later. The chat is told its refusal as before,
  and that you will see it. The item belongs to no chat: no tab shows a hand for it (#1507).
- **A dispatch to another persona asks you once.** The dispatch grant is in place: when a chat
  dispatches to a persona other than its own and nothing covers the pair, nothing starts and a
  Notice on the asking chat's tab says who wants to dispatch to whom and shows the first brief
  as the chat wrote it, with how many lines it is. You choose **Allow for this chat**, **Allow
  for me on this machine**, **Allow for everyone in this project** or **Keep blocked**. After an
  Allow that dispatch starts, and so does every later one the grant covers, with no prompt. The
  persona chat starts with its own persona's hosts and vault, with nothing to allow on its tab.
  A chat dispatching to its own persona needs no grant. Settings › Project › Dispatch lists
  every dispatch grant with its level, who granted it and when, and **Revoke**; the next
  dispatch across a revoked pair asks again, and a chat already running is left alone. A grant
  for one chat ends when that chat closes. A grant for everyone is kept in the project's
  committed file under `[dispatch.grants]`. One a teammate added covers no chat on your machine
  until you allow it there: the project's one-time Notice names what was added and taken away,
  and allows all of it or one pair. Every Allow and Revoke is recorded in purlis's event log
  (#1437).
- **A dispatch waits while this machine is short on memory.** A task or handoff that every
  other check allows no longer starts a new chat when the system reports that memory is short
  (critical memory pressure on macOS; memory stalls, or too little available, on Linux). The
  chat that asked is told it is waiting, the Dispatches tab lists it under *Not started*, and it
  starts by itself once memory frees, checked against the limits as they are then. If memory is
  still short after 10 minutes, nothing starts and the chat that asked is told. A dispatch you
  start yourself from a chat's tab does not wait (#1467).
- **A dispatch can say where its chat works.** `purlis dispatch --in workspace:<name>` starts
  the persona chat in another workspace of the project, with that workspace's todos, memory
  and session records; it is listed under the chat that asked, with the workspace named, and
  reports back to it. `--in worktree` gives the chat a new worktree of the repo the asking
  chat works in, on a new branch. The app cuts the worktree, under a folder and a branch
  purlis names for the dispatch, so two tasks never share either. The `dispatch` tool takes
  the same word as `in`.
- **A worktree task's report names its branch**, from purlis's own record of what it cut.
  purlis merges nothing for a task by itself; you merge it from the task's Changes tab.
- **In a sandboxed project a worktree task commits with `purlis worktree commit`.** A
  worktree's git data is outside the folder a sandboxed chat may write, so its own `git
  commit` is refused there and the app commits for it on the task's branch. purlis tells the
  new chat and the asking chat so as the task starts. With no sandbox the task commits on its
  branch with git.
- **A task's own branch is listed on its row in the Dispatches tab**, with **Discard**.
  Discard removes the branch's folder: it asks first and names every uncommitted file and
  every ignored path of the task's that would go, and is refused while a chat is still open in
  the folder. The branch purlis cut loses no commit: one that holds work stays. A branch that
  is merged is removed with its folder when its chat is closed or the project is opened, and
  only where the folder holds nothing else: a folder holding an uncommitted or an ignored
  file of the task's is never removed for you.
- **`dispatch-isolation: worktree` on a persona** makes a worktree its chats' default place to
  work when a dispatch names none. The key is read again: a persona file that still carries
  the line gets this the moment you update, with no edit, and `purlis persona lint` no longer
  warns about it. Nothing asks before two chats write in one tree.
- **Ask <persona>… asks where the chat works**: this chat's folder, a branch of its own, or
  another workspace.
- **`purlis dispatch list` says the branch a task was given** and how its worktree stands, and
  a task's row in the Chats tree says it works on a branch of its own.
- **A report purlis writes for a chat that ended without one names the task's branch**, as the
  chat's own report would have.
- **A runner chat on a Docker pool has a working browser.** The runner image now carries what
  the browser engine needs, and a Docker pool makes each runner so the engine can start with its
  own sandbox on: Docker's default seccomp profile, plus the user, process and network
  namespaces the engine's sandbox makes. Each runner also gets a quarter of its memory as shared
  memory. Only the browser engine may make namespaces on a runner, and only an image whose
  purlis keeps every other program from making them gets that profile; a team's image gets it
  once it is rebuilt on this version. A runner a chat ran on without the sandbox starts no
  browser and is filled no login until it is made again, and the browsers already open there
  end. A runner made before this version keeps working, but its browsers don't start: remove
  its pool and add it again (#3298).
- **A runner can be a container on this machine.** purlis's core makes a Docker pool's runner
  from the runner image, by its digest, confined the same way every time: Docker's default
  seccomp profile, every capability dropped, no new privileges, a user who is not root, its home
  on a volume of its own and no folder of this machine. It checks the container is still
  confined so before it pairs and before every link. The runner makes a link key of its own when
  it is paired, once, and the desktop keeps its public half; `purlis serve` takes the link from that one desktop
  through `purlis bridge`, which the connector runs with `docker exec`. Adding a pool from the
  window comes next (#2044).
- **A Docker pool's runners have limits and a read-only root.** Each runner container is
  held to its pool's CPU, memory, process and `/tmp` limits (by default two CPUs, 4 GiB,
  1024 processes and 1 GiB). Its root file system is read-only, so its home volume is the only
  place it can write that may hold a program: `/tmp` and Docker's `/dev/shm` are
  memory-backed and run no program. purlis checks both before every link (#2506).
- **An older runner's chats stay reachable until they end.** After a pool moves to a runner of
  the new version, its older runner can still be reached for the chats it keeps, but starts no
  new one. The Pools group says how many chats it still waits on (#2865).
- **A file and line a session record names open from its tab.** A path written as inline code in
  a record, such as `svc/src/lib.rs:42`, is a button that opens the file in the light editor at
  that line, in the repo the path names, or in the workspace's only repo. The record also lists
  the files it names, each with *Open in your editor* at that line. A path the repo's folder does
  not offer is refused, as in the file viewer (#984, #1043).
- **A forge tool names the host it reaches.** A persona's `gh` or `glab` tool takes `host`
  (`host = "github.example.com"`); without it, `github.com` or `gitlab.com`. The run is told
  that host, and a chat's run that names another (a repository as `HOST/OWNER/REPO`, a URL, a
  `git@host:` remote) never runs with the tool's value (#3869).
- **A Panel under both sidebars and the editor, with Repos in its left half.** The left activity
  bar runs the window's whole height, and its Lower icons, below a divider, switch the Panel's
  left half. Repos and branches is a view of its own there, out of Explorer, which keeps
  Workspaces and Files; picking a repo or branch in Repos still chooses where the next chat
  starts and what Files lists. A press of the open Lower icon puts the half away, and with both
  halves away the editor has the whole height. ⌘J (Ctrl+J elsewhere) hides and shows the Panel,
  and so do _Hide the panel_ and _Show the panel_ in the palette. Drag its handle to resize it
  (30% of the window by default, 120px to 70%), and double-click the handle to put it back. Its
  height and whether it is away are kept for each project; after the update it opens once
  (spec #1736, #1737).
- **A persona's tool that is a general-purpose program says so on its Allow.** curl, wget,
  httpie, base64, tee and the like fetch, send, copy, encode or write content as the chat's
  arguments say, so such a program can show the values it receives in the chat's output. It
  stays allowed as a tool; the Notice, Settings › Sandbox and the Granted list now add one
  sentence beside it, so you allow it only for a persona you trust with those values. The list is
  not exhaustive, and a tool without the sentence is not thereby a safe one: any program can show
  what it is handed if its arguments ask it to. Every Allow you made before stands (T-4).
- **A skill's Grade plan lists each Grader extension you installed** (Skill studio preview, #3236).
  The plan names the one you pick, and the grade runs through it, held to the plan's chats, token
  cap and dollar limit. A Grader that fails says why in the window. Grading after each edit runs
  purlis's own runner.
- **A grade compares with the skill's previous version** (SK-57, #3237). A skill with history is
  graded with the skill, without it, and as its previous version had it, read from git's copy of
  that commit. The plan names the version and counts its chats in the cost, and the Grades panel,
  the scorecard and `purlis skill grade` show the difference against it beside the one against no
  skill.
- **Pick the model a grade's chats run on** (SK-60, #3240). The grade's plan offers the models
  the profile's program can run (on Claude Code: opus, sonnet and haiku) beside the profile's own,
  and its dollar limit is priced from the one you pick. Each grade then says the model its chats
  reported, in the Grades panel and in `purlis skill grade`.
- **A Grader extension can grade a skill, its chats run by purlis** (Skill studio preview,
  #3236). A Grader asks for each chat of a grade, and purlis runs it as a grade's chat, held to the
  chats, token cap and dollar limit the plan showed, and tells the Grader what it did, until the
  Grader answers its scores. A Grader that asks for more than the plan, or answers something
  purlis can't read, ends the grade with a sentence saying why, and what ran is still scored.
  Extensions speak protocol 4 for this.
- **A dispatch grant can be limited to one workspace.** When a chat asks to dispatch to
  another persona for a task that works in a workspace, the question now says which, and an
  Allow for you or for the project holds for work in that workspace only. *In any workspace*
  is a choice under the answers for when you mean the wider grant. The workspace is the one
  the task works in, wherever the asking chat is: the one named with `--in workspace:<name>`,
  the one a worktree is cut in, the one a handoff moves into, else the asking chat's own. An
  Allow for one chat covers that chat's tasks in that workspace. Settings › Project › Dispatch
  shows where each grant holds and lets you narrow or widen your own, and a project grant's for
  everyone, each asked first. "Any persona" can be limited the same way. A never is not: it
  holds in every workspace, and so does Keep blocked for a chat. At the project's root there
  is no workspace to limit a grant to, so the question and its answers say an Allow for you
  or for the project holds in any workspace. A question asked again for another workspace
  says where you already allowed the pair. Grants you already have hold in any workspace, as
  before (#1505).
- **An off control's reason links to its harness's card.** Where a Curate row or a First task
  row is off because its harness lacks something, _What opencode can do here_ at the end of its
  reason opens the card's tab: a link in the First task's row, and a row of its own under the
  Curate rows. The first time you start a chat on a harness that lacks something, the picker and
  the First task say what it lacks by Start, once per harness on this machine (#1134).
- **A harness can be declared on this machine alone.** A `[harnesses.<name>]` table in
  `charter.local.toml` declares a harness in the same form as a project's
  `harnesses/<name>.toml`. Its chat runs in its terminal, and it is asked about once, as
  every program that file names is: the question shows the words its declaration adds, and is
  asked again when they change. Under the name of a harness purlis ships (`claude`,
  `codex`, `opencode`) the table replaces that harness's measured facts on this machine: its
  terminal and its card. It never changes how the harness is run or armed: the program, the
  levels, the words purlis starts and resumes a session with, the environment namespace, the
  adapter and the sandbox stay purlis's, and a table that says otherwise is refused with its
  reason. The tables are read only where git would not carry the file. A prompt is typed into a replaced harness on one line only (#968).
- **A chat on a declared harness has its card's button in its header**, as a chat on a harness
  purlis ships has (#1134).
- **A Codex or opencode permission prompt is also asked in purlis's window.** Codex's
  `PermissionRequest` is now armed on each Codex chat, as Claude Code's is, so its approval
  prompt is an ask you can answer with Allow or Deny for this call; Codex asks once to trust the
  new hook. purlis's opencode plugin hands opencode's permission prompt to the app the same way
  and replies on opencode's own client. From the window an opencode command or edit can only be
  rejected; allow it in the chat. Nothing is allowed unless you choose it, in any permission mode
  (#1691).
- **The app's log says where each chat's start at a launch spent its time.** Every chat put back
  at a launch logs one line with the time it waited at the restore gate, then the core's read,
  the sandbox's proxy, its composed line (the package caches with it) and the host's answer, and
  one more line when its harness first reports. A slow launch can now be read from
  `~/Library/Logs/dev.purlis.app/` (#4988).
- **Change a Docker pool's CPUs, memory, processes, `/tmp` and suspend time on its page.** Each change waits for the runner to be replaced, and the page says so. **Replace the runner…** makes a new runner held to the pool's limits: new chats start there, and chats running now carry on on the old runner until they end (#4286).
- **A limit offers its new value in more places.** A profile's row on a pool's page and a chat moving back here now have the form beside the refusal, and `purlis profile sign-in --pool` names the value (#4397).
- **A skill lint extension can answer the whole Skill studio list in one question.** An
  extension whose `contributes.skill-lint` says `"many-at-once": true` is asked
  `findings-of-each`: every skill of the list with its files, in one request, answered with one
  entry per skill in the order asked. Its confined program then starts once per list rather than
  once per skill, and gets the list's whole 200 ms instead of 100 ms per skill, so a lint that
  takes about 150 ms to start now shows its findings on the Library rows and in Needs you. One
  question holds at most 200 skills and 4 MiB of their files. An extension that does not say
  `many-at-once` is asked one skill at a time, as before, and the editor's live lint still asks
  `findings` (#4195).
- **A long proposed change opens in its own tab.** A change a chat proposed to purlis's own
  configuration that is too long for its Inbox row or Notice offers **Open**: a tab with the
  whole change in the comparison view, and Apply there (#1975).
- **Moving a memory from its tab can be undone.** After *Move*, the same Undo line as Delete's
  stands for a few seconds, and Undo moves the memory back to the store it came from, its tab
  following it (#1190).
- **A new host is asked about while the connection waits.** When a sandboxed chat reaches a host
  nothing lists, purlis's proxy holds the connection for about a minute while a Notice asks you.
  Allow lets the same command carry on, with nothing failing and nothing restarting. New hosts
  from one chat within about two seconds are one Notice, each listed whole. If nobody answers in
  time, the connection is refused and recorded, the Notice stays, and a later Allow applies at
  once and tells the chat to run the command again (#1666).
- **Allow for me on this machine is the main button**, for this project on this machine. Other
  scopes… offers Allow only for this chat and Allow for everyone in this project. Keep blocked refuses the waiting connection and tells the chat not
  to try again unless you ask.
- **Policy can turn live asks off, remove Allow scopes, and pin hosts that can never be
  allowed** (`live-asks`, `allow-scopes`, `never-hosts`). The Notice says when policy ruled a
  choice out, and who set it.
- **A page per harness profile in Settings.** Each `[harness.<name>]` profile in this machine's
  local settings file has its own page under Harness & profiles, with its kind, command and
  environment. Add profile asks for a name, a kind and a command. Remove and Rename are on the
  profile's page. A profile the default harness names is not removed or renamed, and the setting
  that uses it is named with a link. What the profile rules refuse is said under the field it is
  about, and a pasted secret is refused with a pointer to the vault. The last add, remove or
  rename can be undone. A new or changed command still asks for approval before its first run.
  New profile… in the default pickers opens the Add form and picks the new profile (ST-4, #1236).
- **A palette row for every Settings group.** Type a group's name to open Settings at that group,
  for example *Project settings: Saving*, *Workspace settings: Repos* or *Your settings: Editor*.
  Your groups are listed with no project open as well (#1201).
- **A pane showing another workspace's chat names that workspace with a badge.** A chat dragged
  into a tab of another workspace stays filed in its own, and its pane head shows that
  workspace's name in the workspace's colour, read to a screen reader as "filed in" it. A narrow
  pane drops the badge with the harness and workspace (#4982).
- **A persona chat that fails, or outlives the chat that asked for it, is handled and never
  lost.** If its program ends before it reported, purlis tells the chat that asked `failed:
  ended without a report`, with the path of its session record where one was written; if you
  close its tab first, that chat is told the operator stopped it. Stopping every
  agent, quitting and restarting a chat report nothing: those chats report when they run
  again. A persona chat stays open after it reports, marked *reported* under the chat that
  asked, and you can still open it and type in it. Closing a chat asks you once about every
  chat at work below it, in the same dialog: *Keep them running*, and a persona chat's report
  goes to that chat's workspace for the next chat to read, or *Stop them*, and they
  are stopped as Stop stops a chat, each after one short turn to write what it did, while the
  chat closes in the same step. The reported persona chats that are at rest close with it,
  each once its session record is written, and the dialog says which. The report of a task
  you started yourself stays with its chat when the tab you asked from has closed, and that
  chat is marked as needing you. A persona chat stopped on a permission prompt or a question
  reads `waiting on the operator` to the chat that asked (#1443).
- **A persona can name the profile its chats start on.** A `profile:` line in a persona's
  definition names one of the project's harness profiles. The new-chat picker moves to it when
  that persona is picked, unless you already picked a harness. The persona view shows it, and
  *Set <persona>'s profile…* on its heading sets it. A chat handed to that persona starts on its
  profile, so a Claude Code chat can hand work to a persona that runs on Codex, and the brief
  reaches it the way that harness takes a first message. Name a built-in or a declared harness
  in a shared project: on a machine that does not offer the name, the chat starts on the asking
  chat's profile and says so. `profile: none` opts a persona out of a profile it inherits. A
  persona with no `profile:` whose `model:` is exactly a profile's name is read the same way.
  Claude Code and Codex profiles are tested; opencode is not yet (#1445).
- **A persona declares its browser, and Always for this persona.** A persona's sandbox section
  may say `browser = "project"` or `"open-web"`: its chats' browser Ask marks that answer "uses
  this", in its place, and you still answer it. The Ask also offers **Always for this persona**,
  kept on this machine for every chat opened as that persona in the project, listed and
  removable in Settings › Sandbox; removing it ends the browsers it opened. An administrator's
  policy without the `you` scope forbids it (#2241).
- **A persona has an icon and a colour, shown wherever it appears.** A persona's definition may
  carry `icon:`, one of purlis's forty persona icons, and `color:`, a palette name or
  `#rrggbb` as a workspace's colour is. Its folder may hold a custom `icon.png` instead. With
  none of these it is its initials, on a colour picked by its name. The mark is on its chats'
  tabs, their rows in the explorer, the Personas panel, its own view, needs-you items, Notices
  that name it and the new-chat picker. The persona's view has the picker, and a pick is
  written to the definition at once. A custom image is treated as untrusted: a PNG of at most
  64 KB, drawn as pixels and never as markup. One that cannot be drawn shows the initials, and
  the persona's view says why. An `icon.svg` is not drawn: the view says to save it as a PNG
  (#1449).
- **A persona says which personas it works with, and one answer allows several.** A persona's
  definition may carry `wants: [devops, qa]`. It grants nothing. When a chat of that persona
  asks to dispatch to another, the question shows, under its answers, "Also let steward
  dispatch to:" with a box for each wanted persona not yet allowed, unticked. Tick the ones
  you want and press an Allow: the asked pair and every ticked one are kept at that level.
  Keep blocked and Never for this pair are about the asked pair only. The question also says
  what the persona you are allowing works with: the names of its vaults, the hosts the
  project declares for it, and the personas it may itself dispatch to, the first few of each
  and how many more. Where the project's sandbox is off it says that no list of vaults or
  hosts holds the persona's chats. Allowing a dispatch does not allow the use of a secret;
  that is asked as before. `purlis persona lint` says which names
  in a `wants` line are not offered (#1502).
- **A persona's tool can be handed several values from its vault.** A tool that needs a key and a
  secret, or a user name and a password, is declared with each under `values`:
  `[sandbox.personas.<persona>] tools = { aws = { vault = "cloud", values = { AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID =
  { key = "aws-access-key-id", as = "env" }, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = { key =
  "aws-secret-access-key", as = "env" } } } }`. A sandboxed chat runs `aws` as it would any tool,
  and purlis hands it every value in the variable or file declared; the program reads them from
  there. The Allow on each machine covers every value, the Notice and Settings › Sandbox name
  each one, and any change asks again. The one-value form is unchanged (T-1). For curl, which
  reads no credential from a variable, the secrets guide shows curl 8.3's own `--variable` and
  `--expand-user`.
- **A persona's MCP server that fails at chat start is tried once more.** When the second try
  fails too, the chat's tab says so with the server's own error and Retry, which restarts the
  chat on its conversation, and the chat is told why its tools are missing (qw381).
- **A persona's tools run through `purlis secret exec` by their plain name.** The project's
  `[sandbox.personas.<persona>] tools = { kubectl = { vault, as, key } }` makes a plain
  `kubectl` in a sandboxed chat running as that persona run through the brokered
  `purlis secret exec`, with the credential handed as a private file or a variable, so the
  chat never reads the vault. The real program is found where no chat writes, and a shell, an
  interpreter, `env`, `sudo`, `xargs` or purlis itself is refused as a tool. A persona's tools
  work on a machine only once the person there allows them, with the persona's hosts, on the
  same Notice. An administrator's policy can forbid persona tools with
  `"persona-tools": false` (#1407, #1362).
- **`--base origin/main` for `purlis worktree add` and `update`.** A piece can be cut from, or
  moved onto, a remote-tracking branch, so a sandboxed chat, which cannot make or move a branch,
  can always reach the remote. `update --base <branch>` moves a piece onto another base and
  carries only the piece's own commits, as `git rebase --onto` does, and records the new base
  (#3836).
- **The window says when a cluster pool starts minting without asking you.** When a pool's admin
  turns on minting in the cluster, you see one Notice saying its chats now get GitHub App tokens
  from the cluster without asking you first, and that the admin controls that. It blocks nothing. It shows once for each
  change, and again if the setting goes off and back on.
- **A pool sets how its runner's browsers are watched over the link.** Add a Docker pool has
  two more boxes: browser frames a second (1 to 60) and browser width in pixels (320 to 3840).
  Leave them empty to keep 15 and 1280. A change holds for the next browser opened there, and
  the runner doesn't have to be made again. A pool that sets either can't be read by an earlier
  purlis (#3297).
- **A pool's limits at the command line** (#4284). `purlis pool limits <pool>` lists them
  (`--json` for a script), and `purlis pool limit <pool> <key> <value>` or `--reset` changes one,
  with the same names and checks as the window. In a chat it changes nothing: you're asked in the
  window, with the old and new value, and only you apply it.
- **A pool's limits have a page.** Under each pool in Settings › You › This machine › Pools, Limits
  lists them by what they affect, each with its unit, its default, a mark on a value you set, and
  Reset. Values are checked as you type (#4285).
- **A moved chat over a pool's limit offers to raise it**, as Start a chat does: saving the value asks
  for the move again (#4313).
- **A pool's own time before its runner suspends itself.** Add a pool… has a
  **Suspends after** box: how long the pool's runner is left without a link from this machine
  before it stops itself, keeping its home, such as `12h` or `90m`, from a minute to 30 days.
  Empty is a day, as before. Each pool's row in Settings › This machine › Pools says its time,
  and `runners.json` keeps it as the pool's `suspendAfter` (#3471).
- **A Docker pool's runner follows purlis's version after an update.** Each release builds
  purlis's runner image with its own version and names it in its update manifest, signed with
  the updater's key. After an update, a pool of purlis's own image gets a runner of the new
  version beside its old one: new chats start on it, and the old runner keeps its chats until
  they end, then is removed. A pool of your own image is never moved, and its row in the Pools
  group says its runner is behind (#2749).
- **⌘⇧H (Ctrl+Shift+H) goes back to the pane's previous chat**, and again to come back. Where
  that chat is on screen in another pane, it goes there instead (#4757).
- **A theme can restyle the welcome's doors and the Get page's repo picks** (#3885). A card
  pressed whole is a theme-parts family of its own, `card-button`: its box's fill, words, edge,
  corners and room, its mark, title and line, as a door or a pick, at rest, under the pointer,
  pressed, with the keyboard's focus and unavailable. A theme's `card.*` keys never reach it,
  even inside a card.
- **Browser logins stay signed in across chats of a profile.** A chat's browser that logged in
  with `browser_login` keeps its logins once it ends, sealed on this device under its profile, and
  the next chat of that profile whose login is allowed starts signed in. A second chat at the same
  time gets a copy. Removing the profile removes them (#2021).
- **A profile pins its harness version.** A profile's first chat pins the version of its harness
  installed, and its chats then run, and its conversations resume, on that version. A profile
  you made follows its harness's minor and patch updates, and the chat's tab says so; on another
  major version a chat does not start, and Update the pin in Settings › You › Profiles moves
  the profile to it. A profile adopted from the harness's own folder follows the harness, and
  the chat's tab says when its version moved (#2038).
- **A profile says why its icon is its monogram.** Where purlis cannot draw the icon a profile
  names, because the file is missing, too large or not a plain file, or its contents are refused,
  Settings › Harness & profiles says so under the profile and `purlis doctor` lists it, in a fixed
  sentence that repeats nothing from the file (#3137).
- **A Claude Code profile signs in on a Docker pool's runner from its line in Settings › Pools,
  with no terminal.** Sign in opens the line in place: purlis runs Claude Code's own login on the
  runner, opens its page in your browser, takes the code the page shows in one field, and says
  Signed in once the runner's own status check agrees. Each step says where it is ("Step 2 of
  3"). Nothing of this Mac's sign-in goes to the runner. Other harnesses still sign in in a shell
  tab for now (#4042).
- **A chat's skill budget shows its program's own skills beside it** (Skill studio preview,
  #3324). The Skills view's line under a chat's set now adds what its program lists of its own
  skills, from your folders and its plugins, such as `Codex's own, not counted: 2 skills, 1,310
  characters`. purlis's budget never counts them: the program lists them against its own limit.
  The studio's Routing page says what the budget counts, and `purlis skill list` shows each
  program's own figure.
- **A project a runner would not hold again is marked in the Pools group.** After its link to a
  runner comes back, a project the runner refuses to hold gets a Notice in the runner's words.
  The Notice goes once the project is held again (#2846).
- **The doctor's dialog lists what each project switch in this window took**: how long to the
  window having drawn it and to that being painted, and how long the core took to answer each
  command it answers on the window's own thread. Kept in memory for the window, and yours to
  copy.
- **purlis tells you when a task goes quiet.** While a task works, purlis watches what its
  harness reports: a turn, a tool starting or coming back. After 15 minutes with nothing, or one
  command running for 30, it says so on the task's tab and to the chat that asked, naming the
  command's program where it can ("running one command for 30 minutes: `cargo`"). The note
  ends nothing, and comes down when the task is heard from again. Both times are settings in
  Settings › Dispatch: _Quiet note after_ and _One command note after_ (`quiet-note-minutes`,
  `one-command-note-minutes`), per project, workspace or persona (#1981).
- **A project this purlis opens read-only says why in its tab.** When a project requires a
  feature this purlis lacks, or declares a format it cannot read, the window names the missing
  feature and the purlis version that has it, once, in the project's tab. Every action that
  would write a committed project file (a workspace, a persona and its icon, a vault, a todo, a
  memory's edit, move or restore, the project's and a workspace's settings, an extension's
  action, an Allow for everyone, the project's save) is turned off with that sentence as its
  reason. purlis already wrote nothing to such a project;
  now the window says so (#826).
- **Fix in a chat, on a save's red pull request.** The red Notice in the Saving view starts a
  chat at once, at the project's root (for a workspace repo, in its workspace), on a message
  purlis writes: the pull request and its page, each failed check with its page, and what
  each one found. For the project, the chat fixes it and saves, and the save goes onto the
  same pull request. For a workspace repo, the chat fixes it and may commit in the clone; it
  does not push, and the fix reaches the pull request with the repo's next save, yours or
  the automatic one. Pressing it again brings that chat forward. If the checks pass or run
  again by then, nothing starts and the window says so. What a check says is quoted to the
  chat as data, and a link is given only into the pull request's own repository.
- **Merge as it stands…**, on a red pull request and on one that waits with no end in sight
  (no check has started where the repository's other pull requests have them, purlis cannot
  read its checks, or a required check has not reported). It looks at the pull request
  afresh and then asks, naming it, the branch it goes into and the checks that failed, and
  merges without waiting for checks. If the pull request changes between the question and
  your answer, nothing is merged and the window shows what is there. A conflict, a required review and every other rule of the forge still stop it, and
  the refusal is shown with a link to the pull request.
- **A red pull request of a save is in the Inbox**, with the same two answers, until it
  merges or its checks pass.
- **A refusal links to the persona that uses the entry.** When a persona's definition is what
  stops a rename or a removal in Settings, the refusal has *Show <persona>*, which opens that
  persona's tab (#1241).
- **A refused theme font can be reviewed and allowed in place** (#2647). When a project's theme
  font is added or changes while the project is open, the theme's Notice offers Review and
  allow. It shows the project's approval question, with what changed first. Allow it, and the
  theme draws with the new font without reopening the project. Cancel, and it stays refused.
  It is offered only when the project asks again about font files alone; anything more is
  reviewed by opening the project again.
- **A vault refused for a chat's persona offers a way forward.** When a sandboxed chat asks for
  a vault that is not tagged for the persona it was opened as, its tab shows a notice naming the
  vault and the persona, with *Allow {persona} to use this vault* and *Keep blocked*. Allow is
  kept on this machine, recorded, listed in Settings › Sandbox › Granted and revocable there;
  the chat does not restart. purlis tells the chat to run the command again when it is waiting,
  or when its turn ends, and otherwise says to ask it. An administrator's policy can forbid the
  Allow with `"vault-grants": false` (#1430).
- **`purlis vault list` works from a sandboxed chat.** The app answers it with each vault's
  name, provider and persona, and whether this chat may use it. No value and no provider
  session is involved (#1430).
- **A right-click in a terminal has Copy, Paste and Select all.** A chat's or a shell's terminal now
  opens a menu of its own: *Copy*, which is off until something is selected and puts on the
  clipboard exactly what the keyboard's copy does, *Paste*, and *Select all*, with a Mac's keys
  said beside them. The rows a right-click on a pane had before (a new tab, the splits, ending
  the chat) follow under a line. *Paste* types the clipboard's text as the keyboard's paste
  does, bracketed when the program asked for that, so several lines cannot run one by one. It
  pastes text only, up to 1 MiB; when it pastes nothing the pane says why. On a Mac a right-click on a word
  selects it first. A full-screen program that turned mouse reporting on
  still gets a plain right-click; **Shift+right-click always opens the menu**. The menu key
  opens it under the cursor, and so does Shift+F10 while no program has the mouse; a second
  Shift+F10 closes the menu and sends the key to the program.
- **A router's grade has a scorecard, and keeps its chats.** On the Skill studio's Routing page,
  Scorecard beside the router's grade opens it: how it ended, each arm's pass rate and what it
  spent, then each skill's trigger tests with the router and with the built-in router. Each chat
  it ran opens read-only, as a skill's grade's do. A router's three newest grades in each
  workspace or persona keep their chats on this machine (#3617).
- **A router's grade plan offers the profile, the model and the cap, and says what it should
  spend.** Grade the router… now lets you pick the profile and the model its chats run on and set
  the cap, as a skill's plan does. It also says what its last grade spent per chat, or that this
  is not known. Where that grade ran on another library, the plan says this one may spend
  otherwise. Pressing Grade consents to the profile, model, cap and dollar limit the plan shows
  (#3618).
- **A skill router can be graded on your library's trigger tests** (Skill studio preview, #3233).
  Where a workspace or a persona chooses a router extension, the Skill studio's router line now
  offers Grade the router…. It shows what the grade runs and costs before anything runs, then
  runs each trigger test of the library's skills with the router in place and with the built-in
  router. The line then says how many tests pass with each, and the library's commit the grade was
  run on. The grade is recorded in the project beside the skills' grades.
- **A router that reads prompts is graded with its pointer** (Skill studio preview, #3619). Where
  you turned reading on for it, each trigger test's prompt is handed to it in its arm, as in a real
  chat. The plan says whether the grade runs so, and the router's line says it did.
- **A skill router that reads prompts suggests skills on each prompt** (Skill studio preview,
  #3231). A router reads prompts only after you turn that on for it, on the Skill
  studio's Routing page, whose line says it reads every prompt; it is off by default. Then each
  prompt of a chat it routes is offered to it with the skills the chat's list leaves out, and the ones it picks reach
  that prompt as a short note naming each with purlis's own description and saying `skill_load`
  loads it. The router stays confined and has 100 ms; past that the prompt goes on without the note and
  the routing record says it fell back. purlis writes no prompt down, and no other chat's prompt
  is handed to a router.
- **Each run in the event log says what it is.** A `run.started` now carries the run's persona,
  harness, profile, sandbox backend and conversation, with the device it runs on, and says
  `unknown` for whatever purlis does not know rather than leaving it out (ADR 0066, #868).
- **A resumed chat knows the chat it resumed.** A session record now also writes `handed-from`
  and `resumed-from`, and **Resume** starts the new chat as having resumed the chat the record
  is of, by its `chat-id` (ADR 0066, #871).
- **A Claude Code chat on a runner has its profile's MCP servers** (#3846). User-scope servers now go
  with a profile's settings, under the same rules: no environment, headers or sign-in, and a server
  whose command shows a credential stays behind. A value a server needs goes in a vault. Plugins are
  not sent yet (#4441).
- **A chat on a runner says which settings were left out of its copy** (#3848, #3867). Its tab says
  what stayed behind and why, once. A variable that only chooses an endpoint or a provider is named,
  with how to give it to the runner, since that chat could otherwise use another without saying so.
- **A runner chat's change to the project waits for you** (#2046). When a chat on a pool's
  runner remembers something, adds a todo or edits its workspace or persona, nothing is
  written. Its tab and the Inbox show the change in words, with **Apply** and **Dismiss**, and
  the chat is told which you chose. A change too long to show whole there opens in a tab of its
  own, where you apply it. A change that carries what looks like a credential is never held.
- **Every other end of a sign-in on a pool's runner** (#4043). Where purlis can't follow a
  login, the strip shows the runner's live terminal in place, and purlis checks the result when
  it ends. A sign-in that fails says the vendor's reason and offers Open the page again. Each
  profile's line says where it stands: not signed in, signing in…, signed in, sign-in failed or
  needs you in the terminal. Sign out on a signed-in line asks first, then runs the harness's own
  sign-out on the runner.
- **The Inbox says when a cluster pool's kept runner will be deleted.** Its operator's notice shows
  as a doctor finding and an Update, with the time. Starting a chat on the pool keeps the runner
  (#3981).
- **The session host takes a runner's chats' sandboxes back when its link to the runner comes
  back.** Once purlis relays your window to a runner, its chats' sandbox asks will reach you
  again after the link drops and comes back, and you will be able to change what a chat reaches
  or forget an Allow you gave it, as before the link dropped (#2511).
- **A runner's chats and browsers say "Reconnecting…" while its link is down.** When the link
  from this machine's session host to a runner drops, each of that runner's chats keeps its last
  screen, and each browser view its last frame, dimmed under "Reconnecting…", and draws again
  from where it is once the link is back (#2496, #2542).
- **What happened on a runner, while you were away.** Each run of a chat that finished, failed or
  was stopped on a pool's runner while you were away is in that runner's section, at its time in
  your time zone, as the runner recorded it, read over the link and never copied onto this
  machine. A runner whose link is down is said to be, not shown as one where nothing happened
  (#3393).
- **A sandbox block is never a dead end.** When the sandbox blocks a chat from reaching a host
  or writing a folder, the Notice on its tab now shows what it would allow, whole, and offers
  **Allow for this chat**, **Always allow…** (**Allow for me on this machine**, or for a host
  **Allow for everyone in this project**, as one of the project's own hosts) and **Keep
  blocked**. The chat restarts on the same conversation once its turn ends, and is told what
  was allowed so it retries by itself; where its harness does not say when a turn ends, the
  pane offers **Restart now** instead. A folder is offered only in the project or in one you
  list in Settings › Sandbox, judged as where it really is, so a link cannot widen it. Vault
  storage, purlis's own state, what only you approve and files later programs load are never
  allowed: the Notice says the way that works instead. For anything else purlis grants
  nothing, and the Notice offers **Start without the sandbox for this chat**, your own choice:
  it restarts the chat now, on the same conversation, and nothing it runs is confined until it
  next starts. Every grant is recorded in purlis's event log (#1342).
- **A sandboxed chat can commit in a branch folder.** A git worktree keeps its index and
  objects in its clone's `.git`, which a sandboxed chat may not write, so `git add` and `git
  commit` were refused there. `purlis worktree commit -m "<message>" --all` (or paths in place
  of `--all`; a new file must be named) now asks the app to stage and commit, on the branch
  the folder is on, with your git identity and the chat's trailers. A chat started in a branch
  folder is told the command when it starts. It only commits: it never amends, resets,
  rebases, merges or pushes, and it asks for no approval, as a commit in a clone asks for
  none. **The repository's own hooks are not run** for such a commit (a `pre-commit` that
  lints or formats, husky's, a `commit-msg` check), and the command says so each time one is
  there; purlis's scan for secrets and personal data does run. Git run this way reads none of
  your global or system git config but your name and email. The app refuses, in a sentence, a
  repository whose own config names a program, one that signs its commits, one that borrows
  objects from another, a folder inside that is a repository of its own, a change to
  `.gitmodules`, a path reached through a link and a name that differs from another only by
  case. **A file your attributes mark for a content filter (Git LFS, most often) is refused
  too**: your filters are in the config this commit does not read, so the file would be
  stored unfiltered; commit such a file from your own terminal. One commit runs in a branch
  folder at a time, and one the app was stopped in the middle of is unstaged by the next. The command works for a chat started in the branch folder itself; a chat that is not
  sandboxed, and any chat in a clone, uses `git commit` as before (#1055).
- **A sandboxed chat on a runner is confined there as on this machine.** `purlis serve` starts
  a chat's egress proxy with the same code the app's own session host runs, a runner composes
  every harness chat it runs with the sandbox it compiles for itself, and a chat's proxy, its
  asks and a withdrawn port reach the window through the link between hosts (#2217).
- **A sandboxed chat is told how to get unblocked under purlis.** At its start, every chat
  purlis runs in the sandbox is told what happens when the sandbox blocks a command: you see a
  Notice on its tab and choose, or you start the chat again with **Start without the
  sandbox**. It is also told that Claude Code's `/sandbox`, `/sandbox exclude` and
  `excludedCommands` do not apply under purlis, so it stops recommending them, and that a
  credential goes through `purlis secret exec` (#1342).
- **A search hit goes into a chat from the keyboard.** In the Search tab's results, Shift+Enter
  on the hit you stepped to opens the chat picker, as _Add to a chat's context_ does in the
  preview. The chat you pick gets a reference to that file and line typed in, unsent, and what
  happened is said in the tab's status line. A hit from another project, or a project with no
  chat open, is said there too, and Escape closes the picker (#1151).
- **A send to a runner leaves out what a save would refuse, and says so** (#2046). What a
  pool's runner gets of a workspace's clones never includes what a save to the forge refuses to
  push: credential files, a file holding a token or a private key, a hard link. Changes names
  what the last send left out under each clone. A workspace's settings gain **Sent to runners**,
  where you can name more files and folders to keep on this machine.
- **A service on this Mac can be allowed by its port.** When a sandboxed chat's command reaches a
  service listening on this machine (`kubectl` against a local cluster at `127.0.0.1:50795`, a
  database in a container, a dev server), the refusal is now a Block whose Notice offers **Allow
  only for this chat** or **Allow for me on this machine**: that one port, never a range or every
  port, and never one of purlis's own. In a Codex or opencode chat the Notice names the port when
  purlis's proxy refused it (a client that uses the proxy, such as curl); for a client that
  connects directly, such as kubectl, its port field is pre-filled from the command's output and
  says to check it. The chat restarts on its conversation to take it, and the grant is listed
  in Settings' Network page with Remove. Codex and opencode chats take it now; a Claude Code
  chat's Notice says its sandbox cannot be given one port alone yet and offers Start without the
  sandbox (qw384).
- **A session's tab wears a chip of its tasks.** After the session's name the tab says how
  many of its tasks are working, how many are waiting (idle, or needing you), how many failed
  and how many are finished, each count with its state's shape, and nothing for a zero. A ring
  means something is at work; no ring means nothing is. The counts move as the tasks do, and a
  task that has ended is still counted until its finished row is cleared. A session with no
  tasks has no chip and its tab is exactly as it was. On a crowded strip the name gives way
  first, then the counts from the end; a tab is never wider for having a chip (#1487).
- **The chip opens the menu of the chats in that tab.** The session's own chat first, then its
  tasks under who asked for them, each with its persona's mark, its name, its state in a word
  that is never cut, how long it has been in that state where this window saw it begin, and
  `in <workspace>` for one that works elsewhere. The chat the tab shows now is marked. Done and
  cancelled tasks fold into **Finished (n)**; a failure, and a task you closed, keeps a row of
  its own. Picking a chat switches the tab to it; picking a task that has ended opens its
  report under its line. The menu opens on a press, and when you move the pointer onto the chip
  and hold it still for about a third of a second. A pointer passing over the strip opens
  nothing, and neither does a chip that appears under a pointer you are not moving, or a tab
  being dragged. A menu the resting pointer opened takes no keyboard, so typing goes on where
  it was, and it closes a moment after the pointer has left both the chip and the menu. A menu
  you pressed or opened with a key stays until Escape, a pick or a press outside (#1487).
- **Keys for the chats inside a tab.** On a Mac: ⌘⇧J opens the tab's task menu with the
  keyboard on the chat it shows, ⌘⌥↓ and ⌘⌥↑ go to the next and the previous chat in the tab,
  ⌘⇧H goes back to the session's own chat. Elsewhere: Ctrl+Shift+J, Ctrl+Shift+] and
  Ctrl+Shift+[, Ctrl+Shift+H. Down on a focused tab that has tasks opens its menu too, and the
  tab says it has one. All four are rows in the palette, which says each key. None is a key a
  terminal turns into anything, so a chat loses nothing (#1487).
- **A short task dispatched onto a cluster pool gets a runner of its own**, on a pool marked as
  yours whose cluster operator is of this release. It starts from a warm runner where the pool
  keeps one. As the task closes, its branches come back to your clones under
  `refs/remotes/<pool>/fresh-…`, and the runner goes only once purlis has checked that your
  project holds every commit and change it holds. Where something is missing, the runner stays
  and the window says what, with Fetch again and Discard. Chats you work in, long tasks, chats on
  a subscription profile and tasks of a project whose folder is not a git repository stay on the
  pool's runner that keeps their work.
- **A skill's Grade plan lists its outcome evals, each off until you tick it** (Skill studio preview,
  #3235). The plan shows the chats each one adds. A ticked eval runs with the skill and without it,
  and a judge chat grades what each chat left, held to the plan's token cap and dollar limit. Outcome
  chats have no shell yet.
- **A grade's scorecard and the Grades tab show its outcome evals** (Skill studio preview, #3235):
  each arm's rate, each run's chat and judge, what the judges found, and why a run failed.
- **A chat's browser marks what a scrolling box or frame does not show.** A snapshot or a find
  marks an element `(out of view)` when a box it is in that scrolls (a list, a chat log, a side
  panel) or the frame it is in lays it out beyond what it shows, even while that box or frame is
  in view, so the agent scrolls over the box to reach it (#2564).
- **A workspace's repo left off its default branch, or on a moved remote, is a Notice with a
  Fix.** The Inbox shows one Notice per repo: a repo itself on another branch than its default
  gets *Switch to `<default>`*, which switches it only when its tree holds no change, every
  commit of the branch is on the remote or another branch and no chat in it is mid-turn, and
  otherwise says what blocks it; a repo the forge said moved, on a fetch purlis ran, gets *Use
  the new address*, which points `origin` at the address the Notice shows (#1985).
- **A tab that shows a chat being stopped says so.** It wears a small square that breathes and an
  amber underline while the chat writes what it did, as its row in the Chats list says
  "Stopping…" (#1459).
- **Finished (n) and Clear finished.** Under each chat in the Chats list, the tasks that came
  out done or were cancelled fold into one "Finished (n)" line with Clear finished. A task
  that failed, was blocked, ended without a report or was stopped or closed by you stays a row
  of its own until it is cleared, whatever its own last report says. Clearing takes rows away
  and nothing else: the dispatch records stay. The rows are there again after the app is quit
  and reopened, and go when the chat that asked closes (#1485).
