- **Reopen a finished task.** Reopen on a finished row resumes the task's conversation as an
  ordinary chat with a tab. It is no longer a task: a `purlis dispatch report` from it is
  refused in plain words, and the chat that asked is told nothing. If its harness cannot bring
  the conversation back, the row stays and says so (#1485).
- **Move to its own tab.** A task lives inside its session's tab. It gets a tab of its own only
  when you ask: from its row's menu in the Chats list, from the buttons at the end of its line
  in its tab's task menu (or `⌘`/`Ctrl`+Enter on that line), from its pane's top line while its
  session's tab shows it, or from the palette. The tab is on the strip of the workspace the
  task works in, and is drawn so it is not mistaken for a session's: the task mark, its name,
  and whose task it is, dimmer (`talk · steward 4`). Its pane says the whole path, as a pane
  switched to a task does (#1489).
- **A task's tab has a minimise button, not a close.** `−` sends the task back into its
  session's tab and ends nothing: the task goes on working, and its session's tab still lists
  it. Nothing on a task's tab ends the task. The key that closes a tab (Delete, or Backspace on
  a Mac) minimises a task's tab. A task whose asking chat has no tab in this window goes back
  to the Chats list (#1489).
- **Open beside.** A task opens beside the session that asked for it, inside that session's
  tab: the session's chat on one side, the task on the other, each pane saying which chat it
  is. Space on a task's row in the Chats list does it, and so do its row's menu, its line in
  the task menu (`Alt`+Enter, or the button at the line's end) and the palette. The task's
  pane has a minimise where the session's pane has its close; it sends the task back to the
  list and the session's pane takes the room (#1489).
- **A setting, "Open tasks in their own tabs"**, under Settings, You, Chats list. It is off:
  pressing a task switches its session's tab to it. On, pressing a task opens it as a tab of
  its own, with the minimise button. Either way the session's tab keeps its chip and its menu.
  It is `chats.tabbed` in `layout.json` (#1489).
- **A task's record says how it ended, what it says it changed and how much the two chats
  talked.** The Dispatches tab now shows a task's own outcome (done, blocked, failed,
  cancelled, or stopped by you), what its report says it changed under the report, and how
  many follow-ups, notes, questions and answers passed between it and the chat that asked. A
  dispatch that has not ended and whose chat is not open says *not open*, with no running
  clock (#1452).
- **`purlis persona stats` counts dispatches again.** `DISP` adds this machine's dispatch
  records to the committed dispatch log's count, so a persona you dispatch to is no longer
  marked *never dispatched*. The records are this machine's and are kept 30 days, and the
  notes under the table say so. Run in a sandboxed chat, which cannot read the records, the
  command says so and counts the log alone (#1452).
- **A team sets a cluster pool's limits** (#4287). A Pool's `spec.limits` sets each limit's highest allowed
  and a default. A default below purlis's holds with no prompt; a higher one is offered, and one press sets
  it. Each person chooses within the highest, a suggestion stops at it, and at the highest the error says
  the team set it and who to ask.
- **A teammate's dispatch grant is shown when it arrives.** When the project's settings come to
  let one persona's chats dispatch to another, after a pull, a branch switch or an edit, purlis
  says so once in the window: "The project now lets steward dispatch to devops." Everything
  that arrived together is one Notice, with **Accept** for the pairs it lists, **Not on my
  machine** for all it lists, and **Decide each in Settings**. Until you answer, nothing
  listed is in force for you, and a chat that needs one of the pairs meanwhile asks on its own
  tab in the same words; answering either clears both. Not on my machine is remembered and
  shown in Settings › Project › Dispatch, and is not asked again. A project's "any persona"
  is told in its own sentence and is accepted in Settings only. When a commit takes a grant
  you had accepted out of the project's settings, purlis says so once and asks nothing
  (#1506).
- **Run outcome evals from a terminal.** `purlis skill grade <name> --run --eval <id>` runs the evals
  you name, and the plan it prints marks each one on or off before you answer. It takes your yes
  only when typed at a terminal, so `--yes` and a piped answer are refused beside `--eval`. An id
  the plan cannot run stops it, with the reason. With no `--eval`, no eval runs (Skill studio
  preview, #4312).
- **A terminal editor opens in a shell tab, at the line.** With `$VISUAL` or `$EDITOR` chosen as
  your editor, *Open in your editor* used to start vi, vim, nvim, nano, `emacs -nw` and the like
  with no terminal, so they exited at once. purlis now opens an editor it knows to need a
  terminal in a shell tab of its own, in front, standing in the file's folder, with `+line` and
  the file. The editor and its words are handed to the tab as they are, never typed into a
  shell, so nothing in the variable or in the file's name is read as a command. An editor that
  opens its own window, such as gvim or `emacsclient -c`, is started as before (#1042).
- **A theme folder may bring its own icons for the rails** (#2337). `theme.json`'s `icons`
  names a file in the folder that draws each view's tab as path data, stroked the way the
  rails draw their icons today. A theme that extends another keeps every icon it does not
  redraw. Purlis Classic keeps today's icons. The Purlis theme's set is Lucide's icons, chosen
  to match the new look's.
- **A theme is a folder, and may have several appearances** (#2322). A theme's `theme.json`
  names a published schema, so an editor completes every token name; it may `extend` another
  theme and hold only what differs, name its colours once in a `palette`, and carry one or more
  appearances, each dark or light and optionally high contrast. A project's theme set to follow
  the system now follows it with your own theme, when that theme has a dark and a light
  appearance. Today's single-file themes keep loading, and today's look ships as
  **Purlis Classic**, unchanged.
- **A theme says how a workspace's colour tints it** (#2329, #2393). `theme.json`'s `tint` can
  turn the tint off, name which tokens a workspace's colour turns, and give any of the eight
  workspace colours a hue of its own. A theme that extends another keeps whatever it does not
  say. The window draws the recipe the theme engine hands it, and the theme check measures
  every tint the theme draws. Purlis Classic's recipe is today's.
- **A theme sets its geometry and fonts** (#2326). A theme folder may give spacing, type sizes,
  weights, line heights, corners, control and strip heights, the focus ring and the two lifts a
  number inside the range purlis documents for each, and bring its window, code and terminal
  fonts as woff2 files in its own `fonts/` folder, which purlis reads and hands the window
  itself. A value outside its range refuses the theme, and the Notice names the range.
- **Density and fonts are yours, in every theme** (#2326). Settings › You › Density and fonts
  draws the window comfortable or compact, and takes a family of your own for the window, for
  code and for the terminal, which beats the theme's. A theme may tune what compact means for
  it; Purlis Classic's compact is tighter spacing and shorter controls and strips.
- **Move a view between its sidebar and its half of the Panel.** Right-click a view's icon, or
  press Shift+F10 on it, and choose "Move to panel" or "Move to sidebar": the view goes to the
  other place on its own side and opens there. Moves never cross to the other side, and the
  Inbox stays pinned to the right sidebar. An extension's panel moves like any view on the
  right. Where each view lives is kept for each project, and _Use the default layout_ puts
  every view back (spec #1736, #1740).
- **A pane's Notice that another chat waits on you can be put away.** "… is waiting on you for a
  permission" and "… is stopped on a prompt" now have **Dismiss** beside Show it. It hides the line
  for that wait only and answers nothing: the tab's hand and the needs-you list still show that
  the chat waits, a new prompt from the chat shows a new line, and the next wait shows it again
  (qw386).
- **A working chat says in one line what it is doing.** Under its name in the Chats list, on
  the second line of its row, with how long it has been at work after it: *running cargo ·
  2m*. While a tool runs the line is in the present (*running cargo*, *editing Notice.tsx*,
  *reading 3 files*, *searching*, *fetching a page*, *waiting on a helper*, *dispatching a
  task*, *asking a question*, *writing its report*, *using a tool*), and once the tool has
  come back it is in the past (*ran cargo*, *edited Notice.tsx*, *read 3 files*) until the
  next tool purlis hears. *thinking* is said only from a turn's start until its first tool.
  purlis says nothing it has not heard: a tool it gets no word of leaves the line as it was.
  The words are purlis's own. The most a line ever names is a file's base name, or a program
  from a short list purlis keeps (cargo, npm, git and the like); a command that starts with
  anything else reads *running a command*, and a file whose name is not plain ASCII letters,
  digits and a few marks reads *editing a file*. Never a command's arguments, what it
  printed, a web address or a file's contents. The line stands in for where the chat works
  while it works and gives the line back when the turn ends; a row never changes height for
  it. It is kept in memory only, and a chat whose harness purlis has heard nothing from has
  no line. A screen reader is told it as the row's description, on demand, and never as it
  changes (#1493).
- **A workspace or a persona chooses the router its chats' skills are listed by** (Skill studio
  preview, #3230). `settings.skills.router` in a workspace's `workspace.json`, or
  `skill-router:` in a persona's definition, names an approved extension that declares
  `skill-router`; the persona's choice wins, and the built-in router stays the default. The
  router is asked at each chat's start which skills to leave out of its list, each with its own
  reason, and has 100 ms: past that, on an error, or on an answer that would hide a pinned skill,
  a chat lists what the built-in router shows. Use skill… and the Skill studio say how long the
  router took and why a chat fell back, and the chat's event log keeps a `skill.routed` record
  that each skill run names.
- **A workspace's chats run on a Docker pool** (#2046). Once this machine keeps a pool, a
  workspace's settings offer **Runs on**: this machine, or a pool. A chat started in a workspace
  set to a pool runs on the pool's runner and behaves as a local one: its tab, input, asks and
  stop work the same. The workspace's code goes to the runner as the chat starts, with your
  uncommitted work. The runner's branches come back when a chat there ends and when you return
  to the window. Changes lists them under each repo, with the commits not on this machine. Chat numbers
  never repeat between this machine and its pools. Shells still run on this machine.
- **The groundwork for opencode chats over ACP.** purlis's core now has an Agent Client
  Protocol client, tested against `opencode acp`. It starts the agent in the chat's worktree,
  hands the session purlis's MCP server, and follows each turn's plan, usage, tool calls and
  reply in the same model it uses for hooks. It gives the agent no file system and no terminal
  of purlis's, and it never answers a login prompt or supplies a credential. A permission the
  agent asks for waits, with no deadline, until you answer it; only you can answer it, and the
  first answer wins. Such a chat starts from the same profile approval and sandbox decision
  as a chat in a terminal, with the same environment and nothing else of the app's. In a
  project that turns the sandbox on, no chat runs over ACP, even one started without the
  sandbox: it starts in its terminal, where its sandbox is shown. Nothing in the window starts
  such a chat yet (HP-2, #669).
- **Add a pool from the window.** *Add a pool…*, in the palette and in Settings › This machine ›
  Pools, asks for the pool's name, its runner image by digest, and its CPUs, memory, processes
  and `/tmp`, each left empty for purlis's default. The image's default is the runner image this
  version of purlis was released with. On the dev channel, where purlis is often behind the
  newest build, it is that build's image, and the dialog says an update of purlis to it is
  waiting. A local build names none, and says so. purlis makes the pool's runner on your Docker,
  confined and held to those limits, and pairs it with this machine. Settings › This machine ›
  Pools is always there: before the first pool it says what a pool is, and then it lists each
  pool with Remove. A runner that answers with another key than the one it was paired with is
  said in a Notice with Remove (#2679).
- **Add a file or folder to a chat's context from its row.** A file or folder row's menu in the
  explorer and the Files tab has *Add to a chat's context*, which picks one of the project's open
  chats and types a reference to the row into it, never sent (#1151).
- **Add a profile from the window, or with `purlis profile create`.** Settings › You › Profiles
  makes a profile of Claude Code, Codex or opencode that every project on this machine can use:
  a folder of its own in purlis's data home, with this machine's harness settings files copied in
  as they are, and a chat on it runs its harness in that folder, where it signs in. Each profile
  says when its settings were imported and offers Import again (`purlis profile import`).
  Remove names the conversations that go and asks first (`purlis profile remove --yes`); a
  harness's own folder adopted as a profile is only forgotten, never deleted (#2034).
- **Add and remove forges in Settings.** Settings › Forges at the Project level has Add forge,
  which opens a small form (kind, owner, host, repos never listed) and writes a new `[[forge]]`
  block to `charter.toml`, and a Remove on each block. What purlis would refuse is said under
  the field it is about, and nothing is written. A forge is not removed while something needs
  it: a catalogued repo on its host, or a save mode that opens a request there. Those are named,
  with a link to the setting. The last add or remove can be undone (ST-3, #1227).
- The core and commands of Agent identity: purlis makes a GitHub App from GitHub's own page, keeps its key straight in a vault where nothing can read it back, and proves a real short-lived token before it adds a tool line. The tab that uses them follows.
- Agent identity, from the palette: give chats their own GitHub identity with GitHub's own page, with no file edited and no terminal. Its row says what it acts as and on how many repos, and removing it takes the tool lines, the key and live tokens at once.
- **`charter doctor --fix workspace-reinit`** runs `charter workspace reinit --all`, which brings
  every workspace up to the current layout and never removes your content. No doctor row offers
  it yet, so bare `charter doctor --fix` does not run it (NO-6, #1238).
- **See what a Claude Code edit writes before you allow it from the Inbox.** A Write, Edit or
  MultiEdit permission ask now shows its change in the same side-by-side view the file comparison
  uses: the whole new file for a Write, and for an edit the text it replaces beside what it puts
  there. Allow is offered for this one edit once the change is drawn, and Deny stays. An edit the
  Inbox cannot show whole (too long, not text, holding characters it cannot draw as they are or
  what looks like a credential, or an input it cannot read) says why and offers no Allow; you
  answer it in the chat (#1146).
- **On Linux, a program that connects straight to an internet address is named in a quiet
  Notice.** In a Codex or opencode chat, a connection that does not go through the sandbox's
  proxy is refused, as before, and the chat's tab now names the address and says to use a
  client that goes through the proxy. There is no Allow on it, and at most one a minute is
  shown (#2423).
- **An empty Inbox lists what was allowed on this machine in the last day,** read-only: the
  hosts, folders and dispatches granted, from a pane's Notice, from the Inbox, or before a
  relaunch, under what was answered in the Inbox itself (#1700).
- **An unused browser stops, and a device runs a budget of browsers.** A chat's browser that
  neither the chat nor you used for ten minutes stops; the chat's next browser call says so and
  opens a new one. A browser you drive, or one waiting for you, never stops this way. The device
  runs at most a budget of browsers from its memory (16 GB: 4, 32 GB: 8, 64 GB: 16), beside the
  three a project's chats hold. All three are set in Settings › This machine › Browsers, and a
  browser refused past a limit says which setting decides it (#2023).
- **Answer a Claude Code question from the Inbox.** When a Claude Code chat asks you one question
  with a single choice, the Inbox lists the question with its answers as buttons, and your pick
  goes back to the chat as its answer. Several questions, a question that takes several choices,
  or one the Inbox cannot show whole is still listed, and you answer it in the chat (#1703).
- **Answer a Claude Code chat's permission prompt from the needs-you list.** When a chat asks to
  run a tool, the prompt also shows in the title bar's ✋ list, with the options Claude Code
  offers: allow, deny, and a rule for the rest of the session. Your choice goes back through
  Claude Code's own `PermissionRequest` hook, so the chat carries on without you opening its
  pane. The pane shows its own prompt at the same time, and either place may answer; left
  unanswered for about a minute, the prompt is the pane's alone. purlis never allows or denies
  anything by itself. Allow is offered only when the list shows the whole command, word for
  word and as it runs. A long command, one over several lines, one holding a credential or an
  invisible character, one asking to run outside the sandbox or in the background, or a file
  edit offers Deny and *Open in its pane* instead. The list never offers an option that saves a
  permission into the worktree's settings, or one that switches the session's permission mode;
  those stay in the chat's own pane (HP-6, #672).
- **Answer a task's question from its row and from its tab's menu.** While a task waits on a
  question to the chat that dispatched it, its row menu in the Chats list, its own tab's menu
  and the palette have an _Answer_ row for it, and its line in its session tab's menu has an
  Answer button at its end. Each opens the same form as the Activity tab, in a dialog: the
  question, a box, _Send_ and _Cancel_. A press outside the dialog does not close it, so what
  you typed is not lost; if the question is answered elsewhere while it is open, the dialog
  says so and keeps your text (#1551).
- **Approve a waiting chat's profile from its Notice.** When a chat did not start because its
  profile's command is new or changed, its Notice offers *Review and approve…*. It opens the
  new-chat picker's own approval sentence with the exact command line, and the file is checked
  against that line again before anything is recorded. Approving starts nothing: *Retry now*
  runs the whole start again (#1246).
- **Ask a persona from a chat's tab.** A chat tab's menu and the palette have *Ask <persona>…*,
  one entry for each persona the project has finished. It asks for a task name and what to ask,
  and starts a chat as that persona under the chat you asked from, with that persona's own
  sandbox, hosts and vaults and nothing the first chat holds. You need no dispatch grant,
  because you are the one asking. So from a `steward` chat, *Ask devops…* starts a chat that
  can use the vault tagged for `devops`, with no handoff brief to write; and the Notice for a
  vault refused to a chat's persona has *Dispatch to <persona>…*, which opens the same dialog.
  Its first message says you asked, and its report reaches the chat you launched it from on
  that chat's next turn, marked as started by you. No command a chat runs starts one. The
  project's dispatch limits hold for it, and so does an administrator's policy: a lock on all
  dispatch takes the entry off every tab, a locked pair takes it off the tabs of chats running
  as the pair's first persona, and the palette's row says who locked it (#1438).
- **Quiet hours for notifications.** Settings › You › Notifications has quiet hours, off until
  you turn them on, with a start and an end time (22:00 to 07:00 unless you pick others). In
  them purlis shows no system notification and what chats ask waits in the Inbox; when they
  end, one notification names the chats still waiting on you. Whether purlis may show
  notifications at all is up to your system's notification settings.
- **What a branch changed, marked in the explorer.** In the explorer's tree, each file a branch
  changed, added, deleted or renamed against the branch it was cut from, committed or not,
  carries a mark, and each folder holding one says how many. A renamed file names where it came
  from, and a deleted file is drawn where it was. The marks follow agents as they write anywhere
  in the branch, even in a folder you never opened, with no refresh. *Changed only* collapses a
  branch's files to what it changed, every folder of it open. A *Filter files* box narrows the
  tree to names that contain what you type, and Esc clears it. A repo's own folder, which was cut
  from nothing, is marked with what isn't committed yet (FM-4, #1107).
- **Focus the explorer on one branch.** *Focus on branch …* in a branch's menu turns the explorer
  into that branch's cockpit: its name, how many commits it is ahead of and behind the branch it
  was cut from, how many files it changed, and Merge and Done; then the chats working in it with
  their live status, and its files. Esc or the breadcrumb steps back out. Each window remembers
  its focus with its view tabs, and ⌘P looks in the focused branch first (FM-5, #1108).
- **A branch's files in the explorer.** Each branch in the left sidebar, and each repo for its
  own folder, has a *Files* row that opens folder by folder into its files, read only as each
  folder is opened. Folders come first, in the order you read names. A file opens in its file
  tab, by click or Enter, and the arrows, Home and End move through the tree. What git ignores
  is hidden until *Show ignored files*, then drawn dimmed and never opened; a file purlis will
  not open, such as a link out of the branch, says why beside it. A file an agent adds or
  removes in an open folder shows up without a refresh. A folder of thousands of files shows
  its first 5,000 and counts the rest (FM-1, #1104).
- **A sandboxed chat can clone a repo and cut a worktree.** In a chat the app started,
  `purlis clone` and `purlis worktree add` now hand the work to the app, which runs the same
  commands and prints what they say. So a clone's git config and hooks,
  and the editor settings a checkout carries (`.vscode/`, `.idea/`, `.claude/settings.json`), are
  written by the app, while the chat's own writes to them stay refused. The app clones only into
  a workspace the chat already works in (any workspace for a chat at the project's top), only
  from a host the chat's sandbox may reach, and credits the worktree to the chat and its persona.
  Git run this way does not read your global or system git config, apart from your name and
  email: an LFS filter, an HTTP proxy or certificate setting and a URL rewrite you keep there do
  not apply to it, so an LFS repository checks out its pointer files, and a clone that needs
  your proxy fails where your terminal's would not. The app also refuses to run git in anything
  but a clone's own repository, or in one whose config names a program for git to run (a
  filter, a diff or merge driver, an include, a helper), and names what it refused. Outside a
  chat, or with no app listening, both commands run as before (#1335).
- **A clone or worktree the app makes for a chat says when your git config would have
  mattered.** It reads none of your git config, by design. A checkout whose `.gitattributes`
  names a filter, the top one or a folder's, now says so (up to eight by name, the rest
  counted): for Git LFS, that the files arrived as pointer files and that `git lfs pull`
  fetches them. A clone that git reports could not reach its host, where your own
  `http.proxy`, certificate setting, extra header or `url.<base>.insteadOf` would have changed
  its route, names the key (never its value) and says to clone it in your terminal. A clone
  the forge answers as not there names none (#1550). `docs/plane-format.md` explains the
  difference (#1413).
- **A `persona_remember` tool** on purlis's MCP server, beside `memory_add`: one memory of the
  chat's persona, or of shared memory, written by purlis for the chat (#1333).
- **`purlis secret exec` from a sandboxed chat runs on Linux.** A persona's declared tool now
  runs through the app on Linux too: in purlis's own sandbox, held by the chat's own profile,
  with the credential handed only to that command, as on macOS. Before, the app refused it
  there (#2342).
- **Browse and restore archived memory in the window.** Each memory list — a workspace's Memory
  section, a persona's tab, the shared list — has an archive button beside its `+`, and the palette
  has *Open <name>'s archive*. It opens the store's archive in a tab of its own: what Delete
  moved out, by title and stamp, each readable but not editable, with Restore memory to put it back
  under its name with its index line (KN-4, #716).
- **A chat's browser downloads and uploads files, inside fences.** A download lands in the
  browser's own holding folder, which no chat reaches, under a name the browser makes, never
  the page's. The agent is told each download's name, size and origin, and a download is
  cancelled past 512 MB, or past 1 GB for a browser's downloads together. Saving one into the
  chat's folder needs your yes for its origin, which purlis does not ask for yet, so nothing is
  saved for now. An upload takes files from the chat's own folder alone, under its read rules,
  following no link out of it; the browser is handed purlis's copy, never the chat's file
  (#2020).
- **The browser engine stays current between purlis releases** (#2073). Once you have used a
  browser on this machine, the session host checks each day's signed manifest of Chrome for
  Testing in the background and takes a newer engine only when its Sigstore signature verifies
  as purlis's own manifest workflow on `main`. An engine still current is no longer refused for
  its age. The network log lists each manifest read as the updater's and each engine download
  as the browser engine's, redirects included. With no update ever received, the engine your
  build pins keeps working.
- **The event log records each browser's life.** It now says when a browser opens, when it is
  closed and by whom (its chat, you, going unused, or the kill switch), when its engine crashes,
  and when you pin or unpin it. Each browser tool call a chat makes is recorded with the call's
  name, the origin of its page and whether it was done, and typing names the page's origin.
  Nothing of a page's content, no typed value, no argument and no address beyond its origin is
  written (#2842).
- **Inspect opens a browser's real DevTools beside it.** On a browser on this Mac, Inspect takes
  the browser over and opens the page's DevTools in a view next to it, drawn by purlis from the
  engine's own DevTools. No chat can open or read them, and they close when you press Done
  (#2028).
- **Attach browser proof to a pull request.** In a chat's browser timeline you pick the
  screenshots to attach, press *Attach browser proof…*, choose the pull or merge request (the
  open request of a save of the chat's workspace, or any other by its address), and see exactly
  what goes before anything is sent: the request, where the pictures are kept and who can open
  them there, a warning that they are public and permanent to whoever can read the repo (and
  whether the repo is public), the comment's words and each picture. Every screenshot is the one
  the agent's browser tool returned, with the fields purlis filled and those you typed into
  already blanked, and nothing the agent wrote goes with them. It is sent with your purlis
  sign-in only, and only while the chat is open. On GitHub the pictures are kept on a branch of
  the repo's own, `purlis/browser-proof/pr-<n>`, in its history for good; on GitLab as the
  project's uploads, which stay after the comment is deleted (#2026).
- **Chats drive a real browser.** Every harness's chat gets purlis's `browser_` tools: a
  snapshot of a page with a reference for each element, clicks, typing, drags, waits and a
  screenshot the model sees as an image, on a browser purlis runs and no script the model
  writes. A chat's first browser tool asks you once what its browser may reach: this project's
  sites and its dev servers, also the open web, or Keep off. A project's chats hold at most
  three browsers together, and a browser's reach follows its chat's reach, including what you
  withdraw (#2013).
- **A chat on a pool's runner has its browser there too.** Its browser runs on the runner beside
  it, so its `localhost` is the runner's, and the browser's chip says so: `localhost:5173 on pool
  builds`. You watch it, take it over and type into it as on this machine. Over the link a view
  is held to 15 frames a second and 1280 pixels wide, sends the newest frame once the last is
  drawn, and never queues what you type behind its frames (#2050).
- **A login in a runner's browser asks first, and only on a runner that is yours.** For now that
  is a Docker pool on this machine's own Docker; a pool on another machine's engine is filled no
  login. The first time a runner chat asks purlis to log its browser in, you are asked about that
  login on that pool; your answer holds while purlis runs and the pool, its runner and its image
  stay as they are. The values go from your vault to the runner's browser for that one login; the
  runner keeps none, and no kept login. With your desktop away, the login waits up to 15 minutes
  for you to be asked, and the chat carries on (#2050).
- **Browsers survive a crash of the app.** A browser a chat used is back under its chat, with the
  name the chat knew it by, when purlis comes back within the grace period, and its view draws
  again at once. A browser you were driving is still yours. One you opened yourself, and any you
  had open in a tab of its own, comes back in a tab. A pinned one whose chat did not come back
  stays under Pinned browsers. A browser nothing takes back is ended, and one signed in with a
  login goes back to its chat only if that chat may still use the login (#2025).
- **The Lower icons carry badges**, as the sidebars' icons do, so they show while their half is
  away: Changes counts uncommitted files, and Repos shows how many commits the clones are behind
  and ahead, only while one is behind (#1739).
- **Every chat the app starts gets purlis's MCP server, whatever harness it runs.** Claude
  Code, Codex and opencode chats get the same tools, for that chat alone, beside your own MCP
  servers: `todo_list`, `todo_add` and `todo_done`, `memory_search` and `memory_add`,
  `session_record_list` and `session_record_read`, `change_status`, and `ask_operator`, which
  puts a question to you through the harness's own prompt. Each tool acts on the workspace the
  chat works in, and none of them reads a vault or a forge (HP-7, #674).
- **A chat that did not start has Retry now and Forget this chat….** Retry now starts the chat
  again, the way a launch does, and its tab opens. If it still cannot start, the line stays and
  says why. Forget this chat… asks first, then drops the chat for good. Until you choose, the
  chat is kept, so a folder that moved never deletes it (NO-3, #1230).
- **Start fresh, for a chat the project's instructions changed under.** The mark on its tab is
  now a button, and the palette and the tab's menu have a *Start chat … fresh* row. After a
  question, the chat starts again on the project as it is now, as a new conversation under the
  same name (NO-3, #1230).
- **See which file a chat is working on.** When a chat's file tool reads or edits a file, the
  explorer and the branch cockpit put a breathing dot on that file and on each folder above it,
  naming the chat on hover. The dot fades a few seconds after the chat goes quiet on the file.
  Claude Code and opencode chats drive it; Codex's hooks see only shell commands, so a Codex chat
  marks nothing. The path stays in memory and is never written to the event log or any other
  store (FM-6, #1109).
- **A filter over the Chats list.** Type a name, a persona, a workspace or a state's word, or
  press the chip for the chats that need you or the ones at work. It finds finished tasks too,
  by how they ended. The session that asked for a task stays above it and is opened, whatever
  fold you had set; the fold is back when the filter is cleared. A line under the filter says
  how many chats it hides, and when one of those needs you it says so and has a button that
  goes to it. Escape clears the filter, and it stays at the top while the list scrolls. The
  palette finds a task that has no tab, too: *Show task …* (#1499).
- **Keys on a row of the Chats list.** Enter opens the chat. Delete on a task (the delete key
  on a Mac) asks to stop it. Space asks for the chat beside the one in front, which purlis
  cannot do yet, and says so (#1499).
- **Two settings for the Chats list**, under You: rows on two lines or one, and the sessions
  grouped by workspace (#1499).
- **Chats survive a crash of the app.** With chats running in the session host (the default,
  #2004), a crash or a kill of the app no longer ends them: the session host keeps every chat,
  its network and its project's saving for ten minutes. Start purlis again within them and every
  tab comes back on the same chat, with what it wrote meanwhile on screen and each chat's state
  and Needs you as the host kept them. After ten minutes the host ends them as a quit would, and
  the next start offers to reopen them. Quitting still ends every chat, and so does an update
  (#2006, #646, #2194).
- **A chat's helpers show under it.** A Claude Code sub-agent or a Codex child is a helper of
  its chat: the chat's row in the explorer says how many it has, and unfolds to each with what
  it is doing. A Claude Code sub-agent or a Codex child reads working, then done when it
  finishes (a Codex chat's hooks gain `SubagentStop`, so Codex asks once more to trust them,
  #1086), and working again when its chat gives it another turn (#2455). The kill switch, or
  closing the chat, stops its sub-agents with it, and a stopped chat's sub-agents read as ended
  with it. A sub-agent's question is its chat's, and its own turns never move the chat out of
  running. opencode reports no sub-agents, and its chat says so (FD-18, #656).
- **Clone a repo the workspace names but this machine lacks, from the window.** Each row under
  *Not cloned here* in the explorer has *Clone* on hover or focus and on its menu, the heading
  has *Clone all* when more than one is missing, and the bottom bar's row offers *Clone* on its
  menu. The palette has a *Clone* row per missing repo and *Clone all missing repos*. A row
  shows its clone under way, moves to the clones when it lands, and shows the core's reason and
  *Retry* when it fails (#1215).
- **A Helm chart for purlis's cluster operator.** `operator/charts/purlis-cluster-operator/`
  installs the operator, its definitions (Pool and Claim, from the chart's `crds/`) and the
  policy on Claims, with the operator's image named by digest; the plain manifests in
  `operator/deploy/` are rendered from it and make the same objects. The chart is not
  published to a chart repository (#2237, docs/cluster-operator.md).
- **A team rolls its cluster operator's signing key without any desktop asking again.** Add
  the next key to the operator's Secret as `next.pem`: every Pool names it as
  `nextSigningKey`, with the current key's word for it (`nextSigningKeyVouch`), every Claim's
  statement is signed by both keys, and a desktop that sees the roll moves its pin. Then make
  `next.pem` the `key.pem`. The operator's pod mounts the whole Secret, so no restart is
  needed (#3305, docs/cluster-operator.md).
- **A cluster operator Pool or Claim can be stopped from kubectl.** `stopped: true` suspends
  every runner of the pool, or the Claim's runner: its pod ends and a kept Claim's volume stays.
  Once `stopped` is false a kept Claim's runner comes back on that volume, paired as it was; a
  fresh Claim's runner starts again with nothing kept. A warm runner made from a pool's earlier
  template is now replaced, so a fresh Claim is never handed one the operator will not vouch
  for. The operator's new right to change a sandbox's mode is narrowed by a second admission
  policy in `policy.yaml`; apply it with the definitions (#2058, docs/cluster-operator.md).
- **A plain guide to setting a pool up on your cluster.** It goes from a cluster with no purlis on
  it to a connected pool, with each step's exact command and what you should see. The add pool
  dialog and the pools settings link to it (#4537).
- **Sandboxed Codex and opencode chats on Linux.** A project that runs its chats sandboxed now
  starts Codex and opencode chats on Linux inside purlis's own sandbox, built from the same
  policy as on macOS, where before they were refused. It needs no extra package, privilege or
  namespace, so it works the same on a Linux desktop, in a Docker container and in a Kubernetes
  pod. It needs Linux 6.12 or later (Landlock version 6). In a project with `mode = "on"`, an
  older kernel refuses the chat and says how to go on; elsewhere the chat starts without the
  floor and its tab says why (#1040).
- **A sandboxed Codex chat raises its own blocks.** A failed lookup, a refused socket or a
  refusal a command printed in a Codex chat now gets a Notice, as it does in Claude Code and
  opencode chats. Codex is armed with one more hook after each shell command, so the first Codex
  chat after the update asks you once to trust purlis's hooks again (#1663).
- **A Report of a sandbox block names the harness's version.** The draft adds the Claude Code
  version this app last heard answer `--version`, in a version's shape only, or says it is not
  known (#1353).
- **Codex and opencode's ChatGPT sign-in finish on a runner by approving in your browser.** Sign in
  on a pool's profile opens the page, and there is nothing to paste: for as long as the sign-in
  runs, purlis listens on this Mac's `localhost:1455` for that one sign-in's redirect and carries it
  to the runner. If another program holds the port, the strip says so and offers a device code
  (`codex login --device-auth` on the runner). Where purlis cannot follow such a sign-in, it restarts in the
  runner's terminal in the strip by that device-code flow, since nothing carries the browser's
  answer to a terminal.
- **⌘P's files draw their icons.** Each file the switcher finds is drawn with its file-type icon,
  in the icon theme of the project and workspace it was found in, as its own tree draws it
  (#1145).
- **A theme can set one part of a control.** A theme's `theme.json` takes a `parts` object of
  keys `<family>.<part>[.<variant>][.<state>].<property>`: `"button.root.corner-radius": "full"`
  draws every button as a pill, and `"button.root.primary.hover.fill": "accent.base"` changes only
  the primary under the pointer. `purlis theme parts` lists every family, part, state and
  property with its bounds, and the published schema completes each key. A state never changes a
  part's size, a control stays at least 24px tall with its words fitting, the floors hold for
  each part, and Allow keeps its edge and never takes the primary look. A theme that names no
  parts draws exactly as before (#2903).
- **opencode's Copilot sign-in on a runner shows its device code in place.** Sign in to GitHub
  Copilot on a profile's line in Settings › Pools shows the code with Copy code and Open page,
  and the line turns signed in once GitHub accepts it. It signs in to GitHub.com; GitHub
  Enterprise stays with Open in terminal.
- **`purlis profile sign-in <profile> --pool <pool>`** signs a profile in on a pool's runner from
  your own terminal, with the same steps as the strip: it says the page and opens it, reads the
  code, or shows the device code, and says signed in. A refusal, or anything it does not recognise,
  says what to do and exits non-zero. So far it follows Claude Code and opencode's Copilot sign-in.
- **Copy diagnostics in About purlis.** One press puts a plain-text report on the clipboard, to
  paste into an issue or a chat: the version and build, the system, each harness's installed
  version, how many chats are open and hot, and the newest 200 slow answers and window stalls
  this machine recorded. Nothing secret goes into it: no vault value, token or folder (#4774).
- **Copy path and Reveal from ⌘P's files.** With a file aimed in the switcher, `⌥⌘C` copies its
  path and `⌥⌘R` shows it in Finder (`Shift+Alt+C` and `Shift+Alt+R` off a Mac). The palette
  stays open, and a refusal is said on its line (#1143).
- **Create a project on GitHub or GitLab, in one step.** The welcome's **Create a project** now
  asks where the project lives: **GitHub**, **GitLab** or **Only this Mac**. On a forge, give it
  a name, an owner (you, or one of your organisations or groups), private or public (private
  unless you say otherwise) and a stack template or none. **Create project** makes the repo with
  your purlis sign-in, lays out the project, commits it, pushes the first commit through
  purlis's own credential helper and opens the project, showing each stage as it runs. Without a
  purlis sign-in to that forge, the page asks you to sign in first, and the guided steps add their
  sign-in step. **Cancel**, or a stage that fails, takes back what this creation made: the repo on
  the forge and the folder, and only those (#1819). GitHub deletes a repo only for a token with
  the `delete_repo` scope, which purlis does not ask for; when it cannot delete the repo it made,
  purlis names it and the page where you delete it.
- **Create the profile a persona names, from its tab.** A persona whose definition names a
  profile this machine does not have (`profile: qa-bot`) now says so on its tab and offers
  **Create profile qa-bot…**: pick the harness and press Create, and the profile is made as
  Settings › You › Profiles' Add profile makes one, ready to sign in with your own account.
  Nothing is made until you press Create. Dispatch lists, the approval of a clone's own
  profiles and the refusal of a command that switches permission prompts off hold for it as
  for any other profile (#2039).
- **A harness declaration lists the plans a subscription signs in to.** `[sign_in] plans =
  [{ provider = "openai", title = "ChatGPT" }, …]` is an allow-list of the plans Sign in offers,
  passed as the harness's own provider id; a harness that lists none signs in to its own
  vendor's plan. opencode's built-in declaration now lists ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot, and
  `anthropic` is refused in any declaration but Claude Code's own (#2039).
- **Database clients and ssh reach allowed hosts from a sandboxed chat.** `purlis secret exec`
  points a vault's connection string (a database URL, a libpq `host=… port=…` string, or
  `host:port`) at a tunnel to exactly that host and port when the chat may reach it, so `psql`
  and `usql` work with the command unchanged; a host it may not reach raises a Block with Allow
  instead of failing at the name lookup. git over ssh, and a bare `ssh` in a Codex or opencode chat, go through the chat's SOCKS port.
  Every tunnelled connection is in the network record (#1667).
- **Messages that name a setting open Settings at its group.** A doctor row whose fix is a
  setting, such as a `[[forge]]` block that does not resolve or a `[plane]` key purlis does not
  read, has a Fix it in Settings button. It opens Settings at that project's level with the
  group shown, such as Forges, Saving or Harness & profiles. A text size or editor in the layout
  file that purlis could not use gets the same button in the alerts drawer, which opens the
  Text or Editor group. A Settings tab already open for that level is brought forward rather
  than opened again. Each level now shows the group you last looked at there until the window
  closes (SE-22, #1172).
- **Some refusals inside dialogs now offer a way out** (NO-8, #1233).
  - When git would carry your local settings file, the Start a chat dialog offers Add the ignore
    line, the fix the doctor's row applies, and then reads its profiles again.
  - The dialog's list of refused profiles links to Settings › Harness & profiles.
  - When the repo picker says a forge's CLI is not logged in, it offers that CLI's login. The
    login is typed into a shell tab at the project root, and you run it yourself.
  - The Extensions dialog's line about an unreadable extension record has Read again.
- **Devices: the disk each pool's runners hold.** The use table under the devices has a Disk held
  column: the size of each pool's runners' home volumes together, a draining runner's included,
  as `docker system df` (or Podman's) reports it. Reading it starts no suspended runner, and a
  slow count holds up nothing else in the view. A home Docker does not list is said apart, never
  counted as nothing (#3493).
- **A chat can dispatch a task to its own persona, and gets the report on its next turn.**
  `purlis dispatch --name "<task>" <<'BRIEF'`, or purlis's `dispatch` tool, starts a chat of its
  own for the task: as the asking chat's persona, on its harness profile and in its folder, with
  the sandbox the project gives that persona. What you allowed the asking chat alone, and a
  start without the sandbox, are not carried to it. Its first message says which chat asked and
  that the brief is a request from a chat. In the explorer it is listed under the chat that
  asked for it. It finishes with `purlis dispatch report --outcome done|blocked|failed "<text>"`,
  and the chat that asked reads the outcome, the text, what changed and the session record's
  path on its next turn, quoted as data. A dispatch to another persona starts nothing until you
  allow the pair (see "A dispatch to another persona waits for your answer"). Where purlis's hook can tell a sub-agent made the call, it is refused
  and told to return to its chat. One chat waits on at most 6 tasks, a lineage holds 16 chats
  that still owe work, and a chain goes 3 deep (#1436).
- **A dispatch to another persona waits for your answer, and starts when you allow it.** Where
  no dispatch grant covers the pair, the task is held: `purlis dispatch` says `held for the
  person` and exits 0, the Notice on the asking chat's tab shows the brief, and **Allow**
  starts exactly that task on the brief you read. **Keep blocked** starts nothing. Either way
  the asking chat is told on its next turn, and a chat that was started again before you
  answered is told the task was not started. A second dispatch across the same pair while
  you are being asked is refused, not queued beside the first. The Notice says that a grant covers the
  helper sub-agents those chats run too (#1437).
- **Dispatch runs under the limits you set.** The limits in force for a dispatch are the
  project's, for the asking chat's workspace and persona, lowered by your own and capped by an
  administrator's policy, read afresh each time. A refusal names the limit and the count it
  stands at. A persona's two own limits are counted across every chat of the project: the
  tasks the chats running as it wait on, and the chats running as it at once. A limit of 0
  says where dispatch was switched off (#1439, #1440).
- **`purlis dispatch --profile <profile>`** starts the task on another of the project's
  harness profiles, and the `dispatch` tool takes `profile`. With none named, a task starts on
  its persona's own profile where the definition names one, else on the asking chat's, as a
  handoff does. Where the persona's own profile is not offered on this machine, the chat
  starts on the asking chat's and both chats are told so (#1436, #1445).
- **A workspace or a persona can have dispatch limits of its own.** Settings › Project ›
  Dispatch has a row for the project and one per override, with Add an override; the same limits
  are on a workspace's settings and on a persona's view. The most specific row wins: a persona's
  over a workspace's over the project's. A persona has two more: how many persona chats the
  chats running as it may have running between them, and how many chats may run as it at once,
  both counted across the project. A
  persona's limits are kept in the project's file, never the persona's own. Your own row, Me on
  this machine, can only lower a limit, and an administrator's policy file can cap each one
  (`dispatch` in `/etc/purlis/policy.json`). The last change on a limits table has Undo (#1440).
- **Dispatch limits, set on Settings › Project › Dispatch.** A project now says how many persona
  chats one chat may have running (6 unless you change it), how many live chats one lineage may
  hold (16), how many dispatches deep a chain may go (3, and never above 8) and how many messages
  a minute one chat may send another (10; set and shown now, and not judged until chats can
  message each other, #1441). A limit of 0 switches dispatch off. The limits are kept in the
  project's committed file, under `[dispatch]`, and a sandboxed chat cannot change them. The page
  also shows what an administrator's policy caps, as locked (#1439).
- **`purlis dispatch list` says whether each task is alive.** Each task in the list, the
  `dispatch_list` tool and the open-task roster at each turn now says whether its program is
  running, when it last ran a command or sent a note, and whether it kept running through a
  purlis restart or was started again on its conversation. A task purlis can no longer reach
  after a restart is marked *orphaned by restart*. When a chat dispatches a second task under
  the name of an open one, the refusal says the open task is alive (#3900).
- **Long-running tasks: `purlis dispatch --long`.** A task started with `--long`, or with
  `long: true` on the `dispatch` tool, works through many pieces and sends progress with
  `dispatch note`. purlis never asks it for a report and never makes one from its last message.
  It ends when it reports `done` or `failed`, or when it is cancelled. `dispatch list` marks it
  long-running and shows its last note. The open-tasks roster marks it long-running too. Plain
  dispatches work as before (#3905).
- **The Dispatch page links to the personas it names.** Each persona in the table of who may
  dispatch to whom, and each persona's row of the dispatch limits, has *Show <persona>*, which
  opens that persona's tab. "Any persona", chats on no persona and a name that is no persona of
  the project now link nowhere (#1388).
- **Tell every task at once, and see who took it in.** `purlis dispatch tell --all "<text>"`
  (or the `dispatch_tell` tool's `all`) sends one numbered instruction to every task of the
  chat still working. A task acknowledges it with `purlis dispatch note --ack <n>` (or the
  `dispatch_note` tool's `ack`), and `purlis dispatch list` shows which tasks have (#3904).
- **The Dispatches tab lists dispatches that did not start**: one waiting on your answer to
  its grant Notice, and one you kept blocked, under **Not started**. They have no record, so
  the list is kept while the app runs (#1456).
- **The window says when a runner's key changed.** When the runner a project's chats run on
  answers with another key than the one it was paired with, a Notice says so once for the
  project, with Open Pools settings (#2752).
- **`purlis doctor` checks each workspace's generated layer.** The `workspace layer` row, which
  said "not checked", now compares the settings purlis generates into every workspace folder,
  and into every clone and worktree in it, with what the project's own settings say today,
  without writing anything. A file that is missing or stale is named with `purlis workspace
  reinit --all`; one purlis did not write, cannot read, or cannot confirm as its own is named
  with what clears it instead (#994, #998).
- **`purlis doctor` checks the Bash guard, shadowed docs and MCP rows.** Four rows that said
  "not checked" now look:
  - `plane-root guard` says whether the Bash guard is declared where a session started in this
    directory loads it: its own `.claude/settings.json` or `settings.local.json`, the user
    settings of the Claude Code folder in use, or an enabled plugin. A guard declared twice is
    named. The chats the app starts are armed by the app either way, so a guard declared
    nowhere is a warning about chats started outside it.
  - `guard seen` says when the guard last ran in this project and under which harness. The
    guard records each run in `guard-seen.json` in the project's state folder.
  - `shadowed docs` names a project's own copy of a page `purlis docs show` serves, or of a
    skill purlis's plugin ships, which drifts unwatched.
  - `mcp` says whether each MCP server a persona's chats are given can start: a launcher on an
    absolute path that is not there is named, with its persona (#994).
- **The doctor finds skills an older project does not publish or keep local.** A project set up
  before LIVE workspaces published their skills keeps them on this machine, and one set up
  before local skills were kept out of git can commit them. The new `live skills` row names
  each LIVE workspace whose skills are not published and the local skills of a project,
  workspace or persona that git does not ignore. `purlis doctor --fix live-skills`, the Doctor
  dialog's Fix button, or bare `purlis doctor --fix` adds exactly the missing lines and nothing
  else (#2875).
- **The doctor fixes what it can, from the terminal and from the window.** A doctor finding that
  purlis can fix carries a fix id, which `purlis doctor --json` prints as `fix` on that row.
  `purlis doctor --fix <id>` applies that one fix. Bare `purlis doctor --fix` applies every fix
  the rows offer, on top of its plugin and ask-rule repairs. Each fix says what it changed or why
  it was refused. The Doctor dialog has a **Fix** button on those rows, which applies the fix and
  checks again. The first fix is `reinit`, offered when the project is missing a baseline folder.
  It adds what is missing and never removes or replaces your content. Removing a git index lock
  is never a fix (FX-1, #1224).
- **Four more doctor fixes, each with a Fix button in the Doctor dialog and an id for
  `purlis doctor --fix <id>`.**
  - `plugin-install`: installs purlis's plugin for chats started outside the app. The
    `plugin install`, `plugin` and `plugin files` rows offer it. Bare `--fix` still installs the
    plugin, and now runs it once even when several rows offer it.
  - `local-ignore`: appends `/charter.local.toml` to `.gitignore` when git would commit that
    file. When git already tracks the file, the fix refuses and tells you to untrack it yourself.
    purlis never runs `git rm` for you.
  - `memory-optimize`: appends a link to `MEMORY.md` for each memory the index is missing, and
    changes nothing else. Collapsing duplicates stays with `persona|workspace optimize --apply`.
  - `discover`: builds an empty inventory from the forges `charter.toml` declares. It goes over
    the network, so it runs only when named, as `purlis doctor --fix discover` or its Fix
    button. Bare `purlis doctor --fix` applies the other three, and `reinit`.
  No fix removes or replaces your content (FX-2, #1234).
- **`purlis doctor` flags a landing the default branch no longer holds.** When the landing log
  names a commit purlis landed for a change, and the clone's default branch (pushed or local) was
  rewritten so it no longer holds that commit, the `changes` row fails, naming the change and the
  member. A commit this clone has never fetched is not read as lost (#878).
- **A missing git identity is fixed from a form.** When `user.name` or `user.email` is unset, the
  doctor's `git identity` row offers the fix `git-identity`. In the Doctor dialog, its Fix button
  opens a small form for a name and an email; in a terminal, it is
  `purlis doctor --fix git-identity --name "Your Name" --email you@example.com`. Both are written
  to git's global config, the scope the row names. Each value is checked first, and a refusal is
  shown under its field and writes nothing (FX-3, #1235).
- **The doctor names the workspaces behind the current layout.** Its new `workspace layout`
  row warns with each workspace's name and offers the `workspace-reinit` fix, the one the
  Alerts drawer's Reinit button runs, so the Doctor dialog has a Fix button for it and bare
  `purlis doctor --fix` brings them up to date. The row and the drawer read the same
  workspaces (#1289).
- **The doctor says who can read what your project pushes.** `purlis doctor`, and the full
  doctor in the app, have a `project remote` row: whether the project's `origin` is public,
  internal or private on GitHub or GitLab, and whether the forge's own push protection (GitHub's
  push protection, GitLab's secret push protection) is on. A public remote without it is a
  warning, and a setting the signed-in account cannot see is never read as on. The session-start
  preflight asks no forge, so it has no such row (SQ-8, #587).
- **`purlis doctor` reads the block that hides purlis's files in a clone.** The `workspace
  layer` row now has a line for each clone's and worktree's `.git/info/exclude`: missing or
  stale (`purlis workspace reinit --all` writes it), keeping a line purlis cannot prove it no
  longer needs, or leaving one out because it would hide a file of yours. It also names a
  machine-local settings file purlis is holding back for that reason, a copied agent or skill
  the next `reinit` takes out, a record purlis could not write there, and a record that
  repository commits. Each is said with what clears it, and nothing is written (#998).
- **`purlis doctor` names an extension still on the old manifest name.** An extension whose
  folder holds `charter-extension.json` and no `purlis-extension.json` gets an
  `extension manifests` row asking for the rename; the old name is read for one more release
  (#1802).
- **`purlis doctor` says when the sandbox drops a forge host.** With the sandbox and its `forge`
  preset on, a `[[forge]]` host sandboxed chats cannot reach gets a `sandbox forge hosts` row, as
  Settings already said (#1405).
- **`purlis doctor` shows the size of a project's sandbox cache home.** Where a project's
  sandboxed chats have a package cache home on this machine, a `sandbox cache home` row says how
  much disk it takes (#1364).
- **`purlis doctor` says when this purlis cannot read the hook spool's keys.** A `keys.json` a
  newer purlis wrote stops every drain of the project's hook spool and every new chat's key.
  That used to be said only in the app's log. Now a `hook spool` row says it and says how to fix
  it. The row reads only the file's version, and drains and writes nothing (#983).
- **`purlis doctor` shows what each workspace repo's forge can do.** A new `forge capabilities`
  row lists, for every clone whose origin is on GitHub or GitLab, each capability purlis uses
  (auto-merge, merge queue, sub-issues, issue types, epics, iterations, boards, dependencies,
  close reasons, item status): yes, no with the reason (a personal account, a GitLab tier, an
  older host), or unknown, and what purlis does instead. The answers come from the same check
  the operations make. Only a doctor you type asks the forge; the preflight does not (#802).
- **`purlis doctor` warns when your git reads any bare repository.** The new `git bare repos`
  row warns while no git config you use sets `safe.bareRepository = explicit`, and says why: a
  sandboxed chat can write a folder git takes for a bare repository, and a git run inside it
  later can run a program its config names (#1100).
- **Drag panes to split, swap and move them.** Drag a pane by its head, a chat's row in the
  sidebar, or a tab pulled down off the strip. Drop it in a pane's outer quarter, by an edge, to
  split on that side, or in its middle to swap. Drop it on the strip to make a tab. The result is
  drawn before you drop. A place that would leave a pane under about 40 columns by 8 rows is
  refused, with its reason. Holding over a tab brings it forward. Esc cancels the drag. After a
  drop, a split or Tile all, Undo or ⌘Z puts the last layout back. A split's separator now stops
  at the same minimum, and double-click or Enter on it makes both sides even (#4763).
- **Each grade's chat is one click from its scorecard** (SK-59, #3239). A row of a skill's Grades
  panel opens the grade's scorecard: each trigger test with the skill and without it, what each
  run started, and each of its chats, which opens read-only in a tab as it showed when the grade
  ended it. purlis keeps a grade's chats on the machine that ran it, for the skill's three newest
  grades. A grade's chat that asks you something is ended there, and the grade says so, in its
  end and on its scorecard, instead of a notice on a chat you cannot see.
- **Edit a project's settings files as TOML in Settings.** At the Project level, an "Edit as
  TOML" link for `charter.toml` and one for `charter.local.toml` sit under the groups. Each
  opens that file's whole text beside them. Nothing is written until you press Save, and
  Discard drops the edit. Text that does not parse, or that purlis would not read, is refused
  with the reason and nothing is written. If the file changes on disk while you are editing,
  the editor tells you, and Save is refused rather than overwriting the other change (SE-19,
  #1169).
- **Two ways to end a task: Stop and get its report, and Close now.** They are on a task's
  row menu in the Chats list, on the breadcrumb's line while a tab shows the task, and in the
  palette. Stop and get its report ends the task's turn and gives it one short turn to say
  what it did. Close now ends its program at once. Neither shows the close dialog, and
  neither offers a Smart close. Delete on a task's row asks for the first (#1488).
- **Ending a task always takes a second step.** A press asks where it was made, on the row or
  on the breadcrumb: "Stop it" or "Close it", beside "Keep", which has the keyboard. Nothing
  ends on one press or on a stray Return (#1488).
- **The chat that asked is told which, in purlis's own words**: stopped by the person, with
  the task's report quoted as data; closed by the person, with no report; or ended without a
  report, for a task whose program died. The first two add "The person ended this task. Do
  not dispatch it again unless they ask." A task cannot say any of this of itself. `purlis
  dispatch wait` returns the same word and `purlis dispatch list` says it (#1488).
- **One dialog, and only where it is needed.** A task in the middle of a turn asks once: "Stop
  task '<name>'? It is working." A task with tasks of its own still working asks, in the same
  question, whether they are ended too or kept. Where purlis may not type into a task, it
  says why and offers Close alone; on a harness purlis never types into, Stop is not offered
  (#1488).
- **Closing a task's tab ends nothing.** The tab goes, and the task goes back to the Chats
  list and keeps working. A close of several tabs sends the tasks among them back and says so
  (#1488).
- **Every handoff leaves a record, and a Dispatches tab lists them.** purlis now keeps one
  record for each chat a chat starts: who asked, which persona it went to, where it worked,
  the brief, the report, when it started and ended, how often it needed you, and the tokens
  and cost its harness reported. Open **Dispatches** from the palette or from the Sessions
  panel's heading to see the running and past ones, filter them by persona and by asking
  chat, and open a row's chat, or its session record once the chat is closed. A session
  record's tab lists the dispatches its chat made. The records stay on this machine, are
  never committed, and are let go of 30 days after they were last written. A sandboxed chat
  can neither read nor write them. In a project with no sandbox, or a chat started without
  it, only the file's own permissions protect them: every such chat can read and change
  them. **Cost (reported)** is what the chat's harness reported; it is shown and never
  enforced, and reads *not reported* for a harness that reports none
  (#1452).
- **Every `purlis dispatch` subcommand is a chat tool.** `dispatch_wait`, `dispatch_tell`,
  `dispatch_answer`, `dispatch_cancel`, `dispatch_close`, `dispatch_note` and `dispatch_ask`
  join `dispatch`, `dispatch_list`, `dispatch_read` and `dispatch_report`, on every harness. A
  Claude Code chat runs each one without its harness asking. Chats are taught the tools first,
  and the command stays for terminals and scripts (#3786).
- **Every running chat of the project is in one tree.** The left region has a **Chats** section
  above the explorer: every chat in every workspace, nested under the chat that started it,
  each with its persona's mark, its name, its workspace, its state and a hand when it needs
  you. A chat whose parent has closed stays at the top and says where it came from. Pressing a
  row brings that chat forward. A handoff opens as a tab, as before. A chat started as a task is listed with no tab of its own; pressing its row shows it
  inside the tab of the session that asked for it (#1447, #1486).
- **Open an extension's view beside a pane.** A view's button has a beside icon after it, and an
  ⌥-press (Alt off a Mac), its right-click menu or ⌥Enter on its palette row opens the view in a
  split beside the pane. Where a side would be under about 40 columns by 8 rows, Open beside is
  greyed with its reason before you press. A view already open is brought forward, never opened
  twice (#4769).
- **An extension can offer its view.** An extension that hears an event may offer one of its own
  views. It opens nothing: you get one quiet note with Open, Open beside, Stop offers and Dismiss.
  A dismissed offer stays quiet until purlis restarts. Stopped offers come back from Settings ›
  Extensions. A removed extension's offers go, and a view of it still open says it is not here
  any more (#4769).
- **Read again on the "extensions unread" Notice.** When purlis could not read which extensions a
  project has on, the Notice in the Inbox now asks once more on a press: once they are read, the
  Notice goes and the extension's theme is drawn (#4871).
- **F6 is in the palette, and every region it stops in is named.** _Focus the next region_ and
  _Focus the previous region_ are palette rows that say their keys, F6 and Shift+F6. The left
  sidebar, the editor and the right sidebar are named regions, as the Panel's halves are, so a
  screen reader says where F6 landed (#1751).
- **File and folder icons.** The explorer's tree and a branch's file tab draw each file with an
  icon for its type, and each folder with one for its name, coloured from the theme so they
  follow light and dark. The icons are an icon theme: purlis's own is a small set from Material
  Icon Theme (MIT), credited with its licence in About. A project picks another under `[theme]`
  as `icons = "<extension>/<icon theme>"`, and an extension contributes one as data under
  `contributes.icon_themes` (FM-3, #1106).
- **A licence check for the app's npm packages.** CI fails when a package the app ships, or an
  asset vendored into it, is under a licence outside `deny.toml`'s allow-list (FM-3, #1106).
- **A file or folder row has a menu, and nothing on it changes a file.** Right-click a file or
  folder in the explorer's tree or in a file tab's tree, or press Shift+F10 on it, to copy its
  path relative to the branch or its absolute path, reveal it in Finder, Files or File Explorer,
  open a file in your editor, or open a shell tab in a folder. purlis offers no create, rename,
  move or delete, so it never races an agent writing the same branch. A link is not followed:
  its row copies only its relative path (FM-10, #1113).
- **⌘P marks the letters you typed.** Each file row marks which letters of its name and folder
  the query matched, so you can see why a file was found (#1131).
- **Hand a file to a chat without typing its path.** Drag a file or folder from the explorer or a
  file tab, a search hit, or the lines you selected in the preview onto a chat's tab or its pane,
  and purlis types a reference to it into the chat in that harness's own words: `@src/main.rs#L10-20`
  in Claude Code, `src/main.rs:10-20` in Codex, `@src/main.rs#10-20` in opencode. It is typed and
  never sent, so you add your own words before pressing Enter. The preview has _Ask a chat about
  this_ and _Add to a chat's context_, which pick a chat, and every file and folder row has
  _Start a chat here_, which opens a chat on that branch with the reference already typed. A chat
  that is mid-turn, asking you something, or not heard from yet is never typed into: the
  reference goes on the clipboard instead, and purlis says why. A file whose name begins with
  `!` or another character a harness reads as a command is written `./!…`, and a name holding an
  invisible or direction-changing character is refused. opencode cannot be typed into yet, so it always gets
  the reference on the clipboard, with a note (FM-9, #1112).
- **Filter settings by name.** A box above the Settings tab's groups narrows them, and the
  settings beside them, to the ones whose name or help holds what you type, whatever its case,
  at the level you are on. When nothing matches it says so; Escape or clearing the box brings
  every group back (SE-21, #1171).
- **⌘P finds a file by fuzzy name** (Ctrl+Shift+P off a Mac). Once you type, a *Files* group
  follows the projects in the switcher. Each file shows its folder, branch and project, and Enter
  opens it in its file tab. The search starts in the branch picked in the explorer, or the
  project in front when no branch is picked. Tab widens it to the project, then to every open
  project when there is more than one, and the scope is shown above the files. Of two equal
  matches, the one nearer your focus comes first. ⌘P never finds files git ignores (a secret
  file git ignores included), links out of the branch, or anything inside git's own folder. With
  one project open, the key now finds files instead of doing nothing (FM-7, #1110).
- **Find in a file.** ⌘F on a Mac, or Ctrl+F elsewhere, opens the find bar over a file tab or a
  file's *What changed* tab: every match is marked, in any case, with Enter and Shift+Enter to
  move between them and a count, as in a chat (#1088).
- **A theme sets the window's gutter and its panels' corners.** Three geometry tokens join each
  appearance: `window.gutter` (the gap between the regions, 0 to 16 px), `panel.corner-radius`
  (a region panel's corners, 0 to 24 px) and `panel.border-width` (the hairline between two
  flush regions, 0 to 2 px). The Purlis theme floats its panels 8 apart with 12px corners and no
  hairline; Purlis Classic is 0, 0 and 1, and draws flush as before (#2913).
- **You can hide any status bar item.** Right-click the status bar, or press the menu key or
  Shift F10 on one of its items, and uncheck an item to hide it; check it to show it again. Your
  choice is kept on this machine. purlis's own items and an extension's are on the bar by the
  same rules: left or right, highest priority first (#2913).
- **A theme colour for warnings that ask for care**: `wash.warning`, the amber wash the
  waiting pill stands on, in every built-in appearance (#2913).
- **Themes reach panels, sections, empty states and status items.** The parts manifest is at
  version 4, with the `panel`, `panel-section`, `empty-state` and `status-item` families
  (#2913).
- **Focus on a repo's own folder.** A clone's menu has Focus on repo, which narrows the explorer to
  the clone as Focus on branch does: the branch it has checked out and how far that is from its
  upstream, the chats working in it, and its files. It has no Merge or Done, which act on a
  branch folder purlis cut (#1152).
- **An asking chat and its persona chats can talk while a task runs.** `purlis dispatch tell
  <chat> "<text>"` sends a follow-up to a task that is still working, which reads it on its next
  turn; one to a task that has finished is refused with its state. A task sends a progress note
  with `purlis dispatch note "<text>"`, and asks a question with `purlis dispatch ask
  "<question>"`, which holds until the asking chat runs `purlis dispatch answer <chat>
  "<text>"`. Every message arrives quoted as data from the other chat, and none is typed into a
  chat. Messages pass only between a chat and the tasks it dispatched itself, ten a minute for
  one pair unless the project's `messages-per-minute` limit says otherwise (#1442).
- **No chat can answer a question a task put to you.** A task that needs you asks in its own
  tab, and `purlis dispatch answer` answers only a question the task asked its asking chat
  (#1442).
- **A report says when you stepped in.** If you typed in a task's chat while it worked, its
  report carries "The operator stepped in" and nothing of what you typed. Picking an option of
  a prompt the task showed you does not count; words do (#1442).
- **A GitLab repo with merge trains joins its train.** Saving a merge request on a repo with
  merge trains adds it to the target branch's train, and the save says so (#805). From GitLab
  19.1 it joins through GitLab's auto-merge. On an older GitLab, or one that does not say its
  version, it joins through GitLab's merge trains API, never through the merge call, which
  merged past the train before 19.1. Where that API is missing or will not take the merge
  request, nothing is merged and the merge request stays open for a person, with the reason.
- **A request budget per forge account.** Every request purlis sends as a forge account is
  counted as its forge counts it (GitHub does not count a `304`, GitLab does), background refreshes
  wait once the account's 1,000 requests for the hour are spent, polling is conditional and paced
  by focus, stops while every window is hidden and backs off below a fifth of the forge's own
  limit, and `purlis doctor` shows each account's budget and its use (FW-4, #731).
- **Get a project from your forge by its URL.** Paste a project's HTTPS or SSH URL on the
  welcome's **Get a project from your forge** page, and purlis clones it into
  `~/Projects/<name>`, or into the place you picked last with **Choose a folder…**. The clone
  shows its progress and can be cancelled. A cancelled or failed clone leaves nothing behind,
  and a bad URL, a missing project and no access each say why, with **Retry**. The project then
  opens through the usual trust question. A private project is cloned with your own git sign-in
  on this machine: your credential helper for HTTPS, or your SSH key (#1815).
- **`gh` and `glab` on a runner.** A chat on a runner of purlis's own image can run both. A persona's
  declared tool whose program a pool's own image does not have now says so, naming the program and the
  image, instead of a bare `command not found` (#4354).
- **A missing git identity is a Notice you can fix where it stands.** When the doctor finds
  git's `user.name` or `user.email` unset, the project's window says so under the strip, with
  Fix. Fix opens the same name-and-email form as the Doctor row: a key already set is shown
  locked, a refusal is shown under its field, and the Notice goes once the doctor checks again
  and finds the identity set. Dismiss lasts until the identity is set, and the Notice shows
  again if it goes missing later (#1250).
- **Git's network calls are in the network log.** A fetch, push or remote listing purlis starts
  is listed with its host, the git operation and whether git finished it. The repo's path, a
  ref and a credential are never listed (#1022).
- **A project that has moved or gone offers Locate… and Forget.** The window's note about a
  project it could not reopen, and the opener's line about a recent project that is gone, now
  have two buttons. Forget takes the project off this machine, so it no longer comes back at
  every launch. Locate… asks for the folder it is in now, checks there is a project there, and
  opens it in the project's old place, with its pins and tab. The project is asked about again,
  as at a first open. Neither happens on its own, because a disk that is unplugged may come back
  (NO-5, #1237).
- **Grade a draft before you accept it.** A draft's page in the Skill studio grades what Accept
  would write against the current version, and shows the score beside Accept, which no grade ever
  blocks (SK-17, #2780).
- **Grade a skill from a terminal.** `purlis skill grade <name> --run` runs a grade in the window
  that has the project open, with the same plan and caps as pressing Grade. It asks before it
  spends (`--yes` skips the question for a script), follows the grade and prints the scorecard.
  Ctrl-C stops it. A chat cannot run it (SK-61, #3241).
- **Grade after each edit, if you turn it on** (SK-58, #3238). It is off for every skill. On a
  skill's Grades tab, _Grade after each edit_ has a _Turn on…_ button, which opens a plan that says
  what each edit runs and may cost and starts nothing; once you press _Turn on grading after each
  edit_ there, each edit you save in the Skill studio's editor grades the skill ten seconds after
  your last save, on the profile and model you picked and within the chats and dollar limit you accepted. A
  grade that would run more or cost more starts nothing and asks you again. Edits from the
  terminal or a chat never grade.
- **Grey tiers held on every ground.** A theme draws words in four tiers, `text.primary`,
  `text.secondary`, `text.muted` and the new `text.quiet`, and marks and disabled words in the
  new `text.faint`. The theme check measures every text tier at 4.5:1 and faint at 3:1 on every
  ground a part draws them on. Line numbers, placeholders, counts, paths and group labels take
  quiet; a tab's ×, separators, the pin and tree chevrons take faint. Purlis draws quiet in
  `#91909d` and faint in `#74727f`; Purlis Classic looks as it did. A theme over Purlis Classic
  that names `text.muted` and not the new tiers draws them in its muted; one over a theme with
  tiers of its own keeps them (#2902).
- **Making a 1Password vault asks how it signs in, tests it, and keeps the token in the
  Keychain.** *New vault* with 1Password chosen is a short set-up: a service-account token
