  pasted once, or the 1Password app on this machine with the account or sign-in address
  chosen; the 1Password vault picked from the ones that sign-in can see; a test that reads
  item names only; then one step that registers the vault and stores the token. No shell
  export and no restart. A token used by several vaults can be ticked for the others, each
  shown with what would be pinned for it. A vault's tab has *Change how this vault signs in*,
  which also converts a vault bound to an environment variable. From a terminal:
  `purlis vault add <name> --provider 1password --op-vault <NAME> --token-stdin` (#1527).
- **Guided steps from the welcome to an open project, picked up where you left off.** The
  welcome now walks you through setting up, one step at a time, and says where you are ("Step 2
  of 4"): the welcome, signing in when you choose to, creating, getting or opening a project,
  installing git when this machine has none, and picking your harness, before the project
  opens. Pick your harness shows the Set up a harness rows for the new project: what is
  installed, Install for what is not, and a word that each harness asks for its own sign-in.
  The sign-in and the harness steps have **Skip for now**, and every step can be done from the
  keyboard. If you quit in the middle, the next launch opens at the same step. Your place is
  kept on this machine only, in `onboarding.json` beside the machine store, and nothing secret
  is ever in it. After the first time through, the harness step comes back only while no
  harness is installed (#1817).
- **Hand several files to a chat at once.** In the explorer's *Files*, pick rows with Cmd or Ctrl
  and a click, a range with Shift and a click, or from the keyboard with Shift and the arrows.
  *Add to a chat's context* under the tree types them all into the chat you pick as one paste,
  never sent. Esc or *Clear* lets the picks go. The one-row *Add to a chat's context* on a row's
  menu works as before (#1151).
- **A handoff is announced where you'll see it.** When another chat hands work to a workspace, a
  card hangs from that workspace's chip, `<chat> arrived from <asking chat>`, with Go to it. The
  card never takes the keyboard, and hiding it leaves a dot on the chip. With no chip for that
  workspace, it's listed in the Notices centre. The Inbox gets an Update, which the ✋ doesn't
  count, and the chat's sidebar row says "new" until you've looked at it (#4759).
- **A task that can't report asks is announced the same way.** A task dispatched on a harness
  that doesn't tell purlis when it's waiting, or on a program purlis has no adapter for, can't
  say when it needs you, so it gets the same card and Update. Its
  row keeps the faint hand, and the chat that asked for it is told you must look at it yourself
  (#4759).
- **What each harness can do here.** A chat's header names the product it runs; pressing it
  opens that harness's card in a tab, *What Codex can do here*: a row for each thing purlis
  does with a chat, yes, no with the reason, or not declared, read off the harness's declaration
  and the adapter purlis ships for it. The new-chat picker shows the picked harness's card, and
  a control that is off because a harness lacks something, such as a Curate row or a first task
  run, says the card's line for it (HP-19, #677).
- **A harness's card from the palette.** ⌘K lists *What Codex can do here* (and so on) for each
  harness the project has, and opens its card in a tab with no chat on it open (#1134).
- **Run a harness purlis does not ship, from one file.** A project declares a terminal
  harness in `harnesses/<name>.toml`: its program, how it starts and resumes a session, and
  what it can and cannot report. It appears in the new-chat picker under its own name, asks
  you once on this machine before its program first runs, showing every word it will run, and
  again after the file changes, and runs in its terminal. `purlis harness show <name>` prints
  any harness's declaration, including the three purlis ships (FD-14, #654).
- **Your Claude Code, Codex and opencode folders are now profiles, with nothing to do.** When
  purlis starts after the upgrade, each harness folder this Mac already uses becomes a profile in
  place, named after its harness (*Claude Code (this Mac)*): the same folder, so the same sign-in,
  settings and conversations. Nothing is copied or moved, nothing in the folder is changed, and
  you are not asked to sign in again. Every chat resumes its own conversation, and profiles in a
  project's `charter.local.toml` work as before. `purlis profile list` shows each adopted profile
  with its folder (#2033).
- **Harnesses have icons** (#2922). Claude Code, opencode and Codex are drawn with glyphs
  purlis draws (a spark, braces and a terminal), never a vendor's mark, beside a profile's name
  in Settings, and on its card in Start a chat once that card draws it. A profile can name its
  icon in `purlis.local.toml`: `icon = "spark"` for a glyph, or `icon = "mine.svg"` for an SVG of
  your own in purlis's `icons` folder in your config home. A profile with no icon shows its
  harness's monogram. The glyphs are part of the theme's icon set, so an icon pack can redraw
  them under `glyphs`.
- **A theme can restyle the Needs-you count on the activity bars.** The new `needs-you.count` and
  `needs-you.count-text` colours draw it, and default to the needs-you colours, so no theme changes
  until it sets them. The theme check holds the words to 4.5:1 on the fill, the fill to 3:1 on each
  bar ground, and the fill apart from a plain count (#3098).
- **Devices: each pool's hours this week.** The use table under the devices has an Hours this
  week column: how long each pool's runners ran since Monday 00:00 in this machine's time, its
  removed runners included. purlis keeps when each runner started and stopped, at Docker's own
  times, in `runner-hours.jsonl` beside `runners.json`, two weeks at most (#3492).
- **Improve a skill from its runs** (#2780). A skill's More menu offers Improve from runs…, which
  opens a chat with its request typed and not sent. The chat reads the skill, its recent runs and
  grades, and what it writes comes back as a draft for you to accept or discard: nothing changes in
  the skill until you accept it.
- **`--in worktree:<repo>` gives a task a branch of its own from a workspace whose clones sit in
  subfolders.** A chat in a workspace's own folder used to be refused `--in worktree`, so its
  tasks shared one checkout. Now `--in worktree` uses the workspace's clone where it holds one.
  Where it holds several, the refusal names them, and `--in worktree:<repo>` (the `dispatch`
  tool's `in: worktree:<repo>`) picks one. The task's branch folder is cut the way `purlis
  worktree add` cuts one, from the remote's default branch as the clone last synced it, and is
  claimed by the task. The task
  then commits, updates and pushes with `purlis worktree commit`, `update` and `push`. The "no
  file locks between tasks" warning names this way out, and a Claude Code chat runs a dispatch
  line that starts with `--in` without asking (#3903).
- **The Inbox lists updates after what waits on you.** A task that finished or failed, a doctor
  finding, a chat that came back, a sandbox block that asks nothing, a dispatch refused while
  you were away and a Smart close that stopped each become an update, newest first, with
  Dismiss, and Go to chat where it is about one. Mark all read and Dismiss all act on updates
  only; nothing that waits on you is ever answered in bulk. Updates are kept for a day on this
  machine, in purlis's data home and never in a project, so a relaunch keeps them (#1693).
- **Install all of a skill source's skills in one review** (Skill studio preview, #4024). A
  source's page offers Install all…: every skill not installed from it yet is ticked, to untick
  and narrow, and those ticked go through one review, land at one level chosen at its top, and
  install together as one commit, all or nothing. Each skill's risky items are on its box, and
  a skill can be left out from the review itself. `purlis skill install <source> --all` does the
  same in the terminal, asking once; `--yes` skips the question. A set larger than one read of
  the source says so and offers to install it in two parts.
- First run's Create a project can start a project from a template when it has only a name.
- **Stop all tasks.** A session's row menu and its tab menu have it beside Stop with
  everything below it, and its tab's task menu has it as the last line of "End a task". It
  asks once, naming how many tasks it ends, stops every task at work below the session as Stop
  and get its report does, and keeps the session running. The session is woken once, when the
  last of them has ended, not once per task (#1498).
- **A limit is shown where it binds.** A session's tab menu ends with `4 of 6 running`. A
  session whose dispatch was refused for a limit says which one under its row (`at its task
  limit (6)`, or its chain's, or a persona's across the project), with a link to Settings ›
  Project › Dispatch, until a slot frees (#1498). A limit other than its own running one is
  said on the tab menu's footer too, and a dispatch into another workspace refused at that
  workspace's limit names it and keeps its line until a slot frees there (#1540).
- **A card row for side views' lists.** The list family draws a row as a small card: its name,
  its tag, Use and ⋯ on its first line, two lines of description or the reason in its place, and
  one fix under it, for the sidebar Skills view (#3669).
- **List groups that fold, and a run of rows folded to one quiet line.** A list's group name
  folds its rows from the keyboard and the pointer, with its count and a waiting tone, and a run
  of rows (the built-in skills) folds into one line that unfolds in place (#3670).
- **A folder a chat's sandbox refused a write in waits in the Inbox.** It offers Allow for this
  chat, Allow for you on this machine and Keep blocked, as its Notice does, and is counted on the
  ✋ with the other asks (#1700).
- **A chat can make your theme** (#2333). Ask any chat for a theme, or use **Create a theme** in a
  workspace's or the plane's Curate menu, or **New theme** and **Edit with a chat** in Settings ›
  Theme. purlis's theme skill builds it from a brand colour, an image, a Figma frame, an
  imported theme or another theme. The chat works on a theme draft that the window draws live,
  and checks it until the check is clean, or tells you which warnings are left and why. You keep
  or revert it from the draft's strip. Each of these opens the chat with its prompt typed, ready
  for you to read and send.
- **Merge… and Discard branch… from a finished task's row.** A task that worked on a branch of its
  own has both on its row's menu in the chats list, and its row on the Dispatches tab has Merge…
  beside Discard once it has ended. Each asks the task's Changes tab's own question first, and a
  merge purlis would refuse is said instead (#1534).
- **Move a chat to a pool's runner and back.** A chat's tab offers *Move chat … to pool …* and,
  on a runner, *Move chat … here*. The move is prepared while the chat keeps working and happens
  at its next pause between turns, never mid-turn: its branch, uncommitted work and conversation
  go with it, and its workspace's chats run there from then on. A move that fails leaves the chat
  where it was and says why. Claude Code chats move today (#2048).
- **Move a memory to the scope it belongs to.** A memory's tab has *Move to* and a *Move*
  button, and the command line has `purlis workspace move-memory <slug> --to-…` and
  `purlis persona move-memory <name> <slug> --to-…` (`--to-workspace`, `--to-persona` or
  `--to-shared`). The file moves whole, with its title and date; nothing is copied, and a
  target that already holds a memory of that name is refused (KN-3, #715).
- **Move a memory from its row's menu and the palette.** A memory's row has a "Move to ▸"
  submenu with each of the project's other stores, and the palette lists one *Move memory to …*
  row per store. It is the memory tab's Move, with the same Undo, and a row into a persona's or
  the shared store says, as the tab does, that those are published with the project (#1190).
- **Move a view from the palette.** Each view but the Inbox has a palette row that moves it to
  its half of the Panel or back to its sidebar, as its icon's menu does. A moved view keeps where
  it was scrolled, and the rows that put a region away name the views that are there now
  (#1752).
- **A narrow window folds panes to rails.** When a split can't give each side about 40 columns
  by 8 rows, the side without the focus folds to a rail beside the other, or a bar above or below
  it. Each folded pane shows its icon, its notices count and ✋ while it asks, and a press opens
  it. The layout comes back when there's room, and the sidebar and the Explorer stay where they
  were. Split right and Split down grey out with their reason where a half would be too small
  (#4766).
- **Needs you in the Skill studio lists problems in the project's own skills.** What the built-in
  lints say of a project, workspace or persona skill a chat gets is a problem in a skill there,
  and its fix, *Open its text*, opens the skill's Text tab in Edit. A new lint says when a skill's
  steps name a `scripts/<path>` its folder does not have (#3780).
- **`purlis doctor` says an administrator's local-port setting.** Where managed Claude Code
  settings turn `allowLocalBinding` on, which purlis's own setting does not outrank, the new
  `sandbox local ports` row names the file (#1699).
- **Two ways to say no to a dispatch, and "any persona" as a grant you set yourself.** The
  Notice that asks whether one persona may dispatch to another has a fifth answer, **Never for
  this pair**: it is kept for you on this machine, and from then on no chat of that persona is
  asked or allowed to dispatch to that persona, whatever the project grants, until you lift
  it. **Keep blocked** now holds for that chat's life: the same chat asking again is told at
  once that you said no, and you are not asked a second time; a new chat is asked. A grant can
  also be "any persona", for you on this machine or for everyone in the project
  (`steward = ["*"]` under `[dispatch.grants]`), which covers personas added later. It is set
  only on purpose, never by answering a question. Settings › Project › Dispatch lists the
  pairs you said never to, each with **Lift** (#1503).
- **One shape for every harness's ask.** A permission request from Claude Code, Codex, opencode
  or an ACP agent is read into the same ask: what it would do, the options in the harness's own
  words, who may answer, a deadline below the hook's timeout, a risk class, a one-line summary
  with credentials masked, and whether it elicits a secret. When two clients answer one ask, the
  first answer applies and the other hears "answered elsewhere"; a late, replaced or withdrawn
  ask refuses its answer and says why. Answering from the inbox builds on this (HP-5, #671).
- **Notices that need a decision.** A Notice has a third tone, attention, for what needs the
  person to choose when nothing failed (a change to review, a draft out of date): its own colour
  in every theme and appearance, a question mark in a circle and "Needs a decision" for screen readers.
  Trouble stays for real failures (#3678).
- **One form for Shared and Local.** At the Project level of the Settings tab, every value that
  either file may hold has a "Shared / Only on this machine" choice: pick the other and press
  Move to take it out of one file and put it in the other, both files or neither. A value
  this machine sets over the team's shows an "Overrides charter.toml" badge and what the team's
  file has. Every value says which level and file it comes from, and a Reset takes it out of
  that file so the value beneath shows through (with Undo). Profiles, the environment passed
  to chats and the default profile stay this machine's; the sandbox is never moved or reset
  (SE-18, #1168).
- **A task's question names its whole path, and one question covers tasks hitting the same
  block.** What a task asks of you is on its session's tab, named by the path purlis recorded
  when it started the task, each name quoted: `“deep” (a task of “steward 4” › “talk”)`.
  When several tasks of one session are blocked on the same host, or on writing the same
  folder, one Notice asks once ("3 tasks want to reach registry.npmjs.org"), lists each task, and its one answer applies to
  each of them: **Allow for these tasks** gives each task its own grant, never the session
  that asked them, **Always allow…** keeps one grant for every chat here, and **Keep blocked**
  answers each. Every task allowed restarts on its conversation once its turn ends. A task
  blocked after the question was shown joins it visibly, and a press just after a question
  appears or changes does nothing (#1508).
- **One table of who may dispatch to whom.** Settings › Project › Dispatch now lists every
  persona and, under it, each persona its chats may dispatch to, with every grant that covers
  the pair and where it comes from: one chat, you on this machine, or the project. Each source
  has its own action. **Revoke** takes back a chat's grant or yours. A project grant offers
  **Remove for everyone**, which changes the project's committed file and says so first, and
  **Not on my machine**, which stops following it here and leaves the file to your team. A
  teammate's grant you have not accepted is shown as waiting, with **Accept**. "Any persona"
  is set and cleared here, per persona, and nowhere else. The pairs you said never to are rows
  with **Lift**, and a pair kept blocked for one chat is shown with that chat. Every press
  asks first and says what it will do. Taking a grant back stops new dispatches only: tasks
  already running are left as they are (#1504).
- **Open each change of a file in your editor.** A file's *What changed* tab offers *Open in your
  editor at line N* beside each change's *Open at line N*, so your editor opens at that change
  rather than at the first one (#1043).
- **Open a file in your editor at the line you are reading.** A file shown in the light editor
  has *Open in your editor at line N*, for the line the cursor is on. Choose your editor in
  Settings: VS Code, Zed or a JetBrains IDE, through their own links, or `$VISUAL` /
  `$EDITOR`, started with `+line` and the file and never through a shell. Only a file the light
  editor would open is handed on (RC-20, #709).
- **Open an unreadable extension record in your editor.** When purlis cannot read this
  machine's extension record, the Extensions dialog's line now has Open in your editor beside
  Read again (#1296).
- **A sandbox block in an opencode chat raises a Notice too.** When a shell command an opencode
  chat ran fails because its sandbox refused it, the chat's tab offers Allow for this chat,
  Always allow and Keep blocked, and the block is counted in `purlis doctor`. opencode hands
  back a command's output and errors as one stream, so purlis reads the whole of a failed
  command's output, not only its errors as for Claude Code. Because of that, an opencode Notice
  pre-fills a host or folder only from the sandbox's own report, and otherwise asks you to type
  it (#1353).
- **The cluster operator's image carries build provenance and an SBOM.** As the runner image
  does, each published operator image now has SLSA build provenance on its index and a
  CycloneDX SBOM of each architecture's image, both verified before `main` moves. See
  `docs/cluster-operator.md` for the `gh attestation verify` commands.
- **The cluster operator can mint a GitHub App token for a vouched runner.** On a Pool opted in to
  minting, a runner proves its link key and gets a token covering only the repos on both its Pool
  and its Claim. The operator asks the cluster before each mint whether the requester may still use
  the Pool, and logs every mint and refusal. No chat uses this yet (#4206).
- **Outcome evals can use files that aren't text** (Skill studio preview, #4230). An eval's PDF or image is staged into its chat's folder, and its judge gets the files of that kind the chat left, each up to 1 MiB. The plan names any file purlis can't check for hidden characters.
- **A pane can show nothing.** An empty pane says how many chats run in its workspace and offers
  New chat, and it comes back after a restart, in its place in the split. A tab whose only pane
  held an unsaved new memory comes back as an empty tab rather than not at all (#4755).
- **Find past tasks by workspace and by date.** The Dispatches tab now narrows by the workspace
  a task worked in (or the project root) and by when it started: today, the past 7 days, or
  earlier. Opened from a workspace, it starts narrowed to that workspace, and _Every workspace_
  widens it. A task whose chat has closed is listed with its report for as long as this machine
  keeps its record (#1510).
- **`purlis persona lint` checks the skills a persona names** (Skill studio preview, #2934). Each
  entry of a persona's `skills:` list is read as a chat's start reads it, and lint warns, with the
  fix, of one that names nothing, one written with the old `charter:` prefix, a built-in skill
  purlis has none of, and a plugin skill or skill name that no skill the persona's chats reach and
  no harness on this machine has. Without the preview, lint says the line is read only with it on,
  where it used to say `skills:` was no longer read.
- **A persona carries the hosts its chats reach.** `[sandbox.personas.<persona>] hosts` in the
  project's `charter.toml` lists hosts, private addresses and ports included
  (`10.100.39.145:6443` for a cluster over a VPN), that a chat you start as that persona can
  reach, as can a chat on no persona when it is the project's default persona. Because anyone
  who can change the project's settings can change that list, a persona's hosts reach nothing on
  your machine until you allow them there: the project view shows each persona's hosts with
  **Allow** and **Not now**, and Settings › Sandbox has the same Allow. Your Allow is for exactly
  the list you were shown, and for whether the persona is the default: if either changes, its
  chats reach none of the list until you allow it again, and Settings › Sandbox › Granted lists
  the old Allow as waiting, with Revoke. Allowed hosts reach chats started after the Allow; a
  running chat takes them when it restarts. A chat on another persona doesn't reach them. A chat
  that another chat opened by a handoff runs with the asking chat's grants, and a chat resumed
  from a session record as a persona wider than the default runs with the default's, until you
  press **Allow** on its tab; **Restart now** then starts it again, resuming its conversation,
  once its turn ends. A handoff or a Resume never widens what a chat reaches. Each host is
  checked as the project's own hosts are (a private address only as one exact address and
  port), a chat can't write the list, and policy can forbid persona hosts (#1362).
- **The new-chat picker shows each persona's one-line description** (`agent-description`, else
  `description`) on its row (#1460).
- **The persona mark picker takes any colour as `#rrggbb`**, typed under the palette's swatches
  (#1454).
- **`purlis persona approve-mcp`** approves the MCP servers of a persona that take a
  credential from its vault: it shows the line each would run and asks, on a terminal.
  `--persona` narrows it to one, `--yes` approves without asking, `--dry-run` records nothing.
  It is refused inside a chat (#1451).
- **Pick a project from your repos.** Signed in to GitHub or GitLab in purlis, the welcome's
  **Get a project from your forge** page lists the repos you and your organisations or groups
  can reach, on every account you signed in to, with purlis projects first and marked. Search
  it by name or owner, and press a repo to clone it and open it the same way a pasted URL is.
  A forge you have not signed in to says so, with **Sign in…** on the page itself, and the URL
  box is always there. purlis finds a project by reading the top-level file names of up to 50
  repos per account, inside its request budget, and clones nothing until you pick (#1818).
- **Pick the file icons in Settings.** Appearance, at the Project and the Workspace level, has an
  *Icons* list: purlis's own icons and every icon theme an extension approved on this machine
  contributes. A pick that cannot be drawn stays shown, with the reason purlis's own icons are
  drawn instead (#1145).
- **Search results show file icons.** Each file in the Search tab is drawn with its project's
  icon theme, as the file trees draw it (#1145).
- **The Extensions dialog says what an icon theme got wrong.** A contributed icon theme with a
  path that is not path data, a colour that is not an icon token, or a name mapped to no symbol
  is listed on its extension's row, at most three complaints at a time (#1145).
- **Pin a chat's browser, hand it to another chat, and see where browsers were at quit.** From a
  browser's row in the Chats list or the command palette, Pin keeps a chat's browser running
  after its chat closes; it is then listed under Pinned browsers by what its chat was called,
  and runs until you stop it, Stop all ends it, or purlis quits. A pinned browser no chat uses
  can be handed to an open chat, whose browser tools use it from their next call; one signed in
  with a login goes only to a chat that may log in with that login now. When purlis quits, the
  next start says where the project's browsers were, each address a button, and loads nothing by
  itself (#2022).
- **Place a pane with the keys or single presses, wherever a drag could put it.** Press a pane's
  grip, the first control in its head, or press Enter or Space on it, or ⌘⇧M (Ctrl+Shift+M off a
  Mac), to pick the pane up. ⌘⇧M on a chat's row in the sidebar or on a tab picks that up
  instead, and so does Place… on a chat's menu, on a tab's right-click, or on a chat's row under
  the pointer. Every other pane then shows five targets, and the strip a New tab. Arrow keys
  choose a side, Tab goes to the next pane, Enter drops and Esc puts it back. Each target says
  what dropping there would do, or why it can't, and the result is drawn before the drop. A
  screen reader hears the pick-up, each target, the drop and a refusal. The drops follow the
  same rules as a drag, with the same Undo (#4764).
- **On the plane root's tab, Files lists the whole project's files.** Open a folder to read the
  next level, and a file to read it in a tab. What purlis keeps to itself is not listed or
  opened: the vaults and their keys, and its own records that no chat reads. A workspace's repo
  is one row that takes you to that workspace's tab, where its files are. What git ignores is
  hidden until *Show ignored files*, and never opens (#1916).
- **A pool can declare its price per hour, and Devices shows its money this week.** A Docker
  pool's row in `runners.json` takes `"pricePerHour": {"amount": "0.40", "currency": "EUR"}`.
  The Devices use table then has a Money this week column: the pool's hours this week times its
  price, worked exactly from the decimal it declares and shown in its currency, never converted.
  A pool that declares no price shows no money (#3491).
- **Record a profile on a pool from your terminal.** `purlis pool add-profile <pool> <profile>…`
  records what Pool setup's Sign-ins button records, with the same checks of the profiles, and
  sends nothing. See what this does on that step now shows it for the profiles you tick, followed by
  each sign-in, and the step picks up a profile recorded this way (#4718).
- **Pool setup sets up the agent's identity in its own step.** The Agent identity step uses the
  same flow as the Agent identity tab, so you never leave Pool setup to give the agent its own
  GitHub identity. An identity that is already there shows as done, with what it acts as and on
  how many repos. Repos on another forge host are told plainly, with the commands and the tool
  line to add by hand, in a vault of the agent's own. A tool still to allow on this machine opens
  Settings. The step can always be skipped. Try it proves the identity with a read-only token it
  revokes at once. It doesn't yet run `gh` or `git push` in the chat itself. With no repo in the
  project, Try it says gh and git push weren't checked, and the end reads "works, except for
  this" (#4490).
- Pool setup's Pool step has Options, with the runner image and limits and the recommended value marked, and See what this does, with the exact command its button runs. A team's own image is checked against the runner image contract before anything is made.
- `purlis pool add` adds a Docker pool from the command line, and Pool setup notices a pool you made that way.
- Pool setup's Sign-ins step lists your profiles with the ones in use ticked, shows each one's size against what the pool lets a profile send, raises that limit in place when one is over, and signs each in inside the step. It can be skipped and come back to.
- `purlis pool setup [name]` shows each step of Pool setup for a Docker pool: its state, what purlis found and what to do next, read fresh each time. `--json` prints the same.
- Pool setup: a guided tab, opened from the palette, that finds Docker, recommends it and makes a Docker pool step by step, with no terminal. The other steps show what purlis finds and what to do next for now. The add pool form stays until the whole Docker path is in.
- **Pool setup ends with Try it.** Its own button starts a real chat on the new pool and closes it
  once the chat's harness reports that it started. The last screen lists what passed, reads
  "works, except for this" where a step was skipped, and has one button that opens a chat on the
  pool. A chat that doesn't start says why and what to do next, with Go to Sign-ins or Try again
  right there (#4483).
- **Your profiles go with you to a pool's runner, and each is signed in there once.** Adding a
  Docker pool now ends with this machine's profiles, each kept on the pool's runner, with Sign in
  for each not signed in there yet. Sign in runs the harness's own sign-in on the runner from a
  shell tab; the runner keeps it, and nothing of this machine's sign-in is copied there. Your own
  Claude Code, Codex and opencode folders are the runner's own default folders there, so a runner
  you signed in before stays signed in. A chat started on a pool, a moved one too, starts
  silently on a profile signed in there; one that is not waits in the Inbox as *Profile <profile>
  on pool <pool>*, with *Sign in on pool <pool>*. Settings › Profiles says where each profile is
  signed in: this Mac, and each pool. For now this is for pools on this machine's own Docker, and
  for profiles signed in by a subscription (#2049).
- **`purlis profile list` shows the sign-in purlis can see each profile has**, or `unknown`. A
  harness declaration says which sign-in kinds its profiles support (subscription, API key,
  cloud, local), the folder variables it uses, whether its credentials can be kept from the
  commands it runs, and how a conversation is exported and resumed; Claude Code, Codex and
  opencode declare all four, and a project's `harnesses/<name>.toml` may too (#2031).
- **Add your project's own hosts, and your own, to a sandboxed chat's Internet access.**
  Settings › Sandbox lists the project's hosts with Add and Remove. They are kept in
  `charter.toml`, and every chat of everyone who opens the project reaches them with no
  approval. Settings › Sandbox › Your hosts holds hosts for this machine only, in
  `charter.local.toml`; one Settings did not add here waits for your Confirm. A host is a
  domain, `*.domain`, an IP address or any of them with `:port`, private addresses included
  (`10.100.39.145:6443` for a cluster over a VPN). Each is checked as you add it, and refused
  with the reason: this machine, link-local and cloud metadata addresses are never hosts, and a
  name is never reached at one of them, whatever it resolves to. Every harness reaches them:
  Claude Code through its own sandbox, and opencode and Codex through purlis's egress proxy.
  When a project's hosts change, each teammate sees one Notice naming what was added and taken
  away. A chat can never change either list (#1341). The first time a project with hosts is
  opened after this upgrade, each teammate sees one Notice listing them, the `[[forge]]` hosts
  the forge preset reaches included.
- **Start chat says when a workspace's chat is its first on a pool.** Before anything is sent, the
  Runs on row says that the workspace's code will be copied to that pool's runner, and that the
  chat's work comes back here when it ends (#4591).
- **Teammates are told when a project's Internet access presets change.** When the presets a
  project's settings turn on change, or its certificate checks, each teammate sees one Notice
  naming what was turned on and off, and what it widens past its hosts: Package registries also
  lets chats write the project's package caches, and certificate checks let the system fetch
  addresses a certificate names. "Got it" records what was shown, so a later change is told
  again; a change you make in Settings, a move between the shared and local files included, is
  not told back to you. A pull while the window is open is told then, for the presets and the
  project's hosts alike. A project on the default presets tells nothing (#1385, #1550).
- **A project can name the pool its chats run on.** Settings › Project › Runs on sets a default for
  this machine, and a workspace can follow it, stay on this machine or name its own pool. If the pool
  is gone, the chat doesn't start and purlis says why (#4536).
- **`sandbox.proposed-changes` in this machine's policy file.** `"off"` turns proposed changes
  off: a chat's change to purlis's own configuration (the project's manifest, a persona's
  `mcp.json` and `persona.md`, a `.claude/skills` file) is refused as before and never shown
  to you to apply. `"on"`, or no key, leaves them on. Any other value refuses the policy file.
  The window that shows a proposed change comes next (#1975).
- **A project that lives only on this machine says so, and publishes to GitHub or GitLab.** Its
  tab, and the Project level of its settings, read **This project lives only on this machine**
  when its folder is no repository yet or has no remote, with **Publish to GitHub or GitLab…**
  beside it. Publish asks what Create on a forge asks (the forge, the name, the owner, private
  unless you say public), then commits what is not committed yet, makes the repo with your
  purlis sign-in, scans the project's history for anything credential-shaped, pushes it through
  purlis's own credential helper and makes the repo the project's remote, which the push record
  holds for its saves. Each stage is shown as it runs. **Cancel**, or a stage that fails, takes
  back what the publish made: the repo, the remote it named, and the repository it started. A
  repo GitHub would not delete is kept, with a link to its settings, and **Retry** pushes into
  it (#1820). A project created on a forge now records its remote for its saves too.
- **Publish a skill, or export it** (Skill studio preview, #2781). `purlis skill publish` opens a draft pull or merge request on a skill source with the skill, the skills it refers to and a summary of their grades, after you review everything that would go and say yes at a terminal. `purlis skill export` writes a folder or zip that works outside purlis. Anything that looks like a secret stops both.
- **Publish or export a skill from the Skill studio** (Skill studio preview, #2781). A skill's "…" menu now has Publish to a source…, a review page of everything that would go with a button that opens a draft request, and Export…, which writes a zip or a folder.
- **Theme tokens for a plain control's edge and the filled primary.** `border.control` draws the
  edge of a secondary button, a field and a select; `accent.fill`, `accent.fill-hover`,
  `accent.fill-edge` and `accent.fill-text` draw the primary; `accent.wash` and `accent.text` draw a
  chosen activity button and words in the accent; `radius.control` is an md control's corner. A
  theme over Purlis Classic that leaves them out keeps drawing as it did: each follows the token it
  was drawn with before.
- **Purlis has a light high-contrast appearance.** Choose "light-high-contrast" as Purlis's
  appearance in Settings, or let Purlis follow the system: on a light system that asks for more
  contrast, Purlis now draws light high contrast instead of standard light. Its text, focus ring,
  borders and marks are at least as strong as in Purlis's dark high contrast (#4677).
- **Purlis light and Purlis high contrast are ready to use.** Choose either as Purlis's appearance
  in Settings, or have Purlis follow the system: it draws light on a light system and high contrast
  when the system asks for more contrast. With no choice made, Purlis stays dark (#2924).
- **A project marked by `purlis.toml` is found.** Ahead of the rename to purlis, a project is
  found by `purlis.toml` as well as `charter.toml`. This build opens it read-only, because some
  of its parts are still read only under the charter names. When a project holds something
  under both names, the doctor's *renamed leftovers* row names both. Keep both for now: the
  `rename-plane` fix will reconcile them (RN-1, #1254).
- **Try Purlis, the new theme, as a preview.** Settings › Theme has a Purlis card marked
  Preview, beside Purlis Classic: a dark appearance from the designer's foundation, a light one
  derived from it and a high-contrast dark, set in IBM Plex Sans and JetBrains Mono with Lucide's
  icons, all bundled with purlis. Purlis Classic stays the default (#2336). The theme id
  `purlis` now names the built-in theme, so a theme folder of your own named `purlis` is behind
  it: rename that folder to keep choosing it.
- **purlis removes a chat's finished branch folder for it when nothing would be lost.** In a
  chat, `purlis worktree remove <repo> <piece>` and the new `worktree_remove` tool are run by
  the app, without asking, for a branch folder of the chat's own workspace. The folder goes only
  when it holds no uncommitted change and no commit that no other branch reaches, or when its
  branch landed by a squash merge, here or on the remote. A folder holding files git ignores,
  such as a `.env`, is kept too. Otherwise the answer names what would be lost and nothing is
  removed. A folder another live chat holds is not removed for it, and a removal ends the
  folder's claim. `--force` stays the person's, from the window (#3879, #3969).
- **A sandboxed Claude Code chat starts on a runner.** `purlis serve` arms each chat it starts
  with purlis's plugin, found beside its binary, and purlis's git hooks, and hears each held
  project's hooks on the same channel, with the same checks, as the app's own session host. The
  runner image ships the plugin at `/usr/local/lib/purlis/plugin`, and the runner image
  contract asks for it (#2447).
- **The app starts its session host.** Opening purlis starts one session host for every open
  project, run by the app's own program so nothing new asks for the Keychain, and quitting ends
  it. It listens on a socket in a folder of your own under your runtime or temporary folder,
  admits the window, and refuses another user, a wrong credential, and the programs a chat
  starts. No chat runs in it yet. `purlis serve` runs the same host on a machine with no window
  (#1997).
- **`purlis theme import` and `purlis theme export`.** `import <file>` makes a theme folder from
  a VS Code colour theme, a base16 or base24 scheme, an iTerm2 colour preset, a Ghostty theme or
  a theme folder's zip, through a fixed mapping table per kind. It lists every key of the source
  no token takes, shows the new theme's check, and never replaces a theme folder without
  `--force`. `export <theme folder>` writes the folder as a zip that `import`, or unzip, gives
  back file for file. `purlis docs show themes` has the tables (#2334).
- **`purlis theme list` and `purlis theme check`.** `list` shows every theme available on this
  machine, with its appearances and where it comes from: built in, your own `theme.json`
  (`mine`), or an approved extension. `check <theme>` (an id, or the path of a theme file or
  folder) says why a theme is refused, what was left out of it, its contrast warnings in each
  appearance (each pair with its ratio, in every workspace tint) and its hard floors, as text or
  as `--json` for a chat, and exits 1 when the theme is refused. `purlis docs show themes` has
  the details (#2321).
- **An extension's theme says what is wrong with it.** Why purlis refused an approved
  extension's theme, or what it left out of one it draws, is shown on its row in Extensions
  instead of being dropped (#2321).
- **The `purlis-building-ui` skill.** An agent changing purlis's own window loads it for the
  component families, their parts and states, the prototype and accessibility rules, the stories
  and the checks that make UI work done (#2928).
- **purlis brings a sandboxed chat's clone, branch folder or project root up to date for
  it.** `purlis worktree update` now works in a workspace's clone as it did in a branch
  folder. It fetches, then fast-forwards or rebases, with `--continue` and `--abort` after a
  conflict. At the project root it runs the window's own Update for the chat. In a chat the
  app runs it without asking, from the command or the new `worktree_update` tool. It refuses
  uncommitted changes and any move that would overwrite a file that is not committed. A move
  that would write a file the chat's sandbox denies is still left to the person. The refusals
  that sent a chat's `git pull` to the person now name the command (#3831, #3862).
- **`purlis worktree prune` clears a workspace's finished branch folders.** It removes every
  folder that is finished, task folders and plain ones, in every repo or the one you name: no
  uncommitted changes, every commit on its base or squash-landed, its task ended, no open chat
  holding it, and no other folder linking into it. A folder that links into another goes first.
  Each removed folder's branch is deleted unless you pass `--keep-branches`, and `--dry-run`
  lists what would go and why each other folder stays. A chat can run it too (ADR 0110, #5168).
- **A chat can read what its task said and ran.** `purlis dispatch read <chat>` prints a task's
  last three messages and its last twenty shell commands with their exit codes, as its harness
  handed them to purlis, quoted as data with credential shapes masked. Only the chat that
  dispatched the task can read it, while it runs and after it ends. The whole conversation stays
  yours, in the task's tab (#1981).
- **Remove a repo the workspace names but this machine has not cloned.** Each row under *Not
  cloned here* in the explorer has *Remove…* beside *Clone*, and the row's menu (and the bottom
  bar's) has *Remove <repo> from workspace…* below the line. Settings › Workspace › Repos lists
  the same repos under *Not cloned here*, each with *Remove from workspace…*. Each one asks
  first, then takes only the repo's row out of `workspace.json`; nothing is deleted. A repo
  that is being cloned is not offered it, and a cloned repo still goes through the existing
  removal, which refuses work that is not pushed (#1228).
- **Rename a harness profile and what uses it in one go.** In Settings, a profile that this
  machine's own `[harness] default` names can now be renamed: Rename first says which settings
  would change with it, and *Rename everywhere* renames the profile and them in one write, so
  nothing is left half-renamed. Undo renames both back. A default in the project's shared file
  is every teammate's, so it still stops the rename, naming it (#1380).
- **Keychain items move to the purlis names, checked before they are used.** `rename-local` now
  copies each keyring vault's secrets and each stored 1Password identity token from its
  `charter/…` keychain item to a `purlis/…` one, reads every copy back, and only switches the
  vault or the identity to the new items once all of them read back the same. An item that is
  already under the purlis name is never taken on trust: when its value differs from the
  original, that vault stays on its old items and the run says so. The old items are kept, so
  `purlis migrate --undo` just reads them again, after first copying back any secret written
  since the switch. On macOS the app does the copy at launch, where reading its own items asks
  nothing, and `purlis migrate` in a terminal copies only the vaults the command wrote itself.
  1Password items keep their `charter-<vault>` titles (RN-6, #1264).
- **Local state moves to the purlis names, and can be put back.** At launch, the app moves this
  machine's config home, the session host's folder in it, the data home, and in each project it
  remembers, `charter.local.toml` and `.charter/`, to their purlis names. `purlis migrate` and
  `purlis doctor --fix rename-local` do the same from a terminal, and move the log folder too.
  Approvals, pins, the device id, the update channel and the kill switch come along. Every move is
  journalled. A move that fails leaves the old name in place, where it is still read. Nothing
  moves while any charter or purlis window, chat or terminal is running, and that includes
  anything named charter or purlis, such as a dev build: quit them all first, and the app tries
  again at its next launch. Git ignores the new names through the repository's own
  `info/exclude`, so no committed file changes. `purlis migrate --undo` puts every move back, and
  an undo that cannot finish says what is in the way and finishes when run again. Going back to an
  older build on the same machine needs the undo first (RN-5, #1263).
- **`charter doctor --fix rename-plane` moves a project to purlis's names in one commit.** It
  renames `charter.toml` to `purlis.toml` and `.charter-scan-allow.toml` to
  `.purlis-scan-allow.toml`, rewrites the managed blocks' markers, a committed `workspace.json`'s
  digest key, the harness variable in `.claude/settings.json`, and personas' `charter:` skill
  references, but never inside quoted code or in an image name such as
  `ghcr.io/acme/charter:v1`, and changes nothing else. Hook commands keep `charter`, which runs on every build. The project then requires the
  `purlis-names` feature, so a build without it opens the project read-only. It runs only when
  named, never from inside a chat, and refuses with uncommitted changes, outside git, or with a file under both names; a
  step that fails puts every file back (RN-7, #1265).
- **The consent rules are written under both names.** `init`, `reinit` and `rename-plane` write
  `purlis handoff`, `purlis report --yes` and `purlis … todo promote` ask rules beside the
  `charter` ones. Where the settings a chat runs under hold the `purlis` spelling at least as
  strictly as the `charter` one, the guard lets it through instead of refusing it; anywhere
  else it still refuses it.
- Reorder the status bar's items: drag an item along its end of the bar, or use Move left and Move
  right in the bar's menu from the keyboard. The order is remembered on this machine, including
  for items that aren't on the bar today.
- Reset order in the status bar's menu puts every item back in its shipped place. It shows only
  after you've moved an item, and what you hid stays hidden.
- **Resolve a save's conflict from the window.** Where a save stopped because the project's
  own commits and the remote's change the same lines, the Saving view offers _Resolve_: purlis
  replays the commits itself and stops on the conflict. Settle the files yourself or with
  _Resolve in a chat_, which starts a chat that only edits them, then press _Continue_. purlis
  checks no conflict marker is left, stages exactly those files, carries on and pushes. A
  binary file, or one a side deleted, is settled in a terminal. _Skip_ drops a commit that
  settling left empty, and _Abort_ puts the project back where it was.
- **Restart a task from its row in the Chats list.** A task with no tab of its own now has
  Restart chat on its row's menu, asked first on the row as its tab's menu asks. Why a restart
  was refused, or why it waits, is said on the row, so you need not open the task to read it
  (#1462).
- **Restart a chat to pick up changed sandbox settings.** A chat keeps the sandbox it started
  with, so a change in Settings › Sandbox used to reach a running chat only if you closed its
  tab and resumed it. A chat's tab menu now has **Restart chat**: its program ends and starts
  again on the same conversation, with the project's settings as they are now. Mid-turn the row
  reads **Restart chat … when this turn ends**, and the chat restarts then; while it restarts,
  its pane says so. A chat that reports no state restarts at once, and its row says that purlis
  cannot tell whether it is mid-turn. After a sandbox setting changes while chats are running, a
  Notice says how many keep the old sandbox until they restart, with **Restart them** and
  **Dismiss**; it appears once for each change, and not at all when no running chat is behind.
  It counts what settings decide (the hosts, what the presets widen, and the folders every chat
  may write), so revoking a folder in Settings › Sandbox › Granted raises it, and a clone or an
  install in the project does not. Settings › Sandbox now says that a change applies to a chat
  from its next start. A chat you started without the sandbox restarts in the sandbox, and its
  tab says so: that choice lasts for one start (#1428).
- **A chat on a pool's runner runs the harness version its profile pins.** The first chat on a
  pinned profile there downloads that version from the harness's own release, checks it against
  the digest its vendor publishes, and keeps it on the runner's volume. A version that cannot be
  checked is not installed, and the chat says why (#3446).
- **A profile's settings reach the pool's runner that keeps it.** Its instructions, agents,
  commands and other settings files go with each chat's start or move there, so a runner chat
  behaves as one on your machine. No sign-in and no file named like a credential is sent, and
  only to a pool shown to be your own (#3448).
- **Adding a pool ends by choosing which of your profiles sign in on it.** The project's
  default profile is ticked; Sign in N profiles signs each in on the pool's runner, one after
  another, in the same place, and Not now leaves each profile's line offering Sign in (#4048).
- **Move to runner waits for the chat's profile to sign in there.** Where the chat's profile is
  not signed in on that pool, the move notice shows the sign-in under it while the chat keeps
  working here, and the move goes ahead by itself once it is signed in. Cancel move keeps the chat
  here (#3477).
- **Code crosses to a pool's runner and back as git bundles** (#2046). Over the link to a
  runner, the desktop sends a chat's branch and a snapshot of its uncommitted work, and takes
  the runner's branches back as `refs/remotes/<pool>/<branch>`. Your own branches, work tree
  and index are never touched. A runner keeps each project it holds for you in
  `<data>/projects/<project id>`. It takes only the branches and snapshots it was sent, runs no
  hook, checks every object as it arrives, and holds no forge credential. Session protocol
  1.34.
- **Runners while you are away.** "While you were away" has a section for each runner your chats
  ran on: what finished there, what waits for you, and the branches ready to push, each a link.
  **Stop all reaches every runner** this machine keeps, names any it could not reach and tries it
  again, and the re-arm names the runners it re-arms with this machine before you press it. A
  Docker pool's runner left a day without a link from this desktop suspends itself and keeps its
  home, and starts again as purlis next links to it for a chat (#2051).
- **Choose where one chat runs as you start it.** Start chat has a Runs on row that says where
  the new chat runs and why (its workspace, its project, or this machine), and takes a pool or
  this machine for that start only, without changing a setting. When the pool is gone, stopped
  or not reached, nothing starts: it says why and offers Try again, Pool setup, or Run on this
  machine this once (#4536).
- **`purlis dispatch --pool <name>` and `--this-machine`** name where a task runs, before its
  workspace's and its project's own. When a chat names a place other than its workspace's, the
  task waits for your Approve, and the ask and any grant Notice say where it would run (#4536).
- **A sandbox block shows on the chat's tab, and `purlis doctor` counts blocks.** When a
  sandboxed chat's sandbox blocks a command, the chat's tab now shows a notice saying what was
  blocked: the operation and the kind of path or host, such as "a write to the project's own
  files". It never shows the path, the command or its output. If purlis itself was the program
  the sandbox blocked, the notice says it is a purlis bug and offers **Report…**. That shows a
  draft naming only the operation, the kind of path and the versions, and the app files it under
  your own `gh` login only when you press **File report**. Nothing is sent before that.
  `purlis doctor` has a new `sandbox blocks` row with a count per operation over the last 7 days
  (#1338).
- **`certificate-checks` under `[sandbox]`.** Set it to `true` to let Go tools such as `gh`
  verify certificates in a sandboxed chat on macOS. It also lets a chat reach hosts named inside
  a certificate, so it is off by default (#1337).
- **The Sandbox changed Notice says when this machine's policy is the cause.** A policy that
  requires the sandbox now lists each chat running without it, a chat its person started without
  the sandbox included, and says who set the policy and in which file. Such a chat's own tab says
  so too, with Restart this chat. purlis reads the policy file again every few seconds, so a
  policy that lands is told without the project's settings or its chats moving (#1431).
- **Codex chats run sandboxed on macOS.** In a project with `[sandbox]` `mode = "on"`, a Codex
  chat now starts inside the sandbox purlis writes, as an opencode chat does, instead of being
  refused (#1123).
  - **Codex's own sandbox is off inside it.** macOS applies one sandbox to a process, so Codex's
    own cannot run inside purlis's. purlis's holds what Codex's held, and what Codex's could
    not: a folder moved aside, changed and moved back, and a folder swapped for a link.
  - **A Codex home of the project's own.** A sandboxed project's Codex chats keep their Codex
    state in a home of their own, outside the project, seeded with your Codex login. They
    neither read nor write your own Codex home, so nothing they write in Codex's own state
    reaches a conversation you resume outside the sandbox. Files they write in their own
    folder, such as an instruction file, are still read by a later Codex started there.
  - **Writes.** The chat can write its own folder and a temp folder of its own. In the
    project's Codex home, only what a turn writes: its sessions, history, state, log and a
    refreshed login, and the memories, goals and queue Codex's own screen needs. So one
    sandboxed Codex chat can influence what a later sandboxed Codex chat of the same project
    loads, but never your own Codex state. It cannot write Codex's config, skills or
    plugins.
  - **Trust.** purlis marks each chat's folder untrusted for Codex, so Codex loads no
    project-local config, hooks or exec policies there and asks nothing, and it trusts exactly
    the hooks purlis arms, so purlis's own hooks run and no other does.
  - **Network.** Its traffic, Codex's own requests included, leaves through purlis's proxy,
    which carries only the hosts of the project's egress presets. Codex checks certificates
    against the system's authorities.
  - **Linux.** purlis cannot wrap Codex on Linux yet (#1040), so there such a chat is still
    refused, with a sentence that says so.
- **An administrator can forbid "on this machine, for every project".** The machine policy's
  `sandbox.allow-scopes` has a word for that scope, `machine`, beside `chat`, `you` and
  `project`. A policy that lists scopes and leaves it out removes it from every Notice and
  refuses an Allow at it, saying who set the policy; a policy with no `allow-scopes` key
  changes nothing. `once`, the scope of "Allow once", is a word of the list too, and a Notice
  names each scope a policy removed (#1927).
- **New projects run their chats sandboxed.** A project that `purlis init` or the app makes
  now has `[sandbox]` with `mode = "on"` in its `charter.toml`. Its sandboxed chats can reach
  model providers, your forges and package registries (SD-2, #1056).
  - **Existing projects.** A project made before this keeps running as it did. The first time
    you open it, a notice offers to turn the sandbox on. "Turn the sandbox on" adds the same
    block to `charter.toml`, and "Keep it off" changes nothing. The notice does not come back
    either way.
  - **One chat without the sandbox.** The new-chat picker has "start without the sandbox", for
    that one chat, with a box for your reason. The chat's tab says it runs without the
    sandbox. A relaunched or resumed chat does not inherit the choice: it starts sandboxed, or
    not at all where the sandbox cannot be applied (a Codex chat, or a program the sandbox
    will not bind). Only a new chat can start without the sandbox; continuing an opted-out
    chat's conversation without it is not offered yet (#1098). If the sandbox cannot be
    applied on this machine, the picker shows why, and its button says "Start without the
    sandbox".
  - **Installing what is missing.** On Linux, if bubblewrap or socat is missing, the picker
    shows your distribution's install command. "Type it in a shell tab" opens a shell at the
    project root with the command typed. It needs sudo, so you run it yourself.
  - **Programs the sandbox will not bind.** A profile whose program is anywhere a chat can
    write or is named by a relative path, or a Claude Code profile whose program does not
    answer as Claude Code, is refused in a sandboxed project; the picker says why before you
    start it. It checks a profile's program only once you have approved the profile.
  - **Codex.** purlis cannot keep a Codex chat inside its sandbox yet (#1123), so in a
    sandboxed project the picker says so and a new Codex chat starts only without the sandbox.
  - **Windows.** There is no sandbox on Windows yet (#565), so chats there start without it
    and their tabs say so.
  - **Recorded.** Each start without the sandbox is a `trust.sandbox.off` event in purlis's
    event log on this machine. The sandbox coming back on for that chat is `trust.sandbox.on`.
    The chat's session record says `sandbox: off`.
  - **How often.** `purlis doctor` and Project settings show how many new chats in the project
    started without the sandbox on this machine. The count is never sent anywhere.
- **opencode chats run sandboxed on macOS.** In a project with `[sandbox]` `mode = "on"`, an
  opencode chat now starts instead of being refused. opencode has no sandbox of its own, so
  purlis runs the whole harness inside a profile it writes, which starts from "deny
  everything".
  - **Writes.** The chat can write its own directory and a temp directory of its own. Of
    opencode's own files, it can write only what a turn writes: its sessions and log. Its state
    is kept in the chat's own temp directory.
    It cannot write opencode's credentials, plugins or packages.
  - **Snapshots.** A sandboxed opencode chat makes no snapshots (#1075).
  - **Network.** Its traffic leaves through a proxy purlis runs for that chat, including
    opencode's own requests to its model provider. The proxy carries only the hosts of the
    project's egress presets.
  - **Keychain.** The profile also keeps the chat away from the keychain, so a project with a
    keyring vault can run sandboxed opencode chats.
  - **Hook reports.** A report purlis's hooks could not hand to the app is shown in the chat's
    window, not dropped.
  - **Linux.** purlis cannot wrap opencode on Linux yet (#1040), so there such a chat is still
    refused, with a sentence that says so (SD-2, #695).
- **`purlis secret list` with no vault lists the vaults.** It shows what `purlis vault list`
  shows, and says how to list one vault's keys. Before, it stopped with a usage error (#1345).
- **`purlis doctor` names vaults whose file is outside the project or gone.** A new `vault files`
  row lists each plain-file vault whose registered file is outside the project. It warns when a
  file is missing, gone or in a temp directory: each one still gets a deny rule in every
  sandboxed chat. The row names vaults and paths, never a value, and says how to remove a
  leftover (#1345).
- **Saving a theme folder repaints the window** (#2324). Edit a theme in use — your own, the
  project's or a workspace's — and the window draws it as soon as you save, with no new window.
  A burst of saves is one repaint. A save that is not a theme draws Purlis, with a Notice that
  says what is wrong, until it is fixed. A project's font file that changed since you approved
  the project is drawn once you approve it again, and a Notice says so.
- **An extension that brings only themes needs no approval** (#2324, ADR 0098). Installing one
  asks nothing, editing its themes asks nothing, and the Extensions list says it is themes only.
  An extension with commands, panels, views or a program is approved as before.
- **Turn screen-reader mode on or off from the palette, and it is kept.** The command palette
  has *Turn screen-reader mode on* (or *off*, when it is on), which switches every chat's
  terminal at once. The window's layout file keeps the choice as `screenReader`, so the next
  launch starts with it. *Use the default layout* leaves the mode as it is (#629).
- **⌘⇧F searches the content of your files** (Ctrl+Shift+F off a Mac, outside a chat). It opens a
  Search tab on the branch picked in the explorer, or the workspace or project in front, and you
  can widen it to the workspace, the project, or every open project. Literal or regular
  expression, match case and whole word. Hits stream in grouped by project, branch and file,
  with the matching lines and a count per file; a large result stops at a page and _Show more_
  carries on, and a new query stops the one before. ↓ steps from the box into the hits, ↑/↓ move
  through them, and Enter opens the hit in its branch's file tab at its line. The search never
  looks inside what git ignores, links, vaults, files named like a credential, binary files or
  files past the preview's 2 MiB. A file with a line longer than 256 KiB is listed as not
  searched. Search tabs are not reopened at the next launch (FM-8, #1111).
- **Search in files from the palette.** ⌘K lists *Search in files*, with its key (⌘⇧F, or
  Ctrl+Shift+F) beside it, and opens the same Search tab the key does, as narrow as where you
  are: the branch you picked, else the workspace in front, else the project (#1137).
- Any chat can ask you for a credential it lacks, declared or not, with the `secret_ask` tool
  or `purlis secret ask <KEY> --purpose "<what for>"`, and every chat is told to at its start
  instead of asking you to paste one. The ask shows the chat's purpose in its own words, says
  when the persona does not declare the key, and goes to the persona's vault unless the chat
  names another. A key the vault holds already answers at once. The chat hears only filled
  (under the name you stored it as) or declined, never the value. The tool doesn't stop on
  Claude Code's permission prompt first, since you answer the ask in the window.
- **A chat can ask you to replace a value that doesn't work.** When a key it uses is refused (a
  401, an expired token), the chat asks again with its reason (`purlis secret ask <KEY>
  --replace "<why>"`, or the `secret_ask` tool), and the window shows its words as the chat's.
  Type a new value, or pick an entry you keep: for a Linked entry the ask names the entry it
  reads, a new value goes there, and a pick re-points the link (#5075).
- **A Linked entry whose entry is gone asks you, instead of failing.** When a chat's command, a
  browser login or a profile reads a key that links to an entry you have since deleted or
  renamed, purlis asks you in the window, naming the entry that is gone. Give the key a value,
  or pick another entry to link it to, and the command carries on. The chat is never told which
  entry the link read (#5075).
- A browser login whose password or user name is missing from its vault, and a profile whose
  credential is missing from its vault, now ask you for it the way a missing secret for a command
  does: the same ask in the Inbox, filled in the window. The login goes ahead once you fill it;
  a chat on that profile starts once you fill it and start it again (#5074).
- A Secret ask still open when purlis quits is there again when it starts: it is listed with
  the other asks, and each chat that waited on it is told once you fill it or choose Not now.
- A chat on a pool's runner that misses a key asks you for it in the window like any other
  chat. The value is stored on your desktop, and the runner gets it only the way a runner chat's
  tool always has: you allow that run, and purlis records it as forwarded. A runner that can't
  receive secrets is told the key was declined and why, and the ask still lets you store the
  key for chats on this machine. A runner purlis couldn't reach to confirm just now is told it
  waits on you instead, and nothing is declined.
- **A vault key can read another entry's value: a Linked entry.** When a chat asks you for a
  secret, choose **Use an entry I have** and pick one of your entries from a list grouped by vault,
  with a filter on top. The key reads that entry's current value every time, so the value is
  never copied and rotating the entry reaches every key linked to it. The chat hears that the key
  was filled and its name, never which entry it reads. The vault view shows a link under its name,
  `purlis vault verify` reports a link whose entry is gone, and deleting an entry says how many
  links will break (#5069, #5073).
- **A missing secret asks you instead of failing.** When a chat's `purlis secret exec` finds its
  key missing from the persona's vault, the Inbox asks you for it: type the value into a masked
  field and the waiting command runs with it, or choose Not now and the chat hears "declined".
  Only the window answers, and the chat never sees the value (#5068, ADR 0109).
- **A command waits on your answer only as long as its harness lets it.** It ends with "waiting
  on you for `<vault>/<key>`; retry once answered" before its harness would kill it, and the
  chat is told when you answer. Chats missing the same key share one ask that says how many
  wait, and a chat you declined isn't asked about that key again (#5071).
- **Secret fill takes Allow for this chat and Always allow.** Always writes one line naming the
  key and the site in the persona's tools, shown on the notice before you press it, and
  `sandbox.proposed-changes = "off"` holds it back. A key marked `card = true` is offered Allow
  once only, and a key missing from its vault goes to the Secret ask (#5116).
- **A multi-line text box or an editable area of a page asks you each time** before a secret goes
  into it, whatever you allowed before, since text there is often posted (#5120).
- **Secret fill works on a pool's runner.** You answer the notice in this window, and it says the
  secret goes to that runner; the fill and its hold run there (#5122).
- A persona can declare the credentials its work needs, one `secret-need.<KEY>: <purpose>` line
  each in its definition. An ask for a declared key shows that purpose. After you fill a key
  the persona does not declare, purlis offers adding it as a proposed change you apply or
  dismiss, so the next teammate's ask arrives named and explained. A first fill into a vault you
  don't have yet makes it in the system keyring; a persona with `vault: none` gets a vault named
  after it, and the proposed change sets it.
- **A runner chat's tools get their vault values from your desktop, one run at a time.** When a
  chat on a pool's runner runs one of its persona's declared tools, the runner finds the tool it
  armed, and your desktop checks it is declared and allowed here and that the pool is yours (for
  now, a Docker pool on this machine's own Docker). Then you are asked about that run, and the
  command waits for your answer. On Allow it runs on the runner with the values your desktop sent
  for that run alone; the runner keeps none. With your desktop away the command waits up to 15
  minutes, says so, and you are asked once you are back; the chat carries on meanwhile (#2047).
- **The session protocol, split from the UI RPC.** The link to `purlisd` now has two protocols on
  one control lane. The session protocol is small, public and versioned: list, attach and detach,
  write, resize, answer, stop, start, and subscribe from a cursor, with events pushed after that.
  Its version is the one the link negotiates. A host refuses a command it does not know and keeps
  going, so a client and a host one version apart can still talk. A recorded frame of every kind
  holds that promise in CI. It names a project by a stable id, `[project] id` in `charter.toml`,
  minted once the first time it is asked for, and never by a path. Beside it, the UI RPC carries
  the app's own commands, with a typed TypeScript client generated from the same list as the
  window's. Only the app's window of the same build can use it, and it is left out of the
  compatibility tests. Nothing serves either protocol yet: `purlis serve` will (FD-26, #663).
- **Add a dispatch grant in Settings, with no dispatch waiting.** Settings › Project › Dispatch
  has **Add a grant**: pick the persona whose chats ask, the persona they may dispatch to, for
  you on this machine or for everyone in this project, and in one workspace or in any. Until
  now a grant was only made from the question a dispatch raises on a chat you are at, so a
  chat nobody is at (its permission prompts off) had nothing to run under until someone
  dispatched from another chat first. Its refusal now says to grant it under Settings ›
  Project › Dispatch (#1465).
- **Add a service on this Mac by its port in Settings.** Settings › Sandbox › Network has *A
  service on this Mac*: type one port and allow it for every chat of this project on this
  machine, or for one open chat only. It is judged, audited and kept exactly as an Allow on the
  Notice a refusal raises, so the same values are refused (a range, every port, a port purlis
  itself listens on, a scope past those two, a policy lock), and it shows in the Allowed list
  with Remove (#1970).
- **A settings gear on the project and the workspace you are in.** The project in front's tab and
  the focused workspace's tab each carry a gear that opens that one's settings. It shows only
  while the pointer is on that tab or the keyboard is on it, so the window stays quiet. Tab
  reaches it from its tab. Right-click and the palette still open settings too (SE-23, #1173).
- **Settings links to where an extension, a vault and a persona live.** The Extensions group, at
  the Project and Workspace levels, has *Go to Extensions…* and is offered even while no
  extension is installed, saying so. The sentence about vaults has *Open vault…*; the default
  persona's picker, a persona's hosts under Sandbox and the Granted list have *Show <persona>*
  and *Open vault <vault>* (#1387, #1388).
- **Settings lists a workspace's own opencode plugins.** At the Workspace level, the opencode
  group also lists the plugins and configs in the workspace's own `.opencode/`, in each folder
  between the workspace and the git top, and in each of its clones, each named by its place in
  the project. A `.opencode` or plugin folder purlis finds to be a link there is named, not
  followed (#1590).
- **Settings › Sandbox › Granted lists every grant, each with Revoke.** It shows what was
  allowed past the project's sandbox at every level (one chat, me on this machine, everyone in
  this project), who granted it and when, and the chat it came from. Revoke takes it out of
  every later start and is recorded; revoking a project host is an ordinary change to
  `charter.toml` that teammates follow. The same page lists the folders outside the project
  that chats may be granted, such as a tool's cache, kept on this machine only; it warns when
  one holds what other programs load code from, and drops one that comes to lead elsewhere
  through a link (#1348).
- **Settings lists the project's harness declarations.** *Harness & profiles* at the Project
  level now shows each `harnesses/<name>.toml` the project declares, read-only, with **Open
  file**, and each declaration purlis would not read with the reason (#1389).
- **Add and remove a persona's hosts in Settings.** Settings › Project › Sandbox has a Persona
  hosts page. It lists each persona's `[sandbox.personas.<persona>] hosts` with Remove, and its
  Add form takes a persona of the project and a host. The host is checked as you type it, as the
  project's own hosts are. Adding a host grants nothing by itself: a chat as that persona
  reaches the list only after the person on each machine allows the list as it stands, and a
  list that changes must be allowed again. The page also says which listed hosts the machine's
  policy keeps every chat from (#1407).
- **See the profiles listed for dispatched chats.** Settings › Project › Dispatch shows each
  persona's `[dispatch.profiles]` list next to the persona's own profile, read-only. Change the
  lists with Edit as TOML (#1522).
- **Settings' standing refusals link to the setting they are about.** Each line Settings shows
  under "charter does not take this from the files as they stand" that names a setting now has a
  Go to button, which shows that setting's group and puts the focus on the setting. The Saving
  view's line about a pull-request mode on an origin with no known forge links to Settings ›
  Saving › Mode (NO-7, #1232).
- **Edit as JSON at the Workspace level.** Settings at a workspace's level has an Edit as JSON
  link for its `workspace.json`, beside the Project level's Edit as TOML. charter checks the text
  before saving it, and refuses to save over a file that changed on disk since you opened it
  (NO-7, #1232).
- **Settings › Sandbox › Network shows what chats here can reach.** The page that was Granted
  is now Network, with three lists. **Open hosts** spells out every host of each Internet access
  preset in force and the project's own hosts. **Allowed** is the old Granted list: each host,
  folder, vault or persona's hosts you or a teammate allowed, with its scope (this chat, this
  project on this machine, or everyone in the project), who allowed it and when, and **Remove**
  in place of Revoke. **Blocked lately** lists what chats here were refused in the last 30 days,
  with the host, the chat and the time, and **Allow** for a host, kept for this project on this
  machine or for everyone in it. Each chat also has a **Network** view on its tab's menu: what it
  can reach now, by Open, Persona and Allowed hosts, and what it was refused. A chat started
  without the sandbox says "Not sandboxed: can reach anything". Nothing about what a chat may
  reach changes (#1662).
- **Settings › Saving offers Discover for a repo that is not catalogued.** A repo gets a save
  policy once `inventory/repos.json` catalogues it: the row says whether any is, and *Discover
  repos* runs the doctor's `discover` fix and reads the settings again (#1390).
- **Project settings in the Settings tab.** Its level switcher now offers Project beside You,
  with the project's settings in eight groups: General, Saving, Harness & profiles, Sandbox,
  Forges, Extensions, Appearance and Plugins; a group with nothing to set is left out. Each
  change is written to its file as you make it — a pick at once, a typed value when you leave
  the field — keeping every other key and comment, and the last change has an Undo. A value
  purlis refuses is said beside its setting, which keeps showing what is in the file. Keys
  the old page reached only as raw TOML have a control here: the sandbox, the Assisted-by
  trailer, the icon theme and the environment passed to chats. Project settings stays where it
  was for now (SE-17, #1167).
- **Locate… a moved project from Settings too.** Settings › You › This machine offers Locate…
  beside Forget for a recent project that has moved or gone, as the window's and the opener's
  notices do: pick the folder it is in now, and the entry is re-pointed there (#1291).
- **Settings › You › This machine.** A new group lists what purlis remembers on this machine
  and lets you take each thing back. Recent projects have Forget, including one that has moved or
  gone. Pinned projects and workspaces have Unpin with an Undo that puts the pin back in its place.
  A pin to a workspace that is gone is listed as kept dormant, with Forget to remove it for good. Approved projects have Revoke, so the next
  open asks again. The update channel can be changed here as well. The core gains the calls to
  forget a recent project and to revoke an approval (ST-2, #1226).
- **Your later word overrides an agent's.** When a task's asking chat answers a question you had
  open, the quiz closes quietly and leaves one line saying who told the task what, with Go to
  task and Say otherwise. It stays until you dismiss it. What you say reaches the task as your
  word, marked as replacing the chat's answer, and the chat is told. Only Say otherwise
  replaces it: an answer you send from the quiz just after the chat's is not sent, so you see the
  chat's answer first. Anything you had typed in the quiz is kept in the box (#4566).
- **A short pause before the next quiz.** After you answer, the quiz's place says where your
  answer went for about a second before the next question appears, so a second click can't land
  on it (#4566).
- **A task's question the window can't draw** (a prompt in its own terminal) takes its place in
  the same queue at the top, as a line linking to the task's pane (#4566).
- **Show what changed in a file.** In a branch's file tab, a file the branch changed has *Show
  what changed* beside it in the preview. It opens a tab with the file against the branch it
  was cut from, committed or not, its changed lines marked as `git diff` marks them. A file
  the branch did not change has no such button, and a binary file, one past 2 MiB or one
  purlis cannot read is said in a sentence rather than drawn as an empty diff (FM-11, #1114).
- **Sign in a profile through its harness's own sign-in.** A profile made in Settings › You ›
  Profiles says how it signs in, on this Mac, and whether its harness says it is signed in.
  **Sign in** opens a shell tab running Claude Code's, Codex's or opencode's own sign-in with
