  the profile's folder set, and `purlis profile sign-in <name>` does the same in your terminal
  (`--check` says whether it is signed in). An opencode profile is signed in to ChatGPT or
  GitHub Copilot, never a Claude plan. purlis reads none of it: the harness keeps its sign-in in
  the profile's folder. A chat on a profile its harness says is not signed in is refused before
  it starts, and one Ask, Sign in <profile>, waits in the Inbox until it is (#2035).
- **Sign in to GitHub or GitLab with a token, on any host.** Settings › You › Accounts lists
  this machine's forge accounts, with Sign out, and **Sign in with a token…** takes github.com,
  gitlab.com, a GitHub Enterprise server or a self-managed GitLab. purlis lists the exact scopes
  and opens the forge's page that makes the token, checks the token with the forge, refuses one
  missing a scope by naming it, and keeps it in your system keychain as an item of its own,
  never in a vault and never where a chat can reach it. Sign out deletes it from the keychain.
  The welcome's **Sign in to GitHub or GitLab** opens the same sign-in, and the forge work you
  do in the window uses the account (#1814, #1816).
- **Sign in with GitHub, in your browser.** The welcome's sign-in page and Settings › You ›
  Accounts have **Sign in with GitHub** beside the token: purlis shows a short code, you confirm
  it on GitHub's own page, and you come back signed in on github.com without ever handling a
  token. The sign-in is kept in your system keychain, renewed by purlis before it expires, and
  never reaches a chat. If GitHub ends it, a notice names the account and offers **Sign in
  again**. A GitHub Enterprise server still signs in with a token (#729).
- **Sign in with GitLab, in your browser.** **Sign in with GitLab**, on the welcome's sign-in
  page and in Settings › You › Accounts, opens gitlab.com in your own browser. You approve
  purlis there, the browser comes back to purlis by itself, and the account is listed with its
  sign-in in your system keychain, never where a chat can reach it. No token to make or paste.
  purlis asks for the `api` scope only. Cancel stops it at once, and a sign-in that cannot
  finish says why and what to do. Signing out ends the token on gitlab.com too, and says so if
  it could not. A self-managed GitLab still signs in with a token (#730).
- **Set a chat's skill budget.** `settings.skills.budget` in a project or a workspace overrides how many skills a chat lists and how many characters they take, from Settings › Skills. A value past a harness's own limit says what that harness would drop, and is never refused (#4610).
- **A skill's checks, in plain words, and one chat to write them** (Skill studio preview). A
  skill's Grades tab speaks of **checks** of two kinds: **Does it get picked?** (its trigger
  tests) and **Does it do the job?** (its outcome evals), each a card with its own results with
  the skill and without it, and its technical name in a small label. Once graded, one sentence
  says how the skill did. A skill with no checks offers **Ask a chat to write checks**, which opens
  a chat with its request typed and not sent; both kinds come back in one draft that waits on the
  tab to be accepted or discarded whole. Write them yourself starts the skill's
  `evals/triggers.json` from a short template and opens it to write in (#3925), and a kind with no
  checks offers a chat to write just those.
- **The window's install review picks where a project skill reaches** (Skill studio preview,
  #4185). An install into the project's skills offers the grant under Lands in, the project's
  root until you pick another, as `purlis skill install --grant` does. The review then says which
  project skill the install relies on and grants to those workspaces too, and Install waits until
  that is shown.
- **A skill whose name is taken can be installed under a new one.** The install review stops on a clash and offers to skip it or to name it `<source>-<name>`, which you can edit. Updates still find it at its source. Skill lists show where each skill came from, as `grilling · mattpocock` (#4530).
- **A skill's page in the Skill studio has a Files tab**, after Text: the skill's whole folder
  (`SKILL.md`, `references/`, `evals/`, `scripts/` …) as a file tree beside the light editor's
  preview of the file you pick. A built-in or third-party skill's files are shown too, read only.
  The page's ⋯ menu gains **Open in Finder** (Files or File Explorer elsewhere), which opens the
  skill's folder (#5183).
- **Each skill source says when it was last checked, and its counts** (Skill studio preview, #3840). A row under Your sources reads, for example, "14 skills, 2 installed · checked 3 hours ago", and a source's page says when it was checked in its lead line. purlis takes this from what the last browse or updates check recorded, so opening Sources asks no source anything.
- **Draft skills in the Skill studio preview** (#2772).
  - **Ask a chat to draft a skill** opens a chat with the request already typed. You finish the sentence and send it.
  - **A chat can't write a skill's files any more.** What it writes becomes a draft skill in the studio, kept on this machine and never committed. The chat's tab only says the draft is ready in the Skill studio, and nothing else asks you about it.
  - **Changes** shows each file the draft writes, against what the project has now.
  - **Try it** opens a scratch chat that has purlis's built-in skills and the draft, and no other skill from the project. It starts in a throwaway folder, on the harness profile the draft's workspace uses or the one you pick. Your own harness skills and plugins are off in it. Closing it removes the folder. All that's left is the skill's run.
  - **Accept** is one commit of only the draft's files. It's refused if the project's copy changed since the chat drafted it. **Reject** deletes the draft.
- **Skills reach the workspaces you grant them to, in the Skill studio preview.**
  - A project skill reaches a workspace's chats once you grant it: `purlis skill grant <name> all`, or name the workspaces.
  - A workspace can turn a granted skill off with `purlis skill grant <name> -w <workspace> --off`. It can't turn on one it wasn't granted.
  - A workspace can keep skills of its own.
  - Every level can keep local skills that stay on your machine. `purlis skill share` or the studio's Share gives one to the team.
  - The studio shows the skills of a chat in any workspace, with one line for each skill left out. Settings › Workspace › Skills counts them and opens the studio (#2767).
- **Install skills from a git repository in the Skill studio preview** (#2773).
  - **Add source** takes a repository's https:// URL, or a folder on this machine, and optionally its branch and the folder its skills are in. Browse lists the skills it holds.
  - **The install review leads with a summary**: the scripts a skill carries and what runs each, the network hosts its files name, its `!` commands, anything it writes outside the workspace, any text hidden from a reader, and any file that is not text. Risky items are marked, every file is one click away with hidden characters shown, and skills it refers to come along in the same review.
  - **An install is a copy, pinned** to the commit you reviewed, all or nothing, and one commit of the skill's files and `skills.lock`. A local install is kept in `skills.local.lock` on this machine.
  - **Updates are never applied by themselves.** A newer commit is offered with what its summary gains and loses, then each file's diff, your own edits beside it, and any skill it now needs; only Accept moves the pin. A source only the team's record names is not contacted from your machine until you confirm it.
  - **A private repository signs in with a vault entry** of your own: the token stays in the vault, is sent to that repository's host alone, and is never shown or written anywhere.
  - The same on the command line: `purlis skill install` prints the review and asks before it copies anything, and `purlis skill update` lists newer commits and shows each one's diff before it asks; `purlis skill update --confirm <url>` confirms a source.
- **Make, edit, rename, move and delete skills in the Skill studio preview** (#2770).
  - **New skill** starts one from a template, in the workspace you opened the studio from, or at the project's root.
  - **Edit** opens a skill in the light editor. A live lint says what would stop it from loading, and Save stays off until the skill is whole.
  - **Rename** also renames every persona's and skill's mention of it.
  - **Moving** a skill is done by dragging its row onto a level, or with Move to. Moving one into the project's skills asks where it reaches.
  - **Delete** says who uses the skill first, and Restore brings it back with its grant. Where the grant can't go with it, the skill stays where it was and you're told why.
  - **A project skill's grant**, and a workspace's switch to turn it off, are on its row. A workspace can't turn on a skill it wasn't granted, and is told which grant would reach it.
  - **Each change is one commit** of only that skill's files.
  - The same changes are on the command line: `purlis skill new`, `edit`, `mv`, `rm` and `restore`.
- **A running chat whose skills changed offers a restart** on the same conversation, so it picks up the new ones.
- **A persona's own skills can be made, edited, renamed, moved, deleted and shared in the Skill studio preview** (#3003), from the studio opened on that persona.
  - **New skill** starts at the persona you came from.
  - **Moving** one of a persona's skills into the project's skills asks where it reaches, and adds it to the persona's skills, so the persona keeps it in every workspace. Moving a project or workspace skill to a persona takes it out of that persona's skills, and says which chats and personas no longer get it.
  - **Rename** also renames every persona's and skill's mention of it.
  - **Delete** says that the persona's chats use it, and Restore brings it back.
  - The same changes are on the command line, with `-p <persona>`, and `purlis skill mv --to-persona <persona>`.
- **A chat's write to a persona's skill becomes a draft** in the Skill studio, as at the project and workspace levels (#3048).
- **Try the Skill studio while it is built.** Settings › You › Previews has a _Skill studio_
  switch for this machine. With it on, every chat gets the project's own skills (a folder in
  `skills/` at the project's root, for chats at the root), on Claude Code, Codex and opencode,
  and the palette's _Open Skill studio_ lists every skill a chat gets and why any other is left
  out (#2765). Each time a chat uses a skill, its tab shows the skill and the tool calls made
  so far until the turn ends, and the skill's own tab lists every run with what happened inside
  it: tool calls, errors, refusals, asks, tokens and time (#2766). `purlis skill runs` prints
  them. A chat can also list, find and load its own skills and see their recent runs, so a
  chat program that has no skills of its own still gets yours. Loading a skill counts as a run,
  and the run says the chat loaded it (#2776).
  _Use skill…_, among each chat's actions (its pane's ⋯, its sidebar row's ⋯ and the palette),
  lists exactly that chat's skills, asks for the arguments a skill declares, and types the
  skill into the chat for you to send, in the way that chat's tool expects it, on Claude Code,
  Codex and opencode alike. The Skills chip on a chat's pane shows how many skills and how many
  characters of their descriptions the chat lists, and warns at four fifths of purlis's budget;
  a manual-only skill costs nothing where the chat leaves it out, as Claude Code does (#2775).
- **Extensions can add to the Skill studio, and run confined when they do** (Skill studio
  preview, #2777). An extension can offer templates for new skills, add its own findings to a
  skill's live lint, add panels to a skill's tab, and offer skills from a source that is not git,
  whose files purlis reviews as it reviews a git source's. Such an extension runs in the same
  sandbox a chat runs in: it reads only its own folder and what purlis hands it, writes only its
  own folder, reaches only the hosts its approval names, and never a host that serves an AI model.
  Its approval says so, and marks its source, lint and template as experimental. Where purlis cannot hold it in
  a sandbox, as on Windows today, it loads none of that extension. A skill's tab draws its Runs
  panel the way it draws an extension's panel.
- **A persona brings its skills into every workspace** (Skill studio preview). A persona's own
  skills, and the skills its definition names, reach every chat as that persona, in any
  workspace, whatever the workspace was granted; the persona's copy wins over a workspace's or
  the project's of the same name. Its page counts them and opens the Skill studio on a chat as
  the persona, where you add a skill by name or remove one. A chat whose persona names a skill
  this machine does not have shows a Notice naming it, and starts without it. Names written the
  old way, `charter:<skill>`, still mean purlis's own skill (#2768).
- **The Skill studio lists each program's own skills and plugins** (#2769): Claude Code's,
  Codex's and opencode's, in your own folders, in their plugins, and in a workspace's repos,
  each with whose it is. Each can be turned off for this project's chats where the program
  allows it, and says plainly where it does not. A project skill that a repo or a program also
  has says that a chat gets both. With the studio on, Settings' Plugins group is a summary that
  opens it. `purlis skill list` and `purlis skill show` list them too, each program's under its
  own heading, with whose each is and whether a chat gets it (#3008).
- **A skill can only narrow a chat** (Skill studio preview, #2771). A skill that asks to
  pre-approve tools or to add commands to a chat's events is handed to the chat without them,
  and says so; one that takes tools away keeps that. Each skill in the Skill studio shows, for
  Claude Code, Codex and opencode, whether everything it asks for applies there, and what is left
  out, carried over or not applied. A skill of a program's own or a repo's that would widen a
  chat is marked. A manual-only skill now stays out of the chat's choice, and costs nothing in
  its budget, on all three. Its badge says it runs only when asked for, and so does a Codex
  skill, its own or a repo's, that Codex's own settings keep out of its choice (#3050). The
  editor's live lint also warns of a description too short to say when to use the skill, a
  skill it names that does not exist, and a program the skill runs that this machine does not
  have. A chat that starts without a skill it would have loaded, because the skill is broken,
  says which and why on its tab, with a way to the Skill studio.
- **Move your project's skills into the Skill studio in one step** (Skill studio preview,
  #2784). `purlis doctor --fix project-skills` moves every skill in the project's
  `.claude/skills` into its `skills/`, shared with every workspace as before. It rewrites the old
  `charter:<skill>` names to `purlis:<skill>`, but never inside quoted code or an image name. It
  all goes in one commit that `git revert` undoes. It checks first that every chat keeps its
  skills, and changes nothing if one would lose one or if two skills or folders differ only in
  case, which a disk that ignores case reads as one. From then on every chat in the project gets
  those skills, the Skill studio switched on or off, and Codex chats get them too. Clones stop
  getting a copy of `.claude/skills`. Your clones lose their copies at once and a teammate's the
  next time a chat starts there, while a copy someone edited is kept and named. It says what it
  changed, and which skills a persona names that no chat can get. It needs the Skill studio
  switched on to run, and refuses while the project has changes that are not committed or its git
  is in the middle of something.
- **A skill's history, state, owners and uses** (Skill studio preview, #2782). A skill's tab
  lists every saved version of it, newest first, with who saved it, the runs that started on it,
  what it changed, and *Revert to this*, which puts the skill back as that version had it in one
  commit. A skill can be **deprecated**, pointing to the skill to use instead: it still works, and
  is listed after the others. A skill can be **archived**: it never loads, and *Restore* brings it
  back. A skill no chat ran for 60 days suggests deprecating it. A skill can name its owners, for
  people to know. The tab lists the skills a skill names, marking one that does not exist, and the
  skills that name it, and a run that started inside another skill's run says so. `purlis skill
  history | revert | deprecate | archive | owners | uses` do the same from a terminal.
- **A skill's grant file that is a link is no longer followed** (#2782). purlis reads what it keeps
  beside a skill's folder (its grant, and now its state and owners) only from a plain file: a link
  in its place grants the skill nothing beyond the project's root, and a change to it is refused,
  so a link can no longer widen where a skill reaches.
- **A skill that changes as it is moved is put back** (#3145). Sharing, renaming, moving,
  deleting or restoring a skill checks, once it has moved, that it moved what was checked; one
  swapped for a link in that instant is put back and the move refused, and a file with a second
  name (a hard link) is never moved. Where a skill could not be put back after a failed move, the
  message says what moved and what stayed, instead of that nothing was moved.
- **A skill's tab totals its runs** (Skill studio preview, #2783): runs, tool calls, errors,
  refusals, asks, tokens and time, by the program each chat ran on, by persona and by
  workspace. Each run says what it ran on, and a run that a curation action's prompt started
  says so, whichever way the chat's program started the skill.
- **The Skill studio offers a way to start** (Skill studio preview, #2785). A project with no
  skill of its own shows three starts above the skills its chats already get: *Ask a chat to
  draft a skill*, *Browse sources* and *New skill*, from the blank template. The sources
  section offers well-known collections of skills (Anthropic's, OpenAI's curated ones, and
  Superpowers), each with why it is on the list. *Add…* fills in Add source for you to
  confirm. Nothing is installed until you review a skill from it. A project whose skills are still where only some chat programs read them is
  offered *Move them*, the same one-commit move as `purlis doctor --fix project-skills`. The
  commit reaches everyone in the project, and a teammate on an older purlis opens it read-only
  until they update.
- **Grade a skill's trigger tests** (Skill studio preview, #2779). A skill can carry trigger tests:
  queries it should start on, and near misses it should leave alone. _Grade…_ on a skill's tab
  first shows what a grade runs: how many chats, each test as the chat will read it (a character
  no reader would see marked), what the skill's last grade spent, and that the chats are paid for
  by the profile you pick, as any chat is. A grade stops once its chats have spent 200,000 tokens,
  or the cap you set in the plan for this machine, or once they cost that many tokens would at
  the dearest price, where Claude Code says what they cost, and says what it spent. Nothing runs until you
  press _Grade_. Each test then
  runs in a chat of its own, three times with the skill and three times without it, in a
  throwaway folder, only in the project's full sandbox, with none of your own Allows, no tools
  but purlis's that only read, and only on a Claude Code profile that keeps its permission
  prompts; the plan says why when a grade cannot run. A chat that asks you something is ended
  there and does not count. A grade of a skill kept on this machine stays on this machine. Those chats get no tab, and each ends as soon as
  the skill starts. The tab says how far the grade has got and offers _Stop_. The skill's
  _Grades_ panel shows each grade: the version it graded, what it ran on, the tests passed, each
  side's pass rate and the difference the skill made. Each version in its history shows its
  newest grade. Grades are kept in the project beside its skill runs, so the team sees them, and
  a run a grade started says so. `purlis skill grade` prints the same plan and the grades.
- **A large library stays reachable without flooding a chat** (Skill studio preview, #2778).
  Once a chat's skills are past purlis's skill budget, it is handed the skills you pinned,
  purlis's own and one index skill that names every other skill in a line, and it loads any of
  them by name when a request needs it. Below the budget nothing changes. Pin a skill for a
  workspace's chats or a persona's with `purlis skill pin <name> -w <workspace>` or
  `-p <persona>`, and the router never hides it. The Skill studio and `purlis skill list` say
  which skills are pinned and why any other is hidden, and _Use skill…_ marks the hidden ones,
  says how many are in the index skill, and still starts them for you.
- **Pin and unpin a skill in the Skill studio** (Skill studio preview, #3232). Each skill's row
  in the studio for a workspace's chats or a persona's has a _Pinned_ switch, one commit each
  way. A skill's tab lists every workspace and persona that pins it, each with _Unpin_. Where a
  chat's pinned skills alone are past the budget, its Skills chip and _Use skill…_ name the
  studio to unpin them in, such as _Skill studio · ops_.
- **A harness that can take no skills says so** (Skill studio preview, #2985). A harness a project
  declares that has no skill format purlis can hand skills by and whose declaration does not say it takes MCP servers gets no
  skills. The Skill studio says why in one line, each skill's badges say skills are not supported
  there, Use skill… on its chats says the same, and so does `purlis skill list`.
- **A Skills view on the left** (Skill studio preview, #3266). With the preview on, the left
  sidebar has a Skills view under Search, on ⌘⇧X (Ctrl+Shift+X). It lists the skills of the
  workspace in the title bar by level, with what needs you on top, and at most one mark on each:
  needs review, off, left out, hidden by the router or lint. Point at a skill, or move to it with
  the keyboard, to read what it does and why it has its mark. A click opens the skill's tab, and
  its right-click menu has Use in this chat, Turn on or off for the workspace, Pin to this
  workspace (or Unpin), and Show in Explorer. Open Skill studio and New skill… are at the top, and
  Only this chat's narrows the list to the chat in front. With the preview off the view isn't
  there, and the sidebar shows Chats until the preview is back.
- **A slow moment in the window is written down, so it can be read afterwards.** Every command
  answer that takes 1 s or longer, and every stall of the window of 200 ms or longer, is
  appended to `slow.jsonl` in the app's log folder (on macOS
  `~/Library/Logs/dev.purlis.app/slow.jsonl`), with how many chats were hot and, for a
  stall, the tab in front and whether a chat's view was opening. The newest 1,000 are kept, on
  this machine only. The window still says an answer is late only at 20 s (#4725).
- **A theme can style the key a button shows.** Start chat now shows the key that presses it
  (⌘↩ on a Mac, Ctrl+Enter elsewhere) after its words. A theme sets that key with the button
  family's new `shortcut` part, `"button.shortcut.text"` and `"button.shortcut.font-size"`, which
  `purlis theme parts` lists and the published schema completes. The theme specimen draws it, so
  `theme_preview` shows it. The key is hidden while the button cannot take it, during an approval,
  a start without the sandbox, and while the chat starts (#3377, #3510).
- **Start a chat's Name field names the next chat's number**, `steward 10`, rather than "steward
  and its number". The number is a guess, and the chat still takes the number it is dealt (#3376).
- **You can stop a chat, or a chat and everything below it.** Every row of the Chats section,
  and every chat's tab menu, has **Stop chat …** and **Stop chat … and everything below it**.
  Each asks first and says what ends. A chat another chat started gets one short turn to write
  what it did, then it ends, and the chat that asked is told you stopped it. Nothing is typed
  into a chat that is showing a prompt: that one ends as it stands. The stop of a subtree ends
  the deepest chats first and touches nothing outside it. Pressing Stop on a chat that is
  already stopping ends it without waiting. Only you stop a chat: a chat can cancel a task it dispatched itself, which asks that task
  for its report, and can stop no other chat. A chat that
  is being stopped, and any chat below it, cannot start another chat or be started again, so
  nothing outlives the stop. The chat that asked reads the stop as purlis's own line, which no
  report can pass for, and its row says the chat was stopped (#1448).
- **The needs-you hand rolls up the tree.** A chat that needs you marks its own row and every
  row above it in the Chats section, and counts on the workspace it works in. Rows with chats
  under them fold, and a folded row still shows the hand for what it hides. Pressing the hand
  on a row above goes to the chat that needs you, opening its tab when it has none (#1448).
- **A chat the Skill studio starts stays linked to its skill and its job, across a restart.**
  Its header names both, "test-design · writing outcome evals", and opens the skill's page. While
  it runs, the skill's page says so above its tabs with Open chat, and the Grades card shows the
  running job in place of its button. Once it is done, the skill's Runs keeps it under "Chats the
  studio started", and its draft offers Open chat (#5185).
- **Tear a tab off into a window of its own.** A tab's *Move to new window*, or dragging it off
  the window, puts it in a **tab window** of the same project: its strip and panes, with no
  sidebar. *Move to window ▸* moves a tab or a pane between the project's windows. Closing a tab
  window sends its tabs back to the project window and ends nothing, and tab windows come back
  after a relaunch, where they were on screen. A chat shown in a tab window is never shown
  twice: a press on it brings that window forward, and a task you are reading there is not ended
  under you, while a minimised window counts as not being looked at (#4768).
- An asking chat can pass a task's question on to you with `dispatch_pass_on`. It reaches your Inbox in the task's own words, with the chat's one-line note marked as its own.
- A task's question nobody handles now reaches your Inbox by itself: 100 seconds after the chat that dispatched it had a turn to see it, or at once if that chat has closed or crashed. If the task ends first, the question closes and you get one Update.
- A task question's line in its task's Activity has a **What happened** fold: when it was asked,
  handed to its asking chat, passed on, reached you, answered and by whom, or closed when its
  task ended. It is read from the audit entries only when you open it, holds none of the
  question's words, and adds nothing to the bell or Updates.
- Each step of a task's question is now recorded in the event log, without its words, so you can see how many reach you, why, and how long they wait. If a question can't take its route, you get one Update and one log line.
- **Tell the chat to retry.** After you allow a host whose held command had already given up
  waiting, its sandbox Notice offers **Tell the chat to retry**: it puts a fixed line in the
  chat's prompt for you to send, so an idle chat runs the command again. purlis never types
  into a chat by itself, and never sends the line for you (#1709).
- **The brief a task was sent can be read.** **Brief** is on a task's row menu in the Chats
  list, on a finished task's row, and on the pane's top line while a tab shows a task. Each
  opens the same read-only panel: the brief as it was sent, who sent it (the chat that asked,
  or you), when, to which persona and where the task works. The brief is shown as text and is
  never rendered: no link in it is live and no image is loaded. A long brief scrolls in its
  box and is not cut, and **Copy** gives it exactly as it was sent. Where a brief holds
  characters that draw as nothing or change how the text around them reads, each is written
  out as its code and the panel says so. The brief is read from the task's dispatch record,
  so a finished task has it too, and nothing new is stored (#1494).
- **The browser's bar says when your key or click was dropped.** While you drive a browser, a key
  or click that reaches the page after the page, or a frame inside it, loaded another document is
  dropped so it never lands on something you did not see. The bar above the page now says so,
  once, and asks you to type or click again (#2304).
- **A chat's browser can ask you to take over.** When a page needs a person (a CAPTCHA, a second
  factor, a consent page), the agent asks through `ask_operator` pointed at its browser, and an
  Ask shows under Needs you. Take over opens the browser with you driving; Done hands it back and
  tells the chat only that you finished, never what you did. If the browser ends first, the Ask
  ends with it and the Inbox keeps an update (#2015).
- **A browser's view marks where purlis filled a secret.** While its page is on the site a vault
  key went to, the bar beside the site says `secret: <key>`, and its hint names the field. The
  chat's browser timeline says which key went to which site. Neither shows a value.
- **The Browsers grid.** *Open browsers*, in the palette and on the Chats view's heading while a
  project has a browser, opens a tab of every browser as a live tile, about a frame a second: a
  chat's, by its chat, and your own. Its switch is the Inbox's: this project (the default), the
  workspace whose strip the tab is on, or every project the window holds, each with its count.
  Pressing a tile opens that browser's view in its own project (#2027).
- **The `purlis` command line reaches the app's built-in extensions.** The binary finds the app
  bundle it shipped in from its own real path, so a built-in's commands run from a terminal,
  and its badges, events and session-start section reach the footer and chats as an installed
  extension's do. A `purlis` outside an app bundle reaches none, and says so (#1366).
- **The cluster operator serves its metrics.** Prometheus can scrape them at `/metrics` on the
  operator's port 8080, through the Service `purlis-cluster-operator-metrics`. They count claims
  by pool, namespace and state, warm runners by pool and namespace, and suspensions and claim
  deletions by pool and cause (#3737).
  Nothing may scrape them until the chart's `metrics.allowFrom` (or a NetworkPolicy of your own)
  says who may.
- **A runner's key is kept once, and removing a runner removes it whole.** purlis keeps each
  Docker pool runner's device id and key in `runners.json` the first time it is paired, and
  refuses a later answer with another key. Removing a runner unpairs it while its link is up,
  then removes its container and home volume. Anything left is named with the `docker`
  command that removes it, and the runner stays listed until it is gone (#2525).
- **Devices: this machine and every runner, in a tab of their own.** Once this machine keeps a
  pool, Devices in the palette lists this machine and each runner it keeps, each with the chats
  and browsers on it, the version it runs, whether it answers or is suspended, and when it last
  answered. Under them, each pool's use: its runners running and suspended, and the CPUs and
  memory they request. A suspended runner is never woken to be asked (#2052).
- **The diff engine can hide whitespace as `git diff -w` does.** Lines that differ only in
  spaces, tabs or line ends count as the same, and the file list stays the same. Where two
  diffs are equally short, a hunk may sit elsewhere than git's (ADR 0084). The Review tab's
  toggle comes with RC-4 (#704).
- **The dispatch question names the task and the profile.** The question a dispatch to
  another persona raises now shows the task's name, which is the chat's own text, apart from
  purlis's own words, and says which profile the other persona's chat would start on. Allow
  starts it on that profile: where the profile would now be another, nothing is allowed and
  the question is shown again. It leads with that persona's mark, and the Notice that a
  teammate's grant arrived leads with the asking persona's where every grant it lists is one
  persona's (#1456, #1454).
- **The first browser shows its engine's download as it goes.** While purlis downloads the
  browser engine for the first browser on a machine, a Notice says how far it has come, and
  **Cancel download** stops it without keeping any of it. A download that fails says what to do
  next (#2207).
- **The event log says who drives a browser, and that someone typed, never what.** Taking a
  browser over, handing it back, a login purlis performs and handing a browser to a chat each
  write an event naming the browser and who drives it now (`agent`, `person` or `purlis`). The
  first key the person types after taking a browser over, and a login purlis filled, write
  `browser.typed`, with no key, count, value, address or page text in it (#2293).
- **A worktree's file tab marks what a chat is touching.** The dot the explorer shows on a file a
  chat is reading or editing now shows in the file tab's tree too, on the file and the folders
  above it, and fades the same way once the chat goes quiet (#1154).
- **A search jump reveals its file in the file tab's tree.** The folders above the file a jump
  picked open, and its row is scrolled into view (#1137).
- **Show what changed in a file's own tab.** A file opened in a tab of its own offers *Show
  what changed* where the branch changed it, as the Files tab's preview does (#1189).
- **Copy path and Reveal beside a file in the file tab.** The header over a file, in the Files
  tab's preview and in a file's own tab, copies the file's path in the branch or shows it in your
  file manager, as a tree row's menu does (#1143).
- **Open a changed line in the file tab.** A file's comparison lists where each change starts,
  and *Open at line …* opens the branch's file tab on that file at that line (#984).
- **The first dispatch on a machine explains the chip, once.** The first time a session you are
  at starts a task, a Notice on its tab says that tasks work inside the tab, and that the chip
  beside its name counts them and switches between them. *Show the task* opens the chip's menu;
  either it or *Dismiss* puts the Notice away on this machine for good. A chat running with its
  prompts off is never shown it (#1501).
- **Opening a repo says what it did to the project's forges.** When the first run or *New
  project* takes a repo in, the window now says "GitLab was added to this project's forges", or
  why the forge was not added and where to add it (#1669).
- **The Inbox has a scope: All projects, This project or This workspace.** A switch at its top,
  the same one the Chats view has, picks whose asks are listed, each scope with its count. It
  opens on This project, and the pick is remembered for the project on this machine. This
  workspace follows the workspace in front on the strip; at the plane root it lists the asks of
  chats filed in no workspace. All projects adds the chats waiting in other windows and each
  ask of the window's other projects, read here and answered there. A scope with nothing in it
  says how many wait in the wider one, with one press to show them.
- **The Inbox's look back lists what you kept blocked.** *Allowed in the last day* in an empty
  Inbox now lists each host you answered **Keep blocked** for a chat, beside what you allowed, so
  both answers to a host ask are there to look back at (#1700).
- **The Inbox: everything in a project that waits on you, answered where you see it.** It is the
  first view on the right side's activity bar, and its icon counts what waits, while the side is
  away too. Each chat that asks is a group under its chain (`steward 12 › #3046 drill`), the one
  waiting longest first. A permission prompt, a choice of several, a sandbox host and a dispatch
  grant are answered in place, through the same path as their Notice, and answering in either
  place clears both. A chat waiting on your reply gets a reply box, a prompt in a harness's own
  terminal says so, and every ask has Go to chat, which opens a task in its session's tab. The
  title bar's ✋ opens it, and so does ⌘⇧I (Ctrl+Shift+I elsewhere). ↑ and ↓ move, Enter presses
  the focused button and Escape goes back to the chat; no single letter does anything. Empty, it
  says "Nothing is waiting on you" and lists what you answered there lately (#1692).
- **The kill switch is in the event log.** As the app starts, each stop, re-arm and tamper in
  the kill switch's journal that the host's event log does not hold yet becomes a
  `killswitch.stop`, `killswitch.rearm` or `killswitch.tamper` event there, saying who wrote the
  line: the window's as a person's, the app's as purlis's own, and `purlis stop --all`'s as
  unattributed. While the app runs, each line is recorded as the switch writes it or its watch
  reads it. A line read again, or at the next start, is not recorded twice (#1375).
- **On Linux, what the sandbox refuses a Codex or opencode chat raises a Notice.** A write, a
  read, a local socket or a service on this machine that purlis's own sandbox refuses is shown
  on the chat's tab as on macOS, naming exactly what was refused, with Allow once, for this chat
  or always where a grant applies. The same refusal again within a minute is one Notice, and the
  refusal stands whether or not the window hears of it (#2344).
- **Going LIVE says whether the remote is public.** The confirmation for making a workspace live
  asks the project's forge who can read its remote, and says public (in bold), internal,
  private, or that it is not known and why. Make live does not wait for the answer (#1369).
- **The window's native parts follow the theme** (#2328). The traffic lights, the menus and the
  dialogs are drawn light for a light theme and dark for a dark one, whatever the system's own
  appearance, and the window opens in the theme's background colour, with no flash of another.
- **Forced colours and more contrast** (#2328). With a contrast theme that forces its colours,
  focus, the tab you are on, the row the keyboard is on and each chat's state mark are drawn in
  the system's colours and with a shape. When the system asks for more contrast, a theme's
  appearance tagged high contrast is drawn for you, and drawn again as soon as the setting
  changes.
- **F6 moves the keyboard from region to region**: left sidebar, editor, right sidebar, the
  Panel's left half, its right half, skipping what is put away; Shift+F6 goes back. Inside a
  chat's terminal F6 is still the chat's (spec #1736, #1741).
- **The Panel's right half holds Memory, Todos and Sessions.** The right activity bar's Lower
  icons, below a divider, switch them, and the right sidebar keeps the Inbox, Personas and
  Vaults, opening on the Inbox. Drag the handle between the two halves to share the Panel's
  width (half each by default, double-click to put it back); it is kept for each project. With
  one half put away the other takes the whole width. Each half is headed by one line: the open
  view's title, its own buttons, and a chevron that puts the half away (spec #1736, #1738).
- **You can answer a question a task put to the chat that dispatched it.** In a chat's
  Activity tab, a question its task is still waiting on has _Answer_: a small form with the
  question, a box, _Send_ and _Cancel_ (Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line). The task is
  handed your answer marked as the person's, and carries on. The chat that was asked is told on
  its next turn that you answered, with the question and your answer, and its own answer to
  that question is refused from then on. A question is answered once: if that chat answers
  first, the form says so and keeps what you typed, and nothing of yours is sent. An answer is
  for the question it was written under, and is never delivered to a later one. Your text is
  sent whole or not at all, never cut; a character purlis will not send is named with where
  it is. If the task ends before it has read your answer, the timeline says so. The timeline says "you" answered. Only the purlis window can send an answer as
  yours: no chat's command, hook or file can (#1496).
- **The picker a chat starts from shows who pays.** Each profile's row says its model (the
  harness's default for now) and what a chat on it is billed to: your plan, your key, your cloud
  account, or nobody for a local model, with the profile's label, or whatever the harness is
  signed in with where purlis cannot see it. A row whose chat would not start says why. A chat's
  run records its profile's sign-in kind as its model source (#2036).
- **A profile of this machine can name its key or cloud credentials by vault reference.** A key
  profile waits for the key proxy, and a cloud profile for #2151; each one's row and start say
  so (#2036).
- **A Docker pool runs on Podman.** The pool's container check takes what rootful and rootless
  Podman write for a correctly confined container, as measured on CI, and still refuses a
  loosened one (#2680).
- **A runner's link comes back on its own.** When the link from this machine's session host to a
  runner drops, or is renewed ahead of its limit, the host links again by itself and carries the
  window's projects, its subscription and its views over, each view drawn again from a snapshot.
  While no link is up, what the window sends is refused in words saying so, and nothing is sent
  later in its place (#2215).
- **purlis starts its session host again if it stops unexpectedly.** Each chat that ran in it
  says on its pane whether its turn was lost or nothing was, with Resume to start it again on
  its conversation. After three unexpected stops within five minutes purlis stops trying and
  says so, with the host's last log lines and Try again (#2007).
- **The session host starts a chat by its names.** A start that names only its profile,
  persona, workspace, the conversation to carry on, its first message and the person's opt-out
  of the sandbox is composed in the session host from the project's own files and this machine's
  profiles, with the code the window's own start runs. The host starts the chat's sandbox
  confinement itself, and the chat's run in the event log says who started it (`started_by`).
  `purlis serve` composes such starts too, and refuses one that would run sandboxed, with the
  reason, until a runner starts a chat's confinement itself (#2217). (#2171, #2306)
- **The Skill studio is ready to try** (Skill studio preview, #2786). Every skill your chats get,
  in one place: see what each chat has and why any other is left out, write a skill or ask a chat
  to draft one, install one from a git repository after reading what it adds, grade it with real
  chats against no skill and its previous version, keep a large library within each chat's skill
  budget, and publish or export a skill to share it. It is still a preview: turn it on in
  Settings › You › Previews with the _Skill studio_ switch, on each machine, and some of it may
  change before it is finished. [The Skill studio](skill-studio.md) explains it from
  the start.
- **The Skill studio's list and Needs you show what your skill lint extensions say of the
  project's own skills.** An extension that declares `skill-lint` used to speak only in a skill's
  Text tab; now its findings are on the skill's Library row and under Problems in a skill, and a
  persona's Skills line counts them the same way. The list asks each extension about a skill's
  files once and keeps the answer while the app runs, asks new questions for at most 100 ms per
  list, and shows nothing from an extension that did not answer in time, asking it again after
  30 seconds. Opening a chat asks nothing (#3940).
- **The team decides how far its people may turn the sandbox down.** In `charter.toml`,
  `[sandbox] policy = "never"` keeps every chat in the full sandbox: "Start without the sandbox"
  and a lower level of your own are refused, with a sentence naming the policy.
  `policy = "local"` (the default) leaves each person their own level.
- **`[sandbox] mode = "off"` turns the sandbox off for the team, by consent.** It no longer reads
  as on with a refusal: each person is asked once, "Your project turned the sandbox off (commit
  <sha> by <author>)", with **Accept** and **Keep it on for me**. Until they answer their chats
  keep their own level; once they accept, a chat with no level of theirs runs with no sandbox
  from its next start. Settings › Sandbox › Your level shows the answer and offers the other.
  Under `policy = "never"`, `mode = "off"` is refused (#2071).
- **A chat waiting on you says what it waits for at the top of its pane, however much it writes
  after.** A permission or a question shows in its own words, which no later turn replaces. A
  chat whose turn ended on you shows its last message, with the few before it a press away, so a
  question a later turn pushed aside is not lost. Show all opens the whole text. The strip never
  takes the keyboard, and goes once you answer (#4563).
- **The window's git signs in with your forge account.** A save, fetch, push or clone the window
  runs, on a host you signed in to in Settings › You › Accounts, now uses that account through
  purlis's own git credential helper, so it needs no `gh` or `glab`. The helper is named only on
  the command line of the window's git, never in a git config, and no other credential helper,
  your keychain's included, is ever handed the token. A chat's git never gets it (#752).
- **The theme check holds more of what the window draws.** Each syntax colour is held on the
  editor's current line, the window's secondary, muted, accent and state words on a theme's
  text selection, and a line of words has to fit the control or strip it is drawn in, in both
  densities: a theme whose text size and line height make a line taller than its box is told the
  sizes (#2522).
- **A chart draws each point in its own colour**, the theme's chart palette in turn (#2522).
- **A chat's theme changes are a draft, drawn only in its workspace.** `purlis theme draft
  <folder>` has the app make the chat's draft in the plane's local folder, never committed, and
  `--save` hands the chat's working copy over and says what the window draws of it. A strip on the
  workspace names the draft and its chat, with Keep, Revert and Compare; ⌘⇧⌫
  (Ctrl+Shift+Backspace elsewhere) reverts at once, and closing the chat asks Keep or Revert. A
  draft that breaks a hard floor is not drawn: its last good version stays, and the chat is told
  which floor (#2332).
- **`purlis theme check` reports the hard floors** of every combination: primary text on every
  surface, the focus ring and the terminal's words, each at 3:1 as the window draws the theme.
  `--json` lists them in `hard_floors` (#2332).
- **Use in the whole project and Copy to my machine** in Settings › Theme move a workspace's
  theme to the project, and copy a project's or a workspace's to your own themes (#2332).
- **Settings › Theme is a gallery.** Each theme you can choose shows as a card with a picture of
  it in each of its appearances; pointing at a card (or moving to it with the arrow keys) draws
  it in the window, and leaving puts yours back. Pressing a card makes it your choice at that
  level, with a badge saying where what is drawn comes from. Under the cards are the chosen
  theme's appearances and options, what the theme check found in it, **Duplicate as my theme**
  (a theme folder of your own that extends it) and **Open folder**. At the You level it is the
  machine default, which had no picker before (#2331).
- **`purlis theme export` takes a theme folder by its level id** (`machine:<folder>`,
  `project:<folder>`, `workspace:<workspace>:<folder>`), as `purlis theme check` does, and never
  exports a farther level's folder in its place (#2612).
- **Themes at every level, and your choices kept per project and workspace.** Theme folders
  can live in your config folder's `themes/`, a project's `themes/` and a workspace's
  `themes/`. Your choice of theme and appearance is kept on your machine per project and per
  workspace, set in Settings › Theme, and survives a re-clone when the project
  has a `[project] id`; a project's `[theme]` and a LIVE workspace's settings commit a default,
  and your choice beats it. Switching workspace repaints with a short crossfade. An old
  single-file `theme.json` is offered, once, a move into a theme folder (#2323).
- **`purlis theme list` and `purlis theme check` know every theme level.** `list` shows your
  theme folders, the project's and each workspace's beside the built-in and extension themes,
  each with its level, and `check machine:<folder>`, `check project:<folder>` or
  `check workspace:<ws>:<folder>` checks a level's folder exactly as the window reads it. The
  check also says which consent floors the window holds when it draws the theme, and which
  tokens it draws as purlis's own for them (#2518).
- **Set a theme's options per project and workspace.** Settings › Theme lets you pick the value of
  each of the chosen theme's options at You, Project and Workspace, kept on your machine with
  your theme choice. The nearest level's values are drawn, and each value's badge names the
  level that chose it (#2527).
- **Theme options.** A theme folder's `theme.json` can declare toggles and choices, each value a
  layer of token values over every appearance (and over one appearance by its id). An option
  nothing chose draws its default. `purlis theme check` covers every combination of appearance
  and option values and names the combination each warning is found in; a theme with more than
  64 combinations is refused with its count. Settings › Theme shows the options of the
  theme drawn, with where each value comes from (#2325).
- **A chat can see a theme without seeing your window.** purlis draws the theme specimen, a
  fixed page of sample content (every control, a chat pane, an editor, a terminal in every ANSI
  colour, a Settings page, a dialog and a Notice), in a hidden window of its own, and a chat's
  new `theme_preview` tool returns its picture in any theme and appearance, alone or two side
  by side (#2330).
- **A theme exports to and imports from the W3C design-tokens format.** `purlis theme export
  <theme> --kind design-tokens` writes a theme folder as one `.tokens.json` file in the Design
  Tokens Community Group's format 2025.10, for a design tool, and `purlis theme import` reads one
  back, from purlis or from a design tool. Exporting and then importing gives the same theme,
  its component parts, grey tiers and files included. `theme.json` stays the format purlis reads
  a theme in (#2926).
- **A theme can colour code, markdown, the selection, the caret, placeholders, scrollbars, charts
  and the window's background.** New tokens: `syntax.*` for the light editor's code, each role
  with italic and bold; `markdown.*` for links, code, code blocks, quotes and headings in a
  markdown render; `selection.*`, `caret`, `placeholder` and `scrollbar.*` for what the platform
  draws until a theme says; `chart.1`–`chart.8`; `window.background`; and the terminal's
  selected text, unfocused selection, scrollbar, cursor style and blink, line height and bold in
  the bright colours. The editor no longer borrows the terminal's colours for code. Purlis
  Classic sets each to what it drew before (#2327).
- **`themes/` is a reserved folder, at the project's root and in every workspace.** It holds
  theme folders, one per theme, each with its `theme.json`, and `purlis doctor` names anything
  there that is not one (#2314).
- **Every third-party crate and npm package purlis ships, with its licence text.** About ›
  Licences now lists, under purlis's own notice and licence, each Rust crate and npm package the
  build was made from, grouped by the licence text it ships. The macOS app and the Linux
  packages carry the same list as `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES` beside `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`. The list
  is generated from the locked dependency graph each time purlis is built, so it cannot fall
  behind, and a build fails when a package it ships has no licence text (#1784).
- **Tile all evens a tab's panes into a grid.** The tab's right-click menu and the palette offer
  it, and a split tab shows it at the right end of the tab strip. It arranges only the panes
  already in the tab, in reading order, and "Undo the last layout change" in the palette puts
  them back. In a tab with one pane the menu and the palette show it greyed (#4765).
- **A todo opens in a tab of its own.** Clicking a todo in the Todos panel, or pressing Enter on
  it, opens it as a tab on its workspace's strip with its whole text, when it was opened, its
  state, and Mark done and Forget. A todo whose tab is already open brings that tab forward, and
  the palette has an *Open todo: …* row for each one (#1214).
- **Optional limits on one task's working time and on a session's tokens.** Settings › Project
  › Dispatch has two more limits, off until set, at the same levels as the others. *Minutes per task* counts a task's working time only (not time it waits on you
  or on its own tasks, nor time purlis was closed, and a task put back after a restart keeps
  what it had); a task past it is asked for its report and ended with its own tasks, never while
  you are answering or typing in it, and the chat that asked is told it was its time limit.
  At *Tokens per session* a session starts no new task, its tasks at work are asked for their
  report (never one you are answering or typing in), and its row shows its figure against the
  limit. A harness that reports no tokens is not counted, and Settings says so (#1512, #1457).
- **How to uninstall purlis.** A new page, *Uninstall purlis* (`docs/uninstall.md`), says where
  purlis keeps its state on a machine and what each step of an uninstall removes: the keyring
  items, what `purlis plugin uninstall` takes back, the app and its command links, and the
  config, data and app folders. It says what an uninstall leaves alone, your projects among
  them, and what to copy out first (#610).
- **Update from remote, in the window.** Where the Saving view and the title bar say how many
  commits came in (`↓N`), there is now an **Update** to press. purlis brings the commits in
  itself, outside every chat's sandbox, from the remote recorded for the project and with your
  purlis sign-in, held as every fetch is. A project that is only behind is fast-forwarded; one
  with commits of its own has them replayed on top. A project with unsaved work is never
  touched and nothing is stashed: the button is *Save, then update* where a save can run. In
  the request modes (`pr`, `pr-merge`), commits an open request carries wait for it to merge,
  as the mode says; commits no request carries yet are replayed.
- **An update leaves the project at the new commit, or exactly as it was.** Nothing starts
  where a file the incoming commits change cannot be written or a file is in the way, and an
  update git stops part-way is undone and checked. Why it was left is a Notice in the Saving
  view, with the files and a way out.
- **A chat refused an update of the project's root asks you for it.** The refusal now names
  the window's Update, and the chat gets a needs-you item that says so.
- **Use skill… has a key: `⌘⇧S`, or `Ctrl+Shift+S` off a Mac.** It opens Use skill… on the chat in front, and Shortcuts lists it (#3954).
- **Use the default layout, from the Alerts drawer.** A layout file purlis could not use, and a
  dismissal it could not keep there, could only be dismissed for one launch. The row now offers
  *Use the default layout…*, which asks first and then moves the file aside to
  `layout.aside.json` (or the next free name), never over a file. The question says what goes
  aside with it: the arrangement, the text sizes, your editor, how chats are listed, the
  Notices you dismissed and the ones seen once (#1289).
- **Use your existing gh or glab login.** Where `gh` or `glab` is signed in to github.com or
  gitlab.com and purlis has no account there yet, the welcome's **Sign in to GitHub or GitLab**
  and Settings › You › Accounts offer **Use my gh login** (or glab). The offer says first what it
  does: the token the tool keeps is copied into purlis's own item in your system keychain, which
  purlis never hands to a chat. A chat that runs the tool itself can still use its own stored
  login, so sign out of the tool if you don't want that. **Not now** comes first,
  and nothing is imported unless you press **Use my … login**. The token is checked with the
  forge like a pasted one, never shown in the window, and never reaches a chat. The tool keeps
  its own login (#1376).
- **Your desktop records each run's vault values it sends to a runner.** The record,
  `secret.forwarded`, names the vault, the keys (never a value), the runner the chat's link
  reached, its pool, the chat, the persona and the tool, and the runner's own record of the run
  says its values came from your desktop, naming the same request. Like every record of a secret
  handed out, it is kept until it is audited (#3406).
- **A chat can wait for a task's report, list its tasks and cancel one.** `purlis dispatch
  --wait` (and the `dispatch` tool's `wait`) holds the command until the report lands and
  prints it as the result, for 100 seconds unless `--timeout` says otherwise and 540 at most;
  a wait that runs out says the task is still running and how to look again, and
  `purlis dispatch wait <chat>` waits on a task dispatched earlier. `purlis dispatch list` (and
  the `dispatch_list` tool) prints each task's chat number, name, persona, place, state and
  age. `purlis dispatch cancel <chat>` ends the task's turn and asks it for one short report,
  which arrives with the outcome `cancelled`. A chat can do these only to tasks it dispatched
  itself (#1441).
- **An asking chat is told when a report lands.** Where purlis may type into it, purlis types
  one line of its own, which starts the turn the report arrives on as context. It types into a
  chat only on a harness it has measured (Claude Code; Codex once you have trusted purlis's
  hooks there), only once that chat has reported since it started, never in a turn that has
  shown you a prompt, and never after a key of yours in its pane until the chat next reports a
  turn. Anywhere else the report waits for the next turn, as before; on opencode it always
  does. A cancel sends Escape and its line under the same rules, and otherwise takes effect
  when the task's turn ends. One chat may have 16 waits under way at once (#1441).
- **purlis estimates weekly users without an identifier.** The first update check of each
  ISO week reads the channel's weekly manifest, `latest-weekly.json` or `dev-weekly.json`, which
  has the same bytes as the manifest. Its download count is the estimate. The request is the
  same from every machine and carries no id. `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` opts out.
  `docs/updating.md` gives the estimator and its biases (OB-17, #688).
- **A project that expects a local socket or a system service asks you once, when you open
  it.** A project's settings can declare what its chats need (`[sandbox] expects`), and a
  declaration allows nothing by itself. Until now you learned of it when a tool failed in a
  chat. Now one notice lists each item not yet allowed on this machine, with what allowing it
  means, and offers **Allow on this machine** or **Not now**. Not now is remembered until the
  project declares something new, and Settings › Sandbox keeps a row, **This project expects**,
  with the same Allow. A chat that starts before you answer says so in its pane. Allow keeps
  each item as the notice showed it: one that changed on this machine since is shown again
  instead. A project declares at most 32 items.
- **Allow a socket or a service for every project on this machine.** A sandbox block on a local
  socket or a system service now offers **Allow on this machine, for every project** beside
  Allow once, so Docker's socket or your SSH agent is not asked about again in each project.
  It is listed under Settings › Sandbox › Network as "Every project on this machine", in every
  project, and Remove takes it from all of them. Hosts and folders stay per project.
- **What a session's tasks used.** The tab's task menu ends with one line that adds up what
  its tasks used: `5 tasks · 310k tokens · 6m`, the tokens of every task, open or ended, and
  how long they worked, added up. Its tooltip says what it adds up, what it leaves out, and the
  session's own chat's figure, which is not in the total. Rest the pointer on a task, in that
  menu or in the Chats list, and it says the task's tokens in and out. They are the figures each
  chat's harness reported; a task that has ended keeps what it used. A missing figure is a dash
  with the reason (nothing reported yet, nothing reported, or not known), never a zero, and a
  total or a time that misses any task's part says `at least`. No money figure is shown.
  Nothing is read on a timer: the figures are read when the menu opens, when one of its chats
  changes state, and when the pointer rests on a task (#1500).
- **What a task changed.** A finished task's row has **Changes** (**Review changes** for a
  task on its own branch), and its report's line about what changed opens the same tab. A
  task on its own branch lists everything its branch changed, each file opening its diff. A
  task that worked in a folder other chats share lists the files its own edit tools wrote
  that are still uncommitted there; it cannot see edits made by a shell command, what the
  task already committed there, or anything after the app is started again, and says so.
- **Merge and discard a task's own branch.** In its Changes tab, **Merge…** lands exactly the
  commit you were shown in the branch it was cut from, as a fast-forward or not at all, and
  **Discard branch…** removes its folder; each asks first. A merge that does not apply
  cleanly changes nothing and says why. Only you can have purlis merge or discard: no chat
  can, through purlis.
- **Two tasks of one chat working in one folder with no branch of their own are named**, both
  of them, when the second starts and on the asking chat's tab (#1511).
- **What is left of a task's branch whose folder is gone.** A dispatch's row whose branch
  folder was discarded or removed has **Review changes**, and the task's Changes tab says
  whether the branch is still in the repo and whether the branch the repo is on holds it.
  Where it does, **Delete branch…** deletes it, asked first; one that holds work stays (#1472).
- **A task's question that reaches you is a quiz at the top of its session's pane.** It says who
  asks, why it reached you (its asking chat passed it on, didn't reply in 100 seconds, or has
  closed), the asking chat's note as its own, and how long it has waited, with a box to answer
  in. One at a time, oldest first, with a count of the rest. It never takes the keyboard or
  switches a tab, and it stays in the ✋ and the Inbox wherever it's drawn (#4565).
- **Where you answer**, in Settings › Chats list: from the top (the default) or from each
  session, where each question waits in its task's own tab. It's offered once, as a quiet line
  above the first question, and a change applies to open questions at once. Any task can still
  be opened and answered either way (#4565).
- **While you were away counts dispatches refused while nobody was at their chat.** "1
  dispatch refused" is a part of the summary, and opens the title bar's list where it is
  answered (#1551).
- **While you were away: one summary of what happened.** When you come back after five minutes
  or more away from the window (in another app or window, or with no key or pointer on it), one
  Notice per project says what happened meanwhile, each project its own: "While you were away: 7 tasks done, 1 failed, 2 waiting on you". Each part is a
  link: one chat goes straight to it, several open a list of them. A chat waiting on you is shown
  where it lives, where its question is answered as before, and a finished task goes to its row
  under the chat that asked; going to a failed task marks it looked at, as its needs-you item
  does. Only what happened while you were away is counted. The summary hides nothing: each task
  keeps its row and its Activity lines, and Dismiss puts away the summary and nothing else. _Away summary_ in Settings, under Chats list,
  turns it off (#1514).
- **`workspace_vision` and `workspace_section` tools** on purlis's MCP server. A chat sets its
  workspace's vision, or adds one decision or one glossary term to its `workspace.md`, at any
  point in a session, not only at smart close. In a chat purlis started, purlis writes it for the
  chat, in the chat's own workspace, and credits it to the chat; what a section already holds is
  kept. `purlis workspace vision "<text>"` run in such a chat hands its write to purlis the same
  way (#1384).
- **Your own sandbox level, per project and per persona** (#2071). Settings › Project ›
  Sandbox › Your level sets how much the sandbox holds for your chats in this project:
  full sandbox, floor or no sandbox, for the project and, if you want, for each persona. It is
  kept in this machine's `purlis.local.toml` under `[sandbox] level` and `[sandbox.personas]`,
  never in a committed file, and a value that is not a level is refused with a sentence. A
  level you pick there counts as yours; a lower one written into the file any other way waits
  on the page with Confirm, since a chat can write that file.
  Chats take it at their start once the floor lands; until then it is saved and shown only.
- **Move a plain-file vault into the keychain.** The same page lists the project's plain-file
  vaults, which a chat with no sandbox could read like any file, and moves each one this machine
  registers into the system keychain: every secret is written and read back before the vault
  is switched and its file goes, a move that stops takes back what it wrote and says anything
  it could not, and a vault the team's file registers is the team's to move.
- **A redesigned first window.** With no project open, the ways in now stay down the left of the
  window and each one opens its page beside them. Recent projects sit in the same place on every
  launch, and a person who has already been through setup is no longer counted through steps.
- **Create a project on this Mac from a name alone**, with no repo and no account. Starting from
  a repo you already have is still on the same page.
- **The event log keeps 30 days and can be followed from a cursor.** The host's event log
  (`<data>/events/<device>/`) is now written in segments: at 16 MiB a segment is sealed as
  `events.<first seq>.jsonl`, and a sealed segment whose newest event is more than 30 days old is
  deleted when the log is opened or a segment sealed. A client subscribes from the last `seq` it
  holds and gets every later event once and in order, across segments and across a host that was
  killed and started again; a cursor older than what is kept is told what it missed (FD-24,
  #661).
- **A first task, beside your first chat.** After the first run opens your repo, a **First task**
  tab sits beside the chat. It gives one small, real task to two chats, on two harnesses or two
  profiles of one, each on a branch of its own in purlis's copy of your repo, with the task typed
  in for you to read and send. The task asks each chat to record what it learned, so the second
  chat starts with the first one's lesson in its briefing, whichever harness it runs on. **Show its
  diff** opens a shell in that chat's branch with its diff. Nothing is written into your repo, and
  the task asks for nothing to be pushed (FR-28, #621).
- **No harness found.** On a machine with no Claude Code, Codex or opencode, opening your repo
  on the first run opens a **Set up a harness** tab instead of the chat picker. It lists each
  harness with its vendor's own install command, and **Install** runs exactly that command in
  a shell tab at the project's root. Each installer puts its harness where purlis looks, so **Check
  again** finds it without a restart, and **Start a chat** opens the picker on it; the harness asks
  for its own login when its chat starts. If Ollama or LM Studio is already answering on this
  machine, the tab says so and names opencode as the harness that can use it with no account.
- **A local network log.** purlis's forge calls, through its own client or through `gh` and
  `glab`, `purlis report`'s filing and the updater's reads are listed in
  `~/.config/charter/network-log/`, a file a day, kept for 30 days. Each line says which feature
  called which host, with the method, the path with names masked, the status and the time it
  took, and whether it went to purlis or to a third party. It never holds a body, a header, a
  token, a query or the names in a path, and nothing sends it anywhere. Without an account, and
  unless you send a report, the only purlis addresses it lists are the updater's.
- **Read any file of a worktree in purlis.** A worktree's menu in the explorer has *Browse the
  files of …*: a tab listing the worktree's files, narrowed as you type, with the file you pick
  drawn beside the list in the light editor, purlis's read-only CodeMirror 6 viewer with syntax
  colours from your theme. *Open in a tab of its own* gives a file a tab to itself. A binary file
  or one past 5 MiB is named rather than drawn. The diff view the Review tab will use is built
  on the same component (RC-5, #706).
- **Agent commits say who made them.** A commit an agent makes in a chat, with its own
  `git commit` in a workspace repo or with `purlis save` in the project, ends with git
  trailers: `Assisted-by: <harness>:<model>`, `Charter-Chat: <chat id>`,
  `Charter-Persona: <persona>`, and `Charter-Change: <change>` when its branch is a change's. A
  trailer purlis does not know is left out, a commit you make by hand gets none, and your own
  `Co-Authored-By` lines stay. Set `assisted_by = "llm"` under `[plane]` or `[repos.<name>]` for
  the Linux kernel's bare `Assisted-by: LLM` (V67, GL-8, #702).
- **Link a chat to a work item.** A chat tab's menu and the palette have **Link to work item…**,
  which asks for the item's tracker key (`github:github.com/owner/repo#12`, or a todo's
  `todo:<workspace>/<todo>`), and **Unlink work item**. A linked chat shows `Work item: <key>`
  in its tab's tooltip and in its pane's corner. A chat works on one work item at a time. The
  link goes in the workspace's work link log, so it reaches your other devices when the
  workspace is LIVE, and it follows a todo when that todo is promoted to an issue. A chat at
  the project root is not offered it (V60, ADR 0088, FW-5, #732, #914).
- **Promote a todo to an issue.** `purlis ws todo promote <slug> --repo <repo>` opens an issue
  with the todo's title and text in one of the workspace's repos, on GitHub or GitLab, as you.
  It names the repo, whether it is public and the workspace label it adds (private repos only)
  before it sends anything, and refuses a repo that is archived or takes no issue from your
  account. The todo is then closed, journalled as `Promoted todo:
  <title> → <issue>`, and an alias in the workspace's new work link log
  (`workspaces/<ws>/work/<device>.jsonl`, committed with a LIVE workspace) makes every work link
  on the todo reach the issue. The Work list shows the issue once, not the issue and the todo
  Claude Code and opencode ask you before
  any spelling of it runs: `purlis init` and `purlis reinit` write the ask rule
  `purlis *todo*promote*` (V42) (ADR 0088, FW-5, #732).
- **The changes view pushes a change and lands a member, and asks first.** Each change in the
  changes tab has a **Push** button, and each member row a **Land** button. Push names every
  repo, branch, commit and destination, and where each pull request or merge request goes, before
  anything is pushed. Land runs every gate first: a refusal is shown beside the row in the same
  words as `purlis change land`, and otherwise it names the request, the head commit its
  checks passed at, and whether purlis merges it now or puts it in the merge queue or merge
  train. Pressing Push or Land does exactly what was shown, and nothing if it has changed since
  (#474).
- **A chat keeps its id across a relaunch.** The app records each chat's id, the device that
  made it and its current run in `.charter/app/reopen.json`, so the event log names a reopened
  chat as the chat it was, and its first event after the relaunch is `run.started` with cause
  `reopen`. A chat that comes back without its conversation, or that **Resume** starts again
  after its harness could not find the conversation, begins a `fresh` run in the same chat
  (ADR 0066, #834).
- **A copied project's chats get ids of their own.** A project copied with its `.charter/`
  directory (`cp -R`, rsync, a backup restore) used to carry its original's chat ids, so the two
  clones' events named one chat. The record now says which clone and device wrote it, and the
  first launch of a copy, at another path or on another machine, gives every chat a new id. A
  moved project keeps its ids. Its chats also get new ids when the project moves to another
  machine, when the machine store is reset, and when a different `PURLIS_CONFIG_HOME` opens
  it. A copy keeps its ids only when its original has
  been deleted and was never opened on this machine (V43,
  amending ADR 0066).
- **The supported platforms are written down.** macOS 27 and 26 on Apple silicon, Ubuntu 26.04
  and 24.04 LTS, and Fedora 44, each with the CI job that covers it and what that job proves,
  are in the README and in `docs/platforms.md`. macOS 27, Ubuntu 26.04 and Fedora are covered
  by evidence jobs, which report and never gate. Windows 11 joins the list when the
  Windows port lands; iOS 16.4 and the current desktop browsers are the floor for clients that
  do not exist yet (FR-25, #619).
- **A project switcher.** ⌘P (Ctrl+Shift+P off a Mac), the new button at the start of the
  project strip's controls, or *Switch project…* in the palette lists the projects open in the
  window, the last one you were in first and already selected, so the key and Enter take you
  back to it. Pressing the key again moves down the list, and typing narrows it by name. The
  button shows once a window holds two projects (FR-27, #620).
- **`purlis change revert` undoes a cross-repo change as a new one.** `purlis change revert
  <change>` creates `revert-<change>`: for every member purlis landed, a branch off that repo's
  default branch carrying `git revert` of the commit purlis recorded, ordered so a member that
  depended on another is reverted first. It pushes and merges nothing; you push and land the
  revert with `purlis change push` and `purlis change land` like any other change. A member
  merged outside purlis is named for you to revert by hand. A recorded commit that is not a
  commit id, or that the default branch no longer holds, is refused by name, and so is a clone
  with uncommitted work. A revert that conflicts is aborted and its branch left for you to
  finish. Run it again once a refusal is put right, and it seeds only the members it has not
  seeded yet. It never force-pushes, deletes a branch or resets one (#473).
- **`purlis change land` lands one member of a cross-repo change.** `purlis change land
  <change> --repo <name>` merges that member's request at the commit its checks passed on, and
  only once every member it needs has landed. Each refusal says which gate stopped it: a
  blocker not landed, checks failed, running, not run or unreadable at that commit, a branch
  that moved after the checks were read, or more than one member named. Where the target
  branch has a merge queue (GitHub) or a merge train (GitLab), the request goes into it at that
  commit, and running `land` again after it merged records the landing. A merge purlis did
  not start, in the browser or before a queue existed, is never recorded as purlis's. It never
  turns on auto-merge. The landing commit carries a `Charter-Change:` trailer where the forge lets
  purlis write the message, and a line goes into the change's landing log once the forge
  confirms the merge. Like `gh pr merge`, it is refused in a session nobody is watching.
  `purlis doctor` now also names a member landed ahead of one it needs, a member's pushed
  branch merged outside purlis, and a request GitLab was left set to merge later (#472).
- **`purlis change push` pushes a cross-repo change.** For each member it prints the repo,
  the branch and where it goes, then pushes the branch, opens its pull request into the repo's
  default branch (or finds the one already there), and writes a block into each request's
  description that lists every member's request, so a partial landing can be read from any one
  repo. Running it again opens no second request, and the block is rewritten in place when the
  members change; the rest of the description is left alone. It commits nothing, never
  force-pushes, sends no tags with the branch, and pushes repos whose save mode is `off` too.
  A repo whose git config sends pushes somewhere other than the URL printed is refused. A
  member that is not a repo in this workspace is refused by name and the others are still
  pushed. GitLab members are pushed and their merge requests opened and updated the same way,
  on gitlab.com and on a self-managed GitLab declared in `charter.toml`; a draft merge request
  is adopted and stays a draft, and one from a fork with the same branch name is never touched.
  When members are on different hosts, a member elsewhere is named by its request's link, so
  a GitLab description never points at a GitHub number as if it were a GitLab one. The guard
  that stops a live substitution in `purlis change create` or `drop` now names `purlis
  change push` as what writes the `why` into requests (#471).
- **The first run lays your project out for the stack you work in.** Project templates for
  Rust, TypeScript, Python, Go, monorepos and docs-only repos each add an engineer and a
  reviewer persona, a review checklist (`REVIEW.md`, in the reviewer's refs), how a change is
  checked in the workspace's `workspace.md`, and the publish and deploy commands, such as
  `cargo publish` or `twine upload`, that Claude Code and opencode ask you about before they run
  them. Codex's command rules live in `CODEX_HOME` or a trusted project's `.codex/rules`, which
  purlis does not write, so purlis's own guard applies there. The first run picks the
  template that fits your repo from the files at its top level, and says which when you type the
  path; pick another, or None, before you open it. Nothing is written into your repo, nothing you
  already have is replaced, and a command you deny stays denied.
