- **A project can say which purlis it needs.** When a newer purlis starts writing something an
  older one would get wrong, it lists the feature in `charter.toml`'s `requires` and sets
  `schema = 2`. A purlis that lacks the feature, or does not understand the project's `schema`,
  or cannot read its `charter.toml`, treats the project as read-only. `purlis` still reads it
  (`status`, `recall`, `statusline`, `doctor`, and the `list` commands of workspaces, personas,
  changes, sessions, harnesses and guards, plus `workspace recall`), saying once that it is
  read-only and why. Every command that could write it is refused, extension commands,
  `doctor --fix`, `init` and `reinit` included, with the version to upgrade to (update the app); `purlis
  doctor`'s `schema` row says the same. Keys and sections purlis does not know are kept when it
  rewrites `charter.toml` or a workspace's `workspace.json`. The window and the chat hooks will
  follow the same rule before any release carries it (#826).
- **A chat that starts in a repo gets a branch of its own.** Start a chat with *New tab in
  <repo>*, or after *Start new chats in <repo>*, and purlis cuts a new branch for it, in a folder
  beside the repo's clone, so two chats in one repo no longer edit the same files. The branch is
  named after the chat, or `chat-1`, `chat-2` and on. Clear *start on a new branch* in the picker
  to work on the branch the repo has checked out, as before. If the chat does not start, the
  branch goes with it. *New branch in <repo>…* on the repo's menu and in the palette cuts one
  without starting a chat, and new chats start on it.
- **A chat in its own worktree leaves an `AGENTS.md` behind for any agent that opens it.** When
  a chat starts in a piece of a repo that has no `AGENTS.md`, purlis writes one there, hidden
  from `git status`. It says which persona the chat was started as and which piece it holds, so
  a Codex, opencode or other agent started there by hand is told the same. It never carries
  memory, todos or session records, and it is never written into a shared clone. A repo that has
  its own `AGENTS.md` keeps it. Because git hides the file by one line for every worktree of the
  repo, `purlis doctor`, a note on the chat's pane and the chat's briefing name any `AGENTS.md`
  of yours that line hides (ADR 0085).
- **purlis keeps a log of every hook call its chats make.** Each state hook and each tool call
  is one line in the event log in purlis's data home (`~/Library/Application Support/charter`
  on macOS, `~/.local/share/charter` on Linux, or `PURLIS_DATA_HOME`). A line records the chat
  and the run it happened in, the tool, what purlis's guard answered and how long it took. A
  tool call's arguments are never written, only a digest keyed to this machine. The log is
  never committed or sent anywhere; a backup of purlis's data carries it, and anything running
  as your user can read it. The coming timeline, audit and fleet views are built from it (#649).
- **The first run offers your repo's agent instructions to its workspace's memory.** When the
  repo you open has a `CLAUDE.md`, an `AGENTS.md` or Cursor rules in `.cursor/rules`, a *Memory
  from the repo* tab opens beside the first chat, showing each file whole. Press Add to memory
  and every chat in that workspace starts with them, whichever agent runs it. Nothing is written
  until you press it, and nothing is ever written into your repo. A link, a file over 64 KB, or
  one that looks like it holds a secret is left out and says which line. A file over 8 KB, or one
  with invisible characters, starts unticked, and the preview shows each invisible character by
  its code point.
- **Where to get help, in the app and the repository.** About purlis now links to Discussions
  for questions and ideas, to the bug report form, and to `SUPPORT.md`, which says where each
  kind of question goes and how soon it gets a first response. The repository gains a Code of
  Conduct (Contributor Covenant 2.1), a `CONTRIBUTING.md` with DCO sign-off, issue and
  discussion forms, and a pull request template (#609).
- **Every release says what it is made of.** Each release carries a CycloneDX SBOM per platform
  (`charter-macos-arm64.cdx.json`, `charter-linux-x86_64.cdx.json`). It lists the Rust crates
  read out of the built binaries and the front end's npm packages from its lockfile. Every
  Rust binary purlis ships now carries its own dependency list, so
  `cargo audit bin` can check an installed copy against the RustSec advisories. `SECURITY.md`
  says how to read both (#584).
- **Every build file a release publishes carries signed build provenance.** Each installer and
  updater archive now has a SLSA build provenance attestation, so you can check that a download
  came out of purlis's own release workflow with `gh attestation verify`. `SECURITY.md` has
  the command (#583). The update manifest (`latest.json`, `dev.json`) is not attested; the
  updater checks each build's own minisign signature, as before.
- **The app keeps a log you can read after the fact.** What the app notices while it runs, such
  as a chat that would not start, a project it could not watch or a record it could not write,
  now goes to `charter.<date>.log` in the app's log directory (`~/Library/Logs/dev.charter.app`
  on macOS, `~/.local/share/dev.charter.app/logs` on Linux), as well as to standard error. An app
  started from the Dock or a desktop launcher used to lose all of it. A new file starts each
  day and the last seven are kept. A line that looks like it holds a credential is replaced by
  a note saying what kind it looked like. `PURLIS_LOG_DIR` moves the log.
- **A kill switch that stops every chat and shell purlis started.** Stop all on the title bar,
  or `purlis stop --all` in any terminal, interrupts and ends every chat's and shell's program in
  every project and every window within seconds. No chat starts again, not even from a relaunch,
  until you re-arm it from the title bar; you can still open a shell to look around. The stopped
  chats stay as tabs to reopen. Each stop, re-arm and tamper is one line in `kill-switch.jsonl`
  in purlis's config directory (ADR 0071).
- **A plane can run every Claude Code chat in a sandbox.** Add `[sandbox]` with `mode = "on"`
  to `charter.toml`, and every Claude Code chat purlis starts there runs inside Claude Code's
  own sandbox, which purlis compiles from one policy. It can reach only the hosts of the
  plane's egress presets. Claude Code's web tools are turned off, because the host list does
  not hold them. The chat can never read a vault's storage or write purlis's own state. A
  plane can turn the sandbox on but never off, and a mistyped `mode` turns it on. If the
  sandbox cannot be applied, the chat does not start, and purlis says what is missing and how
  to install it. `SECURITY.md` says what the sandbox covers and what it does not. Planes that
  say nothing run as before (#695).
  **What this cannot do yet:**
  - A plane with a keyring vault starts no Claude Code chat while the sandbox is on. Keyring is
    the default vault provider, so on most machines this release can sandbox only a plane with
    no keyring vault. That lifts when purlis can wrap the harness, or resolve secrets for the
    chat.
  - opencode chats are not started in a sandboxed plane yet.
- **Codex chats run in the sandbox too.** In a plane with `mode = "on"`, every Codex chat
  purlis starts runs in Codex's own workspace-write sandbox, which purlis selects explicitly
  and compiles from the same policy. It reaches only the plane's egress hosts, through Codex's
  own proxy, and never reads a vault's storage or writes purlis's own state. Codex never asks
  to run a command outside the sandbox, and its web search is off. A Codex chat whose command
  would drop or widen the sandbox is refused, and the refusal names the flag and where it is.
  That covers `-s`, `--add-dir`, `--cd`, `--enable`, `--disable`, an approval flag other than
  `-a never`, and a `-c` for anything but the model and how it is shown. A Codex without the
  proxy feature starts no sandboxed chat. As with Claude Code, a plane with a keyring vault
  starts no sandboxed Codex chat yet (#695).
- **A first run that goes straight to a chat.** On a machine with no project, purlis asks for
  one thing: the repo to work on. It makes a project for you on this machine only
  (`~/.config/charter/local-plane`, with no remote), copies your repo into a workspace named
  after it, and opens the first chat there. When exactly one of Claude Code, Codex and opencode
  is signed in, the chat starts on it without asking. The screen shows what is installed and
  signed in, and offers **Sign in to GitHub**, which runs `gh auth login` in a shell tab. New
  project asks for a repo the same way, and the two-folder form is under Advanced (#603).
- **A chat's commits are scanned for secrets and personal data before they are made, in any
  repository.** Every chat the app starts on a harness commits through purlis's own git
  hooks. Before each commit, including a merge commit, purlis reads the lines the commit adds.
  These refuse the commit:
  - a token or key in a vendor's known shape (purlis's forge-prefix rules plus gitleaks'
    prefix-anchored vendor rules);
  - an email address;
  - a card number;
  - a US Social Security number.
  git prints where each one is and what kind it is, with the value masked, and the chat joins
  the needs-you queue saying why. This holds in a workspace repo, a piece, or a repository
  outside any plane. The repository's own hooks (husky, pre-commit, git-lfs) still run after
  purlis's check, except `post-index-change` and `reference-transaction`, which purlis does
  not forward. The guard also refuses `git commit --no-verify`, `-n`, and a
  `core.hooksPath` or `GIT_CONFIG_*` set on the command line. These are not treated as anyone's
  email: documentation and private-use domains (`example.com`, `.test`, `.internal`, `.local`),
  no-reply addresses, `git@host` remotes, and image names like `logo@2x.png`. The allowlist
  below lets any other false positive through. Commits made by `cherry-pick`, `rebase` and
  `am` are not scanned (#592, ADR 0074).
- **An allowlist for the commit scan.** A repository's `.charter-scan-allow.toml` lets a
  finding through by its rule and paths. A key can also be let through by its fingerprint;
  personal data never is. Every entry gives its reason, and the file is reviewed like code.
  `purlis scan --explain` names a finding's rule and prints the entry that would let it
  through. The file is read as committed. A chat's own commit may not change it, and neither may
  its `git revert` or `git merge --ff-only`, so the operator is the one who commits an entry.
  This is a guard against mistakes; the sandbox is where it becomes a boundary (#784). An
  author's email in `Cargo.toml`, `package.json`, `.mailmap`, `AUTHORS`, `CONTRIBUTORS` or a
  `CHANGELOG` passes with no entry at all, unless `[builtin] enabled = false` turns that off
  (#593).

## Changed

- **A vault refusal is an ask in the Inbox** (#5160). A vault a chat was refused for its persona
  is counted on the ✋ and said in a notification like any other ask. Allow and Keep blocked
  answer it there as they do on the chat's pane, and an answer in either place clears both. A
  chat in no pane has it in the Inbox rather than in the Notices centre.
- **A filled form that posts straight to another site is refused unless the key is approved for that
  site too.** The chat's answer and the page you see in the browser name the site and say how to
  approve the key for it (#5230).
- **`op` no longer sees the `OP_*` variables purlis was started with.** purlis runs the 1Password
  CLI with its own environment less every `OP_` variable, and adds only what the vault declares.
  A token, a session (`OP_SESSION_*`), a Connect server or a settings folder (`OP_CONFIG_DIR`)
  your shell exports no longer decides whose identity a vault is read under: a vault with no
  token of its own signs in through the 1Password app. If you relied on one, declare it on the
  vault as a name when you register it (`--env OP_CONFIG_DIR=<VAR>`) (#1542).
- **After a vault stops reading a variable, purlis asks you to remove its export.** Converting a
  1Password vault from an environment variable to a token kept in the keyring (from its tab, or
  with `purlis vault add --token-stdin`) now names the variable when no vault of any project
  this machine opened reads it any more, and asks for its `export` line to be taken out of your
  shell's startup files (#1542).
- **A sandbox refusal a chat only read back is a quiet line.** When a chat reads the output of
  a command that ran earlier and it holds a refusal's words, the Notice now says so, asks
  nothing, and stays out of the Inbox. *Show what you can do* opens the choices it had before.
- **A save blocked by what looks like a credential says where.** The title bar and the Inbox
  name the file and the line ("Blocked: a secret-shaped value in personas/…/note.md, line 5").
  The Saving view lists each file with its line, the kind of value, and what was matched with
  the value hidden, and offers **Open the file**, which starts your editor at that line, and
  **Save again**. The value itself is never shown.
- **`[sandbox].certificate-checks` now says a project expects certificate checks, and allows
  nothing by itself.** Projects that set it now get one Allow per machine the first time a Go
  tool checks a certificate: the Notice says the project expects it, and Always allow keeps it
  for that project on that machine (ADR 0093).
- **`purlis worktree add` cuts from the remote's default branch** (`main`, most often), brought
  up to the remote where nothing has it checked out, rather than from whatever the clone is on.
  `--base <branch>` names another branch; `--base HEAD` keeps the clone's HEAD (qw387).
- **A branch folder purlis could not read says why.** Where the link check refuses a branch
  folder, or git does not answer in it, the Changes view's branch row now gives the sentence,
  and the explorer's branch row is marked unreadable with the sentence as its tooltip. Before,
  its count was missing with no reason (#1476).
- **A chat's git write that the sandbox blocks in a branch folder no longer raises a Notice for
  you.** When a chat's `git add` or `git commit` in its branch folder slips past the guard and
  meets the sandbox, the chat alone is told to retry with `purlis worktree commit`. The block
  is still kept in the network record (#3861).
- **A host refused while a brokered command ran says the vault it ran with.** The chat's sandbox
  block Notice reads "while running a command with vault <name>", so you can judge whether that
  vault belongs at that host before you allow it. It names the vault, never a value, and says the
  chat's harness as a block of the chat's own command does. Such a host has a Notice of its own,
  apart from hosts the chat's own commands were refused (#1353).
- **A refusals list's Allow says the same words as every Notice.** Settings › Network and a
  chat's Network view now say _Allow for me on this machine_ and _Allow for everyone in this
  project_, the words the Notices and the Inbox use (#1700).
- **A browser login follows the site to its login form before you're asked** (#4995). On a site
  that signs in on another host, the notice shows the page it opens and the host the password is
  typed on, both large, and warns when they differ. The password is typed on that host alone,
  and Always allow records it in the login's line as `form`.
- **A browser login that signs in on another host keeps its signed-in browser** (#5014), like any
  other login. It reopens held to the login's page's site, and reaches the sign-in host again
  once it signs in anew.
- **Every browser's end is in the log.** The window's log says who ended a browser, why, and its
  engine's exit code or signal. Each engine's own log is kept beside its browser's folder,
  `<data>/browsers/<id>.engine.log`, the newest 20 of them (#2745).
- **The browser purlis opens to find a suggested login's form counts toward the project's browser
  limit** (#5015). Where the project is full, the chat is told so, and a chat whose suggested
  pages can't be followed three times has none followed for ten minutes, with a sentence that
  says what to do.
- **A burst of chat events is one redraw of the window, however many it carries.** A chat's
  context gauge reads its record again at every move and every few seconds mid-turn, and each
  answer redrew the chat's pane even when it said what the last one did. An unchanged answer
  now redraws nothing, so what busy chats tell the window in one frame is drawn in a single
  commit (#4882).
- **A busy chat behind the edge of the chat strip no longer redraws the project.** The show-more
  menu lists the tabs the strip has no room for, most recently moved first. That order used to
  be worked out for the whole project view, so every move of a hidden chat redrew all of it. It
  is now worked out by the menu alone, so with many busy chats open, background activity costs
  the window only that menu (#4726).
- **A task's cancel is bounded the way your Stop is.** When a chat cancels a task it dispatched,
  the task now gets the one short turn a stop gives: a line that starts no turn within a minute,
  or a turn still going after 90 seconds, ends it with a report written in its place, still as
  `cancelled`. A task showing you a prompt is still never cancelled under it: purlis waits for
  your answer. From the cancel until its program has ended, the task cannot dispatch or hand
  off; the tasks it started still can (#1459).
- **A save to a changed remote asks which one to keep.** When a repository's remote changed
  since purlis last saved it, the Saving view names both remotes and offers *Save to the new one
  and remember it* or *Keep the old one*. Your choice is remembered, so the next save does not
  ask again (#1852).
- **A sandboxed chat above its branch folders can commit in one.** `purlis worktree commit`
  from a workspace or the project's top takes paths that start with the branch folder
  (`.worktrees/<repo>/<piece>/…`). Claude Code no longer asks before the command when it runs
  alone, a chat is held to 30 brokered commits in ten minutes, a message carrying purlis's own
  provenance trailers is refused, and a commit purlis's scan refuses is a needs-you item
  (#1476).
- **A folder purlis will not read through its git link says why.** A checkout below a workspace
  that keeps its git directory elsewhere is named as such, a folder only named `workspaces` is no
  longer held to a project's rule, and purlis's git reads find your global excludes under
  `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` (#1476).
- **A chat that starts or stops asking for you redraws only what counts it.** The workspace
  tabs' counts, the show-more counts, the hands on the tab chips and the title bar's list read
  the needs-you queue themselves, so the panes are no longer drawn again for it (#1037).
- **A chat does not start when purlis cannot tell what to keep from it.** In a project that runs
  its chats sandboxed, a vault registry that does not read, or a plain-file vault whose file is
  said in a way purlis cannot use, refuses the start for every harness, with a sentence that
  says why, gives the path of the file to put right, and names Doctor. A project with no vault
  registry, with vaults in the keyring, or with a vault this machine has not set up yet starts
  as before, and a chat that is already running is not stopped.
- **`purlis doctor` says what it makes of the vaults it keeps from chats.** A
  `sandbox kept files` row says why the list is not whole, when it is not, and otherwise names
  an entry left over on this machine, a vault of a kind this purlis does not know, and a vault
  not set up on this machine yet. The vault's view says the same of each.
- **A workspace's files leave out what the project keeps to itself.** A vault's file inside a
  workspace's repo is not listed, opened, searched, found by name or compared on that
  workspace's tab, as it is not among the project's own files.
- **A chat isn't a tab.** Every chat lives in the sidebar, and a tab is a layout of panes you
  made. The first launch after this update keeps the tab that was in front and every tab with a
  split, a view or a pin. Each other tab of a single chat closes, and its chat keeps running in
  the sidebar. A workspace left with no tab shows its first chat. The Chats view's This tab
  scope is gone: Workspace and All stay, and a view that was on This tab shows Workspace
  (#4758).
- **A chat's terminal is its own.** A sandboxed chat uses the terminal its session opened and any
  terminal it makes itself; a session's terminal opens for its owner alone, so `write` and `wall`
  from another account do not reach it.
- **A chat's row in the Chats list is one line, and its details are in a card.** A row is its
  state's mark, its persona's badge and its name, with a hand when it needs you. Rest the pointer
  or the keyboard on it and a card says the state in words, what it is doing, its persona,
  harness and workspace, how long it has been in its state, its tasks, its own branch, where its
  work went or came from, and a task's tokens. A chat's tasks are rows under it; folded, it shows
  how many in a small count. A task that comes to need you opens the rows above it (#1675).
- **A chat's commands keep to its own terminal, on macOS.**
- **What a chat wrote reads as text.** In the Inbox, a chat's message, a task's question and the
  note a chat passed on with it, and in a pane, the report of a task that ended, show their bold,
  lists, code and tables instead of raw `**` and `-`, with their own line breaks. HTML in them is
  dropped, a picture is never loaded (its description shows instead), and a link shows the site
  it goes to and opens in your browser only when you press it. A message over six lines folds,
  with "Show all · N lines" to open it (#5214).
- **An Inbox card is quieter.** Its head is one line: what kind of ask it is, the chat, and what
  it waits on, how long and where, with Go to chat and a × that ignores it. A chat's words are a
  step smaller and quieter. Your reply is a strip at the card's foot, always there: it grows as
  you type, Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line, and Esc leaves it (#5214).
- **Starting a chat on a pool sends only the profile settings that changed** (#4088). A profile's
  skills and settings used to cross whole at every start. Now the runner says what it holds, and an
  unchanged profile sends none of them. The runner still checks the
  whole result, and a file changed or added there is put right at the next start. A runner of an
  older version is still sent everything.
- **A chat's Allow on a sandbox block answers only the block it showed.** purlis now checks that
  the chat is still blocked on exactly what the Notice showed before it grants anything. An
  Allow for a block that was already answered, or that a newer block replaced, grants nothing
  and says why (#1538).
- **A chat's commit is held to the project's file as it stands.** A chat's commit is refused
  where the project's file it stages differs in `[sandbox]`, `[chat_env]` or `[dispatch]`
  from that file in the working tree, wherever the project sits in its repository. A staged
  or working file purlis cannot read, or one staged as anything but a regular file, is
  refused too. Committing the file as it stands is not refused (#1464).
- **A chat's GitHub App token is revoked when the chat ends** (#3808). Each installation token
  purlis minted for a chat's `gh` is revoked on GitHub as the chat closes or its program ends,
  and every chat's as purlis quits (it waits up to two seconds for them), instead of living out
  its hour. A revoke GitHub refuses, or one with no network, is logged, and that token still
  expires within the hour.
- **A chat's browser sites are shown apart from what the chat reaches.** Its Network view lists
  them under "Only its browser can reach": the browser sites you allowed for that chat and for
  every chat of the project on this machine. Its tab's sandbox mark says how many it has. A
  browser's site ask says its browser wants to reach the site, and that an Allow is the
  browser's alone, from its next act, with nothing restarting. The ask names each site it
  answers whole; the others wait for the next ask (#2364).
- **A chat's persona is fixed for its life.** `purlis persona use` inside a chat purlis started
  is now refused: it exits non-zero, changes nothing, and names the two ways forward, which are
  the operator allowing the vault on the chat's tab, or dispatching to that persona. `purlis
  persona create --use` is refused there too. Outside a chat both work as before. A persona is
  now defined as a role a chat runs as for its whole life, never a harness sub-agent, and
  ADR 0090 (chats working together by dispatch) is accepted as amended (#1435).
- **A chat's skills chip shows its skills in the Skills view.** Pressing a chat's "N skills" chip opens the sidebar Skills view on that chat. The chip is warning-coloured when the chat's set needs you. It no longer opens Use skill… (#3694).
- **Use skill… is a quick picker.** Its box takes your keys as it opens, and Enter takes the first match. A skill that takes arguments asks for them in a second step, and built-in skills are listed last. The chat's budget, routing and pins are no longer said above the list. The Skills view says them instead: under whose skills it shows, and as the chat's own cards in Needs you, each with one fix (#3694).
- **A chat's skills notices each have one action:**
  - "started without" offers Show in Skills;
  - "drafted" offers Open the draft;
  - "skills changed" adds What changed, which shows what is new, gone and changed in the Skills view (#3694).
- **A chat's tab names the harnesses' instruction files that came back from a runner.**
  `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `GEMINI.md`, Copilot's instructions and the like, in any folder of a
  clone, are named with the other files a tool here reads, since a harness here reads them as
  instructions. A repository the chat cloned on the runner is said to be whole from there (#3990).
- **A chat's terminal opens on its screen and the newest 200 lines of history**, never the
  5,000 a chat keeps, so switching to a busy chat with a long history draws it sooner. Scrolling
  up past them pages the older lines in, 1,000 at a time, with the line you were reading kept in
  view. A session host before this version still sends the whole history (session protocol
  1.70, #4742).
- **A chat's vision or section entry can no longer hide the rest of `workspace.md`.** A text
  that opens an HTML comment or a code fence and does not close it is refused, because a Markdown
  viewer would hide every section after it. A chat's write that would grow `workspace.md` past
  64 KiB is refused too, since every later chat in the workspace reads the whole file. The
  refusal says how to keep it short. Writes that shrink a longer file still go through (#1598).
- **A Claude Code chat holds each repository's git folder as a whole.** A repository folder
  that was there when the chat started stays where it is, as do its git folder and the folders
  above it: the chat's commands no longer move, replace or remove them. Git works in it as
  before. Remove a branch folder with `purlis worktree remove`. A refused write of one of these
  folders says so, and offers no Allow.
- **Switching projects no longer costs more for every pane.** Each pane's ⋯ menu used to set up
  its hidden popover whenever its project came to the front, so a tab split many ways made the
  switch slower. A menu is now drawn only while it is open (#4783).
- **A warm pool scaled with `kubectl scale` no longer keeps that count.** Set the Pool's
  `warmReplicas` instead (#3737).
- **A command over several lines is shown on them in the Inbox.** A permission whose command
  runs over several lines draws each line on its own line in its row, up to five, and counts
  the rest ("and 12 more lines"). The row says why only Deny is offered: "Allow is not offered.
  It runs over 3 lines." The lines are the row's own line split where the command breaks one,
  masked and cut as that line is, so they show nothing it does not. Where they could not be
  shown that way, the line stays as it was and the row says how many lines the command runs
  over (#3502).
- **A project's harness declarations are checked more closely.** A declaration may no longer
  take a name purlis gives a harness it ships (such as `claude-code`), since a chat on it would
  be taken for that harness. `[terminal] newline` must be one of the keys a terminal reads as a
  new line (`"\r"`, `"\n"`, `"\r\n"`, `"\u001b\r"`, `"\\\r"` or Shift+Enter in the kitty
  keyboard encoding, `"\u001b[13;2u"`); anything else is refused with
  a sentence saying so (#1119).
- **Claude Code no longer asks before `purlis dispatch`.** A chat the app starts runs `purlis
  dispatch`, `purlis dispatch report` and the `dispatch` and `dispatch_report` tools without
  its harness's permission prompt. What consents to a dispatch is purlis's own dispatch
  grant: the app asks you once for a pair of personas, on the asking chat's tab, with the
  brief in front of you, and starts nothing until you allow it. A chat dispatching to its own
  persona needs no grant and asks nothing. Your own `ask` or `deny` rule for any of them still
  wins, and the handoff command still asks (ADR 0064, amended).
- **A dispatch waiting on memory is said where you and its chat look.** A chat's row in the
  chats list says how many of its dispatches wait until this machine has memory to spare
  ("1 dispatch waits on memory"), beside the Dispatches tab's *Not started* list. A chat whose
  dispatch you allowed while memory was short is now told at once that it waits, and told
  again when it starts or gives up (#1617).
- **A dispatch into another workspace is held to that workspace's dispatch limits as well as
  the asking chat's.** A workspace with a limit set to 0 is not worked in by a chat that names
  it from elsewhere, whatever a persona's own limits say.
- **A chat nobody is at starts a chat in another workspace only under a grant that already
  stands** for the pair, yours on this machine or the project's, also for its own persona.
  This rule is a dispatched task's: a chat nobody is at still hands off to its own persona.
- **A handoff is held to the dispatch limits of the workspace it moves into** as well as the
  asking chat's, as a task sent into one is. A handoff into a workspace whose limit is set to
  0 opens nothing and says so.
- **A follow-up wakes an idle task, on every harness.** `purlis dispatch tell` to a task at
  rest starts its turn at once, now on opencode too, as it did on Claude Code and Codex. A task
  mid-turn reads it when that turn ends, as before. A stop or a cancel of an opencode task
  mid-turn asks it for its report when that turn ends, since opencode ends a turn on a second
  Escape (#1981).
- **The chat that asked always hears back.** A task whose turn ends without its report is
  asked for it once, in purlis's own line. If the turn that starts also ends without one, purlis sends the chat that asked the task's last message, marked as **a report
  purlis made from its last message** and quoted as data. You see it on the chat that asked,
  and on the task's finished row. The task stays open, and a report it sends later reaches the
  chat that asked too and takes this one's place on its record (#1981).
- **A todo marked done stays, and can be reopened.** Marking a todo done still writes its trace to
  the workspace's journal, and now keeps the todo as done instead of deleting it. In the Todos
  view a done todo is drawn after the open ones, struck through with its box ticked; untick the
  box, or choose Reopen from its menu, to open it again as it was. Delete still removes a todo,
  open or done. In a terminal, `purlis ws todo done <slug>` says how to reopen it,
  `purlis ws todo reopen <slug>` reopens one, and `purlis ws todo --done` lists the done ones. The
  open-todo count, the digest a chat starts with and `todo_list` still count only the open ones
  (#3063, ADR 0106).
- **A finished task folder can be removed without the Changes tab.** `purlis worktree remove`,
  from a chat or a terminal, and the explorer's Remove now take a branch folder purlis cut for a
  task once it is finished: its task has ended, nothing in it would be lost, and no other folder
  links into it. `--delete-branch` goes with it. A task folder that is not finished is still sent
  to its Changes tab, and the refusal now says why (ADR 0110, #5168).
- **A limit that can't change now says so** (#4281). When a stop or re-arm runs out of its wait for
  a runner, or a runner prints more than purlis reads, the message says the limit is fixed, why,
  and what you can do instead.
- **Opening a folder that is not a purlis project offers to make it one.** Picking such a folder
  through **Open a folder on this machine…** or typing its path no longer ends in a refusal: the
  welcome says "This folder isn't a purlis project yet. Make it one?" with the project template
  choice. **Make it a project** opens the folder in a workspace of its own in the project purlis
  keeps on this machine, through the usual trust question; nothing is written into the folder,
  so its code stays where it is. **Not now** leaves the folder untouched (#1822).
- **Uncommitted work inside a submodule no longer shows in purlis.** Git looks into a
  submodule by starting another git inside it, which purlis cannot hold to a repository it
  checked. So git that purlis runs now reads a submodule by its recorded commit only: a new
  commit in a submodule still shows as a change, and edits not yet committed there do not.
  Your own `git status` is unchanged (#1055).
- **Two folder layouts are no longer read by purlis's own git.** A worktree folder moved by
  hand is refused, with a sentence that names `git worktree repair`, until that is run in it.
  A checkout below a workspace that keeps its git directory elsewhere (`git clone
  --separate-git-dir`) is not read. A project's own top, and a checkout outside any project,
  keep whatever layout they have (#1055).
- **A forge host the sandbox does not let through is named.** While a project's sandbox and its
  `forge` preset are on, a `[[forge]]` host that no chat may reach (this machine, a link-local or
  metadata address, a name ending in a number) used to be left out without a word. Saving one in
  Settings now says which host it is and why. A host already in the file does not stop other
  saves, and turning the sandbox on is never refused because of one (#1405).
- **A `gh` or `glab` tool used with GitHub Enterprise Server or a self-managed GitLab needs
  `host`.** Without it the tool reaches `github.com` or `gitlab.com`, and a run naming your
  own host is refused with a sentence that says so: add `host` to the tool and allow the
  persona's tools again (#3869).
- **A frame is judged by the origin of its document.** While a browser's reach is judged, what
  the agent types, presses or drops into a frame is judged by the origin of the frame's
  document, as the browser gives it: a `blob:` frame by the origin that made it, an
  `about:blank` or `about:srcdoc` frame by the origin it takes from the page around it. A frame
  with no web origin of its own, such as a `data:` frame or a sandboxed `srcdoc` frame, is
  judged as opaque, and nothing is typed into it.
- **A blank or srcdoc frame whose origin is not known is not typed into.** While a browser's
  reach is judged, an `about:blank` or `about:srcdoc` frame whose own document has not said its
  origin is judged by the page around it only when it runs alongside that page; otherwise
  nothing is typed into it until its origin is known. A frame showing the browser's own error
  page is judged by the page around it.
- **A memory tab whose memory is gone offers its store's archive.** *This memory is not here any
  more* now has an *Open …'s archive* button, which turns the tab into that store's archive,
  where a deleted memory went (#1191).
- **A dismissed "project gone" line stays dismissed after a relaunch.** Dismissing the line about
  a remembered project that has moved or is gone, in the window or on the opener, is kept on
  this machine with your other dismissed Notices. It shows again once purlis finds the project
  there again, or once you locate or forget it (#1291).
- **A grade's dollar limit is priced from the model its chats run on** (Skill studio preview,
  #3469). The plan says the limit and the price it used: the model's, read from the profile's
  `--model` or `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, or the dearest known price where
  none is named or its price isn't known, so the limit is never set too low. A grade that reaches
  the limit stops, and its record says it stopped at its dollar limit. A chat that says its tokens
  and not its cost counts against the limit at the dearest price. Prices come from a table in
  purlis, never from the network.
- **A grade's chat ends with its window** (#3274). If purlis stops without quitting, the session
  host ends a grade's chat at once instead of keeping it for the window to come back to, and the
  grade is recorded as interrupted at the next start, as before. Your other chats are still kept
  for the window to come back to.
- **A grade's chats run with only purlis's plugin on** (#3468). Every other plugin Claude Code
  has installed is turned off for those chats alone, so a grade measures the skill and not your
  plugins, and the grade's record names the plugins that were off. Your own plugin settings are
  not changed. A grade on an opencode profile is refused with the reason: opencode cannot turn
  its plugins off for one chat.
- **A grade's consent covers the profile, model and limits its plan shows** (#3622). Grade
  starts on the plan you read: if the profile, the model, the token cap or the dollar limit
  changed since it was shown, the press is refused and the new plan is shown to press again.
- **A grade's cost and record are said truthfully** (#3273). The plan says which earlier grade
  its estimate comes from (its profile, its program and the day it ran) and prefers one on the
  profile you picked. A skill whose last grade's chats did not report their spend now reads as
  graded, with its cost not known. A row of the grade record that does not hold together, that
  is out of range or that is stamped ahead of your clock is skipped. The Grades panel, the plan
  and `purlis skill grade` say how many rows were skipped and name any record file too large to
  read.
- **An Allow for one chat is for that task's workspace.** A chat you allowed to dispatch to a
  persona is asked again when it sends that persona to work in another workspace (#1505).
- **A chat nobody is at** starts a chat as another persona in another workspace only under a
  grant that names the pair and covers the workspace it goes into: a grant limited to any
  other workspace, its own included, does not carry it across (#1505).
- **Allowing a folder or a socket restarts the chat at its next pause, and says first what will
  stop.** The Ask, and its row in the Inbox, names each program the chat started that listens on
  a port ("its node on port 5173 will stop") and counts the others, or says plainly that purlis
  cannot tell. A chat whose program ended first is not restarted. Restart now still restarts it
  at once (#1986).
- **A chat started by a handoff or a dispatch remembers which chat started it, by that chat's
  id.** It was kept by number alone, which is dealt again once that chat is gone. The id is
  kept across a relaunch; a chat you start yourself names none (#872).
- **A handoff is a dispatch: its consent is the dispatch grant, on every harness.** Your
  harness's permission prompt no longer consents to `purlis handoff`. The app decides a handoff
  as it decides a dispatched task. To the asking chat's own persona it opens at once and asks
  nobody. To another persona it needs a dispatch grant: the first time, nothing opens and a
  Notice on the asking chat's tab shows the brief in full, and you allow the pair for this
  chat, for you on this machine or for the project, or keep it blocked. The command returns at
  once saying the handoff is held, and on Allow the chat opens then, in the workspace the
  handoff named, which is created then and not before. Later handoffs across the pair open
  with no prompt. Nobody approves the brief: it is the new chat's first message, it is in the
  dispatch's record, and the chat that gets it is told who asked and still asks you for every
  command that asks (#1444). What a project author will notice:
  - `purlis init` writes no ask rule for a handoff, and a Claude Code chat the app starts
    carries an `allow` for one, as it does for a dispatch: by each flag the line can start
    with (`--name`, `--report`, `--persona`, `--create`, `--vision`) and for
    `purlis handoff report`, never a bare wildcard. So the spelling to write puts a flag first,
    `purlis handoff --name "<task>" <workspace>`. A line that starts with the workspace is
    still a handoff; Claude Code asks about it first, as it does for any command it has no
    rule for. An `ask` or `deny` of your own still wins.
  - A project made earlier still carries the rule `init` wrote, so its harness asks a second
    time before every handoff. `purlis doctor` says so on its `handoff gate` row, and
    `purlis doctor --fix handoff-rule` removes exactly that rule from `.claude/settings.json`
    and `opencode.json`, says what it removed, and names every rule about a handoff it left
    because you wrote it (a `deny`, an `allow`, another spelling, anything in
    `.claude/settings.local.json`). It runs only by name and commits nothing: a teammate on an
    older purlis is still asked by that rule and by nothing else, so commit the change once
    they have updated.
  - `purlis handoff` with no `--persona` now runs the new chat as the asking chat's own
    persona, as a dispatched task does. It used to start it as the project's default persona.
  - A handoff is held to the project's dispatch limits, its depth among them (3 unless the
    project sets another), and to an administrator's dispatch locks. A chain of handoffs had
    no depth limit before.
  - A handed-off chat starts with its own persona's hosts and vault, with nothing to allow on
    its tab. It no longer starts holding the asking chat's grants, and a chat that still holds
    another persona's is refused a handoff until you allow it its own.
  - `purlis guard handoff` is retired: it writes nothing and says what consents now. To have
    your harness ask as well, run `purlis guard ask 'purlis handoff*'`, which purlis holds
    under every spelling. The glob `init` used to write, `purlis handoff *`, is read as the
    retired rule: as an `ask` it covers the plain spelling only. A `deny` on it is yours and
    is held under every spelling.
  - `purlis doctor --fix rename-plane` gives a carried handoff ask no `purlis` twin.
  - **An older purlis in a shared project.** Once the rule is removed and committed, a
    teammate on a purlis older than this change is refused the `purlis handoff` spelling by
    their own hook, their `charter handoff` runs with no prompt and no grant, and their
    `init` and `guard handoff` write the rule back.
  - A handoff that was held and then allowed leaves no todo in its workspace yet.
- **A handoff from a Codex chat works.** purlis's hook refused every handoff from a chat whose
  harness reported its permission prompts off, and Codex reports that for nearly every run.
  The hook no longer reads it. The app weighs it instead, from its own mark on the chat: **a
  Codex chat is always taken as a chat nobody is at**, so it is never asked for a grant. To
  its own persona it hands off; to another it needs a grant that already stands and a
  sandboxed project; in a project with no sandbox it hands off to its own persona only
  (#1444).
- **purlis's handoff guard refuses less, and says why in its own words.** It still refuses a
  handoff from a helper sub-agent, one inside a string, a heredoc or a substitution a shell
  runs, one whose two words the shell would rewrite, and a brief the shell would change (a
  pipe, a file, a here-string, an unquoted heredoc, a live substitution). It no longer refuses
  a handoff for being spelt another way than a harness rule matched: a path to purlis,
  `python3 -m`, a `VAR=` prefix or a wrapper, a quoted word and two spaces are read as the
  handoff they are (#1444).
- **A handoff is a row of its own in the Chats list.** It was drawn under the chat it came
  from, like a task. The work moved, so its chat is a session of its own: its own tab with a
  close button, its own row at the top, and no part in the counts, the fold, the needs-you
  hand or "Stop and everything below it" of the chat it came from. Its row says
  `from <chat>`. The row of the chat it came from says `handed off to <chat>` on its second
  line while that chat is not working, with `and 2 more` where it handed off to several, and
  pressing those words goes to that chat. Both follow a rename (#1492).
- **A task you asked for yourself says so.** A persona chat you started with Ask from a tab is
  a task of that session, inside its tab, and its row and its breadcrumb now say
  `asked by you` (#1492).
- **The asking chat is told a task is yours, in those words.** `purlis dispatch cancel`,
  `tell`, `answer`, `wait` and `read` for a task you asked for from that chat's tab were
  refused as "not a task this chat dispatched". They are still refused, and the sentence now
  says the person asked for it and that its report comes to that chat. Any other chat is told
  what it was told before (#1492).
- **A handoff no longer adds a row to the committed dispatch log.** The row said only when a
  handoff happened, whether it stayed in the workspace and whether it made one; the handoff's
  own record, on the machine that made it, already says more and is what `purlis persona
  stats` counts. A handoff now leaves no trace another machine can see, and `persona stats`
  no longer prints a total of the rows older builds committed (#1457).
- **A prompt waiting in a harness's own terminal says what it is.** The ask reads, for example,
  "Waiting in its terminal: a permission prompt", "a form to fill" or "a question", with Go to
  chat. A Claude Code notice that asks nothing, such as a finished sign-in, no longer reads as a
  prompt, and a question opencode asks now counts as one (#1691).
- **A held file is rewritten only under the one name it has on disk.** When purlis writes a
  plain-file vault, a local vault registry or a key file, and that file has a second name (a
  hard link), purlis says so and leaves the file as it was, instead of giving the one name new
  bytes while the other keeps the old ones. The refusal says what to do next: remove the other
  name, or put a plain copy of the file in its place, since a value written through the other
  name reaches both. When the other name is inside the project, the refusal names it. Other
  project files are rewritten as before.
- **A held handoff's Notice says "hand off".** When a handoff waits for your answer, its Notice
  and the Inbox now say the chat wants to hand off its work, not dispatch a task (#1471).
- **A hidden window reads nothing on a timer.** While the purlis window is minimised or out of
  sight, it stops reading the save standing, the alerts, a running chat's context gauge, a
  running dispatch and the time a chat has been in its state. Each is read once the moment the window is
  shown again, so what changed meanwhile is on screen at once (#1392).
- **A hook line no longer starts `ps` on macOS.** To check that a line on the hook channel
  comes from inside its chat, purlis read the sender's parents and start time by running
  `/bin/ps` once per line, and once more as each chat started. It now asks the kernel in its
  own process, as it already did on Linux, so many lines at once no longer queue behind one
  another or delay a chat's start. What is admitted and what is refused is unchanged. Only
  macOS and Linux read a process's parents: on any other unix purlis has no answer, so
  nothing there is taken as inside a chat (#1407).
- **A kept 1Password token says why it is not used.** After the vault's provider or its file
  of references changed since the token was stored, the vault's tab and every read said only
  that no token was kept. They now say which of the two changed, without naming either, and ask
  for the token again from the vault's tab. A token stored before purlis recorded these two
  settings records them at its next read (#1828).
- **A harness declaration's program is refused under a versioned name too.** `ksh93`,
  `tclsh8.6`, `luajit-2.1` and `bash.exe` are refused as the shell, interpreter or launcher
  they name, as `ksh`, `tclsh`, `luajit` and `bash` already were (#1119).
- In the Skill studio's Library, a reason cut short under a skill's name now reads in full in a tooltip, under the pointer and while the keyboard is on the row. A reason that fits shows none, and the row keeps its one line.
- **A line break the shell does not use is marked in a command.** A command holding a lone
  carriage return, a next line (U+0085), a vertical tab, a form feed, or a line or paragraph
  separator now shows it as its mark (`⟦U+2028⟧`, for one) in the Inbox. It used to read as a
  plain space. The row says the character breaks the line there, which is why only Deny is
  offered. Where a command holds several hidden characters, the row names a line break first.
  A control, a bidi override or a zero-width character is described as one a reader does not
  see, no longer as one that looks like another. A forge login line holding any character the
  one rule hides is no longer typed, where before only control characters stopped it. The
  window now asks the core's own generated tables for which Brahmic and Arabic letters and
  viramas a joiner may stand beside, not the browser engine's (#3470).
- **A link and the first chart colour never look like danger in a red, orange or pink workspace.**
  They are held apart from the danger colour as the accent is. In Purlis's dark appearance those
  three workspaces now draw the accent in Purlis's own colour rather than a warm grey, as its light
  and high-contrast appearances already did; the strip keeps the workspace's colour (#3049).
- **A link's calls are answered side by side, and a client's event queue is bounded.** The
  session protocol's host answers each call on a task of its own, so a command that waits (a
  `start` that waits on a harness, or one of the window's own commands) holds back neither
  another command's answer nor a pushed event on the same link. The commands about one chat are
  still carried out in the order they came, so keystrokes never overtake each other, and a link
  has at most 32 calls in flight. A client that subscribes and stops reading now holds at most
  1024 events: past that it lets go of the subscription, and when it reads again it is told the
  cursor to subscribe from, which brings back what it did not keep. Nothing on the wire changed
  (#1081, #1095).
- **A live workspace is published "with the project".** The palette's live switch, New
  workspace's Live setting and New persona's dialog said "the plane" (#1192).
- **A skill only on this machine keeps its grades across a rename and a move** (#4018). Git keeps
  no history of a local skill, so this machine now keeps the names and levels it had, and its
  Grades tab and each grade's scorecard read the grades recorded under them. This holds for a
  rename, a move into or out of the local skills, and a share. The Rename and Move dialogs say its
  grades move with it, and that its History starts again.
- **A browser login that signs in on another host keeps reaching that host, and the chat acts on
  its pages only while it signs in** (#5152). The site's own redirects, hidden frames and token
  refreshes to its sign-in host work after the login. Outside a sign-in, a chat's call on a page
  of the sign-in host is refused with the reason, a frame of it inside the site's page is left
  out of what the chat reads and painted over in screenshots, and a page that asks to sign in
  again tells the chat to log in again. The login's answer lists the hosts the browser reaches,
  and what the chat may do on each.
- **A store's archive tab is searched and paged, and a numbered archive name restores under its
  own name.** An archive holding more than a page shows one page and _Show more_, with a search
  box over each archived memory's title, stamp and text, the way a memory list does. A memory
  archiving likely had to number (`freeze-2`, beside an archived `freeze`) has a second button,
  _Restore as freeze_, besides _Restore memory_, and the tab says which name it came back under
  (#1191).
- **A long proposed change marks the lines it changes.** Its own tab used to draw the whole file
  as one change. Now it marks only the lines that changed, found as a branch's comparison finds
  them, and folds the unchanged stretches between them. Click a fold to open it, so you can still
  read every line before you press Apply (#2121).
- **On Linux, a lookup refused at the system's name lookup is one Notice.** On a host whose name
  lookups go through a local socket (systemd-resolved, nscd, sssd or avahi), a program's failed
  lookup in a Codex or opencode chat is shown once, as a lookup past the sandbox's proxy, not
  also as a local socket. Its words say what letting a chat reach that lookup would mean (#2428).
- **The project-root guard says how to join a `cd`.** A branch switch or reset refused in the
  project root, after a `cd` joined to it by `;`, `||`, `&` or a newline, now says that such a
  `cd` leaves the shell where it was if it fails, and to join it with `&&`
  (`cd <path> && git …`) so purlis reads where git runs. Nothing that was refused is allowed now
  (#1326).
- **A resumed chat that came back fresh no longer shows a conversation id.** When the harness
  could not bring back a session record's conversation, the new chat's note named it by its raw
  id. It now says the harness could not bring back its conversation; the record keeps the id
  (#1646).
- **A memory or a session record saved in the workspace in front redraws only the panel that
  lists it.** The focused workspace's panels are held in a store of their own, and each region
  takes the part it draws, so a memory an agent saves no longer redraws the whole project
  window, and a session record redraws it once, for the palette's rows, where it was twice. A
  memory's or a todo's tab is read again only for a write to its own store, not for every todo
  or memory written anywhere in the project (#1160).
- **A task's report and the messages between a chat and its tasks are sent as written.** A
  call that runs `purlis dispatch report`, `tell`, `answer`, `note` or `ask` beside a live
  `$(…)`, a backtick or a process substitution is refused, on every harness, as the handoff's
  report already was: the shell would have replaced that text before purlis read it. The
  refusal says to write the text out in plain words (#1456, #1463).
- **A never says when you said it, and on which chat's question.** Settings › Project ›
  Dispatch now shows, beside each pair you said never to, when you said it and the chat that
  was asking, as it does for a grant. A never said on an item of the needs-you list says when
  (#1464).
- **Any new chat on a machine with no harness offers the setup tab.** Only the first chat did.
  A new chat from the `+`, the palette or a split now brings forward the _Set up a harness_ tab
  for the directory it would have started in, instead of a picker whose every row fails with
  "not found". With any harness installed, or a profile of the project's own, the picker opens
  as before (#963).
- **A New tab asks git about `charter.local.toml` once, not about seven times.** Opening the
  picker and starting a chat each checked whether git would carry the project's local file
  every time something read that file, and each check is a `git status`. Each now asks once and
  gives every reader that answer, and the next one asks again. The check refuses exactly what it
  refused before (#2179).
- **A page's own document is judged by its origin.** While a browser's reach is judged, what
  the agent types, presses or drops into a page is judged by the origin of the page's own
  document, as frames already are: a blank page another page wrote by the writer's origin. A
  page with no web origin of its own is judged as opaque, and nothing is typed into it; a blank
  page whose origin is not known yet is not typed into until it is. The browser's own error page sends nowhere.
- **A sandboxed frame is judged as opaque by its sandbox.** An `about:blank` or `about:srcdoc`
  frame whose own document has not said its origin is judged by its frame element's `sandbox`:
  sandboxed without `allow-same-origin`, it is opaque and nothing is typed into it.
- **A chat's pane that cannot keep up with a flood of output is sent a fresh screen, not a
  backlog.** The session host now counts a pane's output as delivered only once the pane has
  drawn it, so typing into a chat that is printing a lot stays quick: a pane that falls behind
  starts over from the chat's screen as it is now, rather than working through everything it
  missed (#4733).
- **A refused vault points to the request the chat already made.** When a chat has asked the
  persona a vault is tagged for and that dispatch is waiting for your answer, the vault's Notice
  says so and offers *Show the request* in place of *Dispatch to {persona}…*. The request is the
  first Notice on the pane, with its Allow buttons under its sentence and the brief under them.
  Ask {persona}, opened from a chat's Notice, says that the chat's words are not copied into it
  (#1481).
- **A chat's warnings live inside its pane, and the chosen tab stays joined to it** (#3142).
  A pane is three rows now: a band of its warnings at the top, each a washed card with its
  words above its buttons, two at most and the rest behind "+N more"; a slim header with the
  chat's skills, its harness and its context gauge at the left and the pane's split and close
  at the right; then the terminal. Nothing sits between a tab and its pane any more, and
  nothing is drawn over the terminal's first lines. The terminal keeps its last line in place
  as a warning comes or goes. Esc on a warning puts it away and moves on to the next one, or
  to the terminal; a question about access (Allow or Keep blocked) has no Dismiss and stays.
- **A chat's terminal takes its output once per frame.** A harness streaming a long message
  reaches the terminal as one write per frame instead of one per chunk, so the window does less
  work while it streams (#4732).
- **A pane's notices no longer cover its chat.** Questions, warnings and notes about a chat stand
  in a row of their own at the top of its pane, and the terminal sits under them instead of
  behind them. At most two show at a time; the rest wait behind "+N more", which opens them in
  the same row (#1647).
- **The window restyles itself faster.** Each component's rules are now keyed on classes rather
  than attributes, which roughly halves the style work when the window restyles itself, as it
  does when Skill studio opens from the palette (#4351).
- **Opening a persona's file that leads outside the project says so in the project's words.**
  The window used the terminal's sentence, which named a "control plane"; it now says the file
  leads outside the folders this project keeps its data in. The terminal's words are unchanged
  (#1156).
- **A sandbox grant for a persona the project does not have is refused.** Saving
  `[sandbox.personas.<name>]` in Settings for a persona the project does not define now says
  that it names no persona of this project and grants nothing, instead of being taken without a
  word. Make the persona first; it is read at the next read (#1407).
- **In a sandboxed chat, `purlis secret exec` runs only the persona's declared tools.** A
  command that is not one, a shell or an interpreter among them, is refused with a sentence
  naming the tool to declare in `[sandbox.personas.<persona>] tools`; a declared tool runs only
  with its own vault, key and hand-over. A credentialed MCP server you approved runs as
  approved. Your own terminal is not limited (#1407, #1362).
- **A persona host or tool that policy locks out is refused when the project file is saved**,
  as a project host already was, named with its persona (#1407).
- **A harness profile named by a `[dispatch.profiles]` list links to Settings › Dispatch**
  when a rename or remove is refused over it (#1522).
- **A pool keeps only the profiles chosen for it.** A Docker pool's runner no longer keeps every
  one of this machine's profiles: it keeps the profile a new chat in the open project gets, or
  the ones chosen for the pool, kept in `runners.json` as the pool's `profiles`. Each pool's row
  in Settings › This machine › Pools has **Add a profile…**, and **Remove** on each profile,
  which asks first: the runner forgets that profile, its sign-in there with it. A chat that
  starts on or moves to the pool on another profile adds it (#4047).
- **A chat's dispatch to a pool this machine doesn't keep is refused at once.** It used to wait
  for your Approve, though no start could run it. Now nothing is held, and the chat is told
  that the pool isn't one this machine keeps (#4965).
- Removing a pool whose runner is on another Docker engine now needs Docker to be using an engine
  shown to be yours. Otherwise nothing is removed, and the message says what to do.
- **A pool's code send and waits are now its limits, and running out offers to raise them.** The
  largest code sent to a runner (1 GiB), the longest code send (10 minutes), the longest wait for a
  sign-in (15 minutes), for a cluster runner to be vouched for (5 minutes) and for a runner's answer
  (30 seconds) can each be raised on a pool. Hitting one says so and suggests a value you can edit:
  what is needed plus a margin for the size, double for a wait. Applying it saves the value to the
  pool and tries again. Only the wait changes: every check still runs. What a runner sends back to
  this machine stays held to 1 GiB and 10 minutes, whatever these say (#4282, #4283).
- **Pressing a chat shows it in the pane you're in.** A sidebar row, a task, a Go or a name in a
  breadcrumb replaces what the focused pane shows, and the chat it replaces keeps running. A
  chat already on screen is jumped to rather than shown twice, a view is never replaced (the
  pane you used last takes the chat instead), and a chat from another workspace brings that
  workspace forward. The sidebar highlights the focused pane's chat and faintly marks the chats
  in the tab's other panes (#4757).
- **Settings no longer offers "Open tasks in their own tabs".** A task you press lands in the pane
  you're in, like any chat (#4757).
- **A profile over its pool's limit now says so and offers to raise it.** A pool has limits on what a
  profile may send to its runner, by size (128 MiB by default) and by files (8,192 by default). Going
  over used to leave part of the profile behind, with a note on the chat's tab. Now nothing is sent:
  Start a chat says how much is needed and suggests a value you can edit, and applying it saves the
  value to the pool and starts the chat. A value you never set follows purlis's default (#4279).
- **Renaming or removing a profile names the personas and dispatch lists that use it.** A
  persona whose definition names the profile with `profile:`, and a `[dispatch.profiles]` list
  in the project's file that holds it, now stop a rename, a rename everywhere and a removal, and
  each is named before anything changes. Neither file is rewritten from this machine (#1380).
- **A sandboxed Codex chat runs on a profile for sandboxed chats only.** A sandboxed Codex chat
  with none waits, and the Inbox's *Codex needs a sandbox-only profile here* makes one and opens
  Codex's own sign-in for it. You can also make one in Settings › You › Profiles with *For
  sandboxed chats only* on, or with `purlis profile create --harness codex --sandbox-only`.
  purlis no longer copies your Codex sign-in for a sandboxed chat, and no sandboxed chat writes
  your own Codex home. A project's earlier sandboxed Codex conversations are brought to that
  profile the first time it runs there (#2037).
- **Opening a project no longer waits on another project's cleanup.** The month-old session
  files of a project are collected as it opens, and that collection no longer holds the app's
  lock on its open projects: another project opens, closes and draws while it runs (#1027).
- **Purging purlis removes the browser engine's profile you added.** The profile the Notice about
  the browser engine's sandbox offers to add is unloaded and removed by `apt purge purlis`. A
  plain remove keeps it (#2900).
- **The network log names the host a push goes to.** A push to a remote by its name is listed at
  the URL it pushes to, after the remote's `pushurl` and your `pushInsteadOf` rewrites, and no
  longer at the one it fetches from (#1828).
- **One git process fewer for most git calls.** purlis keeps a repository's config listing, which
  it reads before a git call to turn off the programs the repository names, until a file it was
  read from changes, and checks that before every call.
- **A setting is one line.** Its name, its control and Reset sit side by side at one height.
  Where a group's values are kept is said once, in the group's header, instead of under every
  setting. A setting kept somewhere else, on this machine, for the team or in the workspace,
  shows a small badge; hover or focus it to read where its value comes from. A value set here
  has a small mark, and "Where it is kept" is now a "Move to…" menu (#1840).
- **More of a read-only project's Settings stay on.** What is kept on this machine stays on:
  your own dispatch grants, accepting or declining the project's, Network's folders, and Allow or
  Remove for this project on this machine. Only what changes the committed file is off, with
  the project's sentence as why. A setting kept in the local file stays editable, and only its
  move to the committed file is off (#1759).
- **purlis's own look at a save's pull request uses your purlis sign-in.** A person signed in
  only through the window gets their green pull request merged by the look, with no new save.
  With no sign-in at all the pull request says a sign-in is needed, and offers **Sign in…**.
- **A pull request that waits with no end in sight says so**, in the Saving view and on the
  title bar's save mark.
- **A refusal that names a setting links to it.** Open in your editor from a file's row, with no
  editor chosen, says "Choose your editor in Settings first." with a Choose your editor link to
  Settings › You › Editor. A repo that did not clone into a new workspace links to that
  workspace's Repos settings. The link is on the line under the strip and in the palette
  (#1201).
- **A dispatch refused while you were away says whether it was a task or a handoff.** Where a
  chat nobody was at was refused a crossing into another workspace, its update in the Inbox now
  says whether the chat wanted the other persona for a task there or wanted to hand its work
  over there (#1543).
- **A screen reader hears a refused form once.** When a form will not send, because a field is not
  right or because purlis refused what it was sent, a screen reader says it once, as a summary such
  as "Email: That does not look like an email." or "2 fields to fix: Name, Port.", and the keyboard
  goes to the first field to fix. Each field still says why under its box, as its description. A
  field's error is no longer an interrupting alert as well: it is said politely after what you
  type, and no longer talks over the other fields (#3291).
- **A chat can't keep asking to move its work somewhere you refused.** When you refuse a chat's
  dispatch that would run somewhere other than where its workspace runs its chats, that chat's
  later dispatches to the same place are refused without asking you again, for as long as it
  runs, and the chat is told why. Other places and other chats still ask (#4862).
- **A task's Changes tab lists the paths purlis will not read.** A path a branch changed whose
  folders include one called `.git`, or whose name is not a plain path, used to be left out
  without a word. It is now listed under its place with its mark and the reason. It is drawn
  as text: nothing opens, compares or stages it (#704).
- **A policy file's `0` for a limit that is off until set says how to leave it off.** A policy
  whose `tokens-per-session` or `minutes-per-task` is not a whole number in range is still
  refused whole, and its sentence now ends "remove the key to leave it off" (#1545).
- **A profile the new-chat picker refuses opens its own page in Settings.** Each refused profile
  has its own _Open … in Settings_ link. It opens the profile's page with its command in focus.
  A profile with no page of its own (one committed in `charter.toml`, or one renamed since)
  opens Harness & profiles. Before, one link opened Harness & profiles for all of them (#1296).
- **A link to a Settings page that is no longer there opens the group it was under.** Before,
  it opened the level's first group (#1296).
- **A chat refused a `git pull` at the project root no longer asks you for it.** The refusal
  names `purlis worktree update`, which the chat runs itself. You get a needs-you item only
  when that update is left for a reason no chat can settle: a file the chat's sandbox denies,
  a conflict, or a project not put back whole (#3877).
- **A refused vault names what to do next.** The refusal a chat reads names the ways forward:
  the operator's Allow on the chat's tab, or a dispatch to the persona the vault is tagged for.
  A vault name the project does not register is refused as that, with nothing to press. A
  persona sub-agent is told at start that in a sandboxed chat it runs with that chat's persona's
  vaults (#1430).
- **A repo on a second forge is tracked by the first run's project.** Opening a repo whose
  `origin` is on github.com or gitlab.com, when the project tracks only the other forge, adds a
  forge for it to the project, with the owner the remote names. The repo picker and `discover`
  then see both. A remote on a forge the project already tracks adds nothing, and the forge shows
  in Settings › Project › Forges, where it can be removed (#1094).
- **A self-managed GitLab or GitHub keeps its host.** When a new project's repo is on a host
  whose forge purlis cannot tell, and you name the forge, the project's forge uses the remote's
  host, and the owner its path names, without typing either again (#1094).
- **A report is filed with purlis's own sign-in, never `gh`.** A sandbox block's **File report**
  searches and files on purlis's tracker as you, with the GitHub account you signed in to in
  Settings › You › Accounts, and no longer asks `gh` under whatever login it holds. Without that
  sign-in nothing is sent, and the link that files the draft in your browser is shown instead.
  `purlis report` from a terminal shows the draft and that link: a command holds no sign-in
  (#806).
- **A resumed chat's note names no conversation id.** It said "… was resumed — conversation"
  and a raw id. It now says the chat was resumed where it left off; the session record and
  Activity keep the id (#1646).
- A list measures whether a line under a row is cut only once you rest the pointer on the row or
  the keyboard reaches it, so long lists, such as the Skill studio's Library, open sooner (#4351).
- **The chat's tab says how to push a repository it cloned on a runner.** Move here brings the
  repository back with no remote; the tab now offers the `origin` the runner's clone had, where
  that is a forge's HTTPS or SSH address, with the one command that adds it. Where there is
  none, the tab says why and how to add one (#3985).
- **A runner keeps only the profiles its pool names.** As a pool's profiles are shown, and as
  the first chat of a run starts there, a runner of this version names the profiles it keeps
  for this machine. It forgets, sign-in included, each one no longer chosen for the pool or no
  longer on this machine. A pool made before pools kept only their chosen profiles now names
  every profile its runner kept, so each shows on its row to remove (#4060). Removing a profile
  in Settings › You › Profiles removes it from each pool's runner that kept it; a runner that
  is away is asked again at its next chat or when its pool is shown, and one of a purlis before
  1.52 keeps it, which the removal says (#3849). Removing a profile from a pool whose runner has
  one of the same name of its own now takes it off the pool's record.
- **A runner holds a profile once as it keeps it, and a pool says how much its memory holds.** A
  runner kept up to three copies of what a profile sent while it kept it, and now keeps one. On a
  Docker pool, *Most a profile may send: size* is at most half the runner's Memory: the pool's page
  says so and refuses a larger value as it is typed, and a start over it says what Memory to set
  (#4396).
- A runner mints its device id when it is paired, so two runners started from one image never
  share one. A runner whose home already holds a device id, such as one its image was built
  with, is not paired, and the refusal says why (#2539).
- **A harness chat on a runner will be started there by its names, for the runner connection to
  come, with its sandbox asks reaching you as a local chat's do.** The window starts it by its
  profile, persona, workspace, conversation and first message; the runner composes it with the
  sandbox it compiles for itself, and a host its proxy asks about appears in Asks, answered from
  the window. A shell on a runner still starts from the window (#2446).
- **A cluster runner's pod now has limits**: 4Gi of memory and, for its disk, its home's size and
  2Gi. `perPerson.quota` gains `memoryLimit` (64Gi) and `ephemeralStorage` (16Gi). A runner
  namespace made from now on enforces the restricted Pod Security Standard (#3844, #3824).
- **A sandboxed chat asks you to remove a workspace.** `purlis workspace remove` run in a chat
  the app started under the sandbox now refuses before anything is deleted, and says to remove
  the workspace from the window. A chat without the sandbox, and a terminal, remove it as before
  (#1408).
- **A save commits a file only under the one name it has on disk.** A save of the project or of
  a workspace's repo refuses a file with a second name (a hard link), as purlis's file readers
  already do, and a file that changed or went away after it was staged. It names each one, takes
  it out of the index again, and makes no commit. A file with a second name is refused before
  anything is staged, a refused file's contents are removed from the repository's own store
  where nothing else uses them, and a save of a skill's files stages each file from the one
  open file it checked. On macOS, the sandbox lets a chat make a hard
  link only to a file in the folders it may write, so git, cargo and npm keep making their own
  links as before.
  A commit the app makes for a sandboxed chat in its branch folder, and the files
  `purlis worktree update --continue` stages once a conflict is resolved, hold to the same
  rule; a resolved file refused there is marked as conflicted again. So does Continue on a
  project's save conflict in the window.
- **A red pull request of a save stays open, and says which checks failed.** A failed check of
  any kind, required or not, leaves the pull request open and unmerged. The Saving view names
  each failed check with a link to it, the title bar's save mark turns to the alert, and a
  repo's row says the same. Saving is not blocked: your next save goes onto the same pull
  request. A cancelled or timed-out check counts as failed; neutral and skipped ones pass.
- **A `pr-merge` save no longer turns on the forge's auto-merge.** A branch that lands through
  a merge queue or a merge train is put in it by purlis once its checks have passed.
- **The finished tasks under a chat, a dispatch's brief and report, the tasks menu's Finished and
  a notice's details draw one chevron that turns** as they open, in place of swapping two
  (#3675).
- **`purlis serve` says what purlis does on its standard error.** A runner's host now writes the
  core's `info` lines there as well as its warnings, redacted as the app's log is, so the
  container's log or the service's journal shows an engine update or a browser's end (#2753).
- **A self-managed repo opened into your first project is asked about.** Opening a repo whose
  `origin` is on a host that is neither github.com nor gitlab.com into the first-run project you
  already have now asks whether it is GitHub or GitLab, as a new project does, and adds that
  forge on the repo's host to the project's forges (#1669).
- **A session record names its chat by its ids.** Each record written now carries the chat's
  `chat-id`, the `device` that made it and the `run` that wrote it, as the format has said it
  would, or `unknown` for one the app does not know (#871, #1092).
- **A chat waiting on its tasks says so, and is not in the needs-you list.** A chat whose turn
  has ended while tasks below it still work reads `waiting on 2 tasks`, in the working colour
  with a mark of its own, in the Chats list and the explorer. It needs you only once every
  task has reported or ended and it has then stopped with nothing to do. A task paused on a
  question to the chat that asked reads `asking <chat>` and is not in the list either. A
  permission prompt or a question for you still is, whatever the tasks are doing (#1491).
- **A chat's row counts its tasks.** `2 working · 1 waiting · 1 failed · 3 done`, each part
  only when it is not zero, and `6 of 6 tasks` when it is at the most it may have running.
  Waiting is a task that needs you or is at rest. A folded row says the same count (#1491).
- **A chat that needs you is never left at rest unmarked.** A chat waiting on its tasks is
  looked at again whenever one of them reports, is stopped, is closed or dies, and when a line
  purlis typed into it was never taken. A task you asked for yourself from a chat's tab does
  not hold that chat back (#1491).
- **Only a task that came to nothing flags its chat.** A task that finishes as done, or is
  cancelled, changes the count. One that failed, was blocked, ended without a report or did
  not start puts the hand on the chat that asked: the item says which task and why, and goes
  to that task's row. It goes, one failure at a time, once you have been shown it, open its
  row, clear the row or ignore the chat (#1491).
- **The hand on a tab is pressed.** Where a chat of a tab is waiting for you and is not on
  screen, the hand is on the tab's chip and a press goes to the chat that has waited longest.
  It was a mark that could not be pressed (#1487).
- **On Linux, a desktop portal that did not answer is asked once per login session, not at
