- **A chat's commit message is read for credentials when it commits.** A chat's own commit, and
  a commit the app makes for a sandboxed chat, is refused when its message holds what looks like
  a credential, masked, with the same needs-you item as a refused change. A push now also reads
  every header line of each commit and annotated tag it sends, and reads messages in UTF-8
  whatever the repository's settings ask git to write them in (#1133).
- **A comparison reads attribute files only through the branch's own folder.** The
  `.gitattributes` files that decide whether a file is binary and how its line ends compare are
  now opened from the branch's folder one component at a time, following no link, as the files
  themselves are. A `.gitattributes` that is a link, or one in a folder swapped for a link, is
  not read.
- **A studio extension's program starts programs only from folders it cannot write.** That is the
  system's program folders and the extension's own folder, less its state folder and temporary
  folder, on macOS and Linux. An extension that runs an interpreter installed elsewhere, such as
  under a home folder, needs it in one of those. On macOS it also loads no native library from
  its state or temporary folder, and on Linux it makes no file in memory (`memfd_create`).
- **An Allow starts the brief you read, and no other.** The app keeps the held dispatch as it
  was asked, by its own number, and starts that one. A brief sent afterwards across the same
  pair is never started by the Allow of the first.
- **A chat nobody is at is refused in one place.** A chat whose harness runs with its
  permission prompts off, by what its harness reports or by the command it was started with,
  dispatches to another persona only under a grant that already stands for you or the project,
  and only from inside the sandbox. A grant made for one chat never counts for it, nothing of
  its ask is held, and no Notice is raised (#1446).
- **The persona chat takes its folder from the asking chat, and nothing else.** Not the hosts
  or folders you allowed that chat alone, not its start without the sandbox, and not the
  grants it holds.
- **No chat is started for another chat on a profile that asks nobody.** A dispatch or a
  handoff whose profile's own command switches the harness's permission prompts off is
  refused, whoever named the profile: the dispatch, the persona's definition, or the asking
  chat's own. Codex's `-a never`, `--ask-for-approval never` and `--full-auto` are recognised
  beside the flags already known.
- **What purlis tells a chat about its held dispatch names a task by a task's rule.** A file
  in the store those lines wait in whose task name could end purlis's own heading is dropped
  when it is read.
- **A dispatched chat that lost its conversation keeps its place.** Started again in its own
  place, it still owes its report, at its depth, in its lineage.
- **A chat cannot write the home folders Docker links `docker` into.** `~/.docker/bin`,
  `~/.orbstack/bin` and `~/.rd/bin` are denied to every chat's writes (#2752).
- **purlis's own Docker commands never read your Docker settings as they are.** Each gets a
  checked copy: your registry sign-ins and the credential helpers Docker's own folders hold, and
  no plugin, hook or context, pointed at your engine (#2752).
- **A chat cannot run Colima, Lima or a Podman machine.** Where those engines keep their
  sockets (`~/.colima`, `~/.lima`, a Podman machine's folder) is closed to every chat's
  writes, so `colima`, `limactl` and `podman machine` do not work from a chat (#2752).
- **A test now fails if purlis starts git anywhere but its one runner.** The runner turns off
  what a repository's own config could make git run, such as hooks and an fsmonitor. Every git
  process purlis starts already goes through it. A new call that skipped it now fails a test,
  and another test plants such programs in a repository's config and checks that none of them
  runs. `crates/purlis-core/docs/git-policy.md` lists the call sites, and what the runner does
  not hold yet (#810).
- **The consent and operator-rule checks read every command substitution the shell runs.** A
  command that waits for your consent, or that one of your own ask or deny rules names, is now
  refused inside a substitution at any depth: in double quotes, a parameter's default, backticks
  or an expanding heredoc body. They also read a command in a `case` branch, with or without
  the pattern's leading parenthesis, and in a shell function the command defines. A heredoc
  body written to a file or another reader stays data: only its substitutions are read. The
  refusal says where the command sits and asks for it to be run as a command of its own. Both
  checks read substitutions once per command with the same scanner as the leak guard, and a
  substitution nested past purlis's limit is refused as too big to check. A handoff inside a
  substitution is refused too. A test runs every shape through bash and zsh to confirm which
  ones really run the command (#1417).
- **The leak guard reads a shell function the command defines, and a `case` pattern written
  with its leading parenthesis.** A read inside a function that the same command defines and
  calls is refused, including when the call comes after a change of directory or inside a
  substitution (#1417).
- **Every secret check reads a file the way it reads, not only the way it is written.** The
  commit and push check a chat's git hooks run, a workspace repo's save, and the Edit as TOML and
  Edit as JSON editors now find a credential written with string escapes, as the project save
  does. A file that does not parse (comments, a trailing comma, JSON5, JSON lines, a key given
  twice) and a file of any name are read with their escapes decoded too. The editors and the
  project save now ask one shared check, so they refuse the same documents. A file with
  ordinary escapes and no credential is still saved (#1304).
- **Fetches go only to the remote you saved to.** The window's own fetches and pulls (auto-save's
  fetch, a repo sync, a restore) now use your purlis sign-in only for the remote recorded for
  the clone, as automatic pushes already did. A changed remote is not fetched from, and the
  Saving view asks about it. A remote whose push address differs from its fetch address is
  never signed in for (#1851).
- **The guards treat the two forge CLIs alike.** A persona that declares `gh` is now asked
  before running one of its delete or remove commands, as one declaring `glab` already was. The
  leak guard now refuses a vault file that `glab` would upload to the forge, as it did for `gh`,
  and reads more of the ways either CLI uploads a local file. Every guard table that names a
  forge CLI pairs each row with the other CLI's, or says why that CLI has none, and a test fails
  on a row added for one forge CLI alone (#1068, #1080).
- **`gh` and `glab` refuse more of their credential commands in a chat.** After an audit of each
  command line's whole command set, `gh secret` and `gh repo set-default`, and `glab variable`,
  `securefile`, `duo`, `mcp`, `opentofu init` and `download`, `cluster agent` token commands,
  `runner-controller token`, `ci --with-variables` and `repo view` as JSON, each under its aliases
  too, never run with a vault's value from a chat; nor does `api` on the forge's own host where
  its route does what a refused command does (keys, secrets, tokens, CI/CD variables), or GraphQL
  that asks for a credential. The audit is `docs/forge-tool-refusals.md` (#3894).
- **A fresh runner's proof is hardened.** It also counts a file outside the runner's home that the runner's user may write but does not own, and names in its notice show each character a reader would not see as `⟦U+XXXX⟧` (#5103).
- **Every git call purlis makes uses a bare repository only where it is named.** Not only the
  git the app runs for a sandboxed chat: `purlis worktree add` from your own terminal and every
  other call too, so a bare repository made in a folder a chat writes is never found in place
  of the clone meant. A clone or worktree the app makes for a chat is also held to the very
  git directory it checked, not only to its path: one replaced between the check and the run is
  refused (#1415).
- **purlis's git turns off hooks a repo names in its config.** Newer git (2.54 and later) can
  run a hook named in a repo's config, which the runner's turned-off hooks folder did not cover.
  Each such hook is now turned off by its name on every git call that could fire it, including
  one that only writes a branch or a ref (#1805).
- **The git purlis runs connects only through its network entry point.** A fetch, push, clone or
  other verb that can reach another repository is refused by every other runner before git
  starts, so none skips the one-credential rule or the network log. Two more config keys that
  start a program are held: a remote's helper (`remote.<name>.vcs`) and the commands a gc runs
  (`gc.recentObjectsHook`) (#1853).
- **The git purlis runs starts no program a repository's own config names.** A repository's
  config can name a filter, a diff or merge driver, a signer, an editor, a trailer's command, or
  what a remote starts at the other end. purlis's own git turned off only the repository's hooks
  and fsmonitor. Now it turns off every one of these that a repository sets. Your own global and
  system config is not affected, and the standard Git LFS filter still runs. Where turning a
  program off cannot leave the command working, purlis stops instead: a merge that needs the
  repository's merge driver stops on a conflict, a signed save in a repository that names its own
  signer is refused, and a fetch or push in a repository that names a remote's program is not
  run (#1805).
- **A dispatch's brief is held to the same rule as a handoff's.** In a Claude Code chat, a
  `purlis dispatch` whose brief does not come from one quoted heredoc in the same call is now
  asked about. That covers a pipe, a file, a here-string, an unquoted heredoc, or no brief at
  all (#1471).
- **A redirection that writes a file beside a dispatch or a handoff is asked about.** It is
  treated like a second command in the call. A duplicated descriptor (`2>&1`) and `/dev/null`
  are not asked about (#1471).
- **`purlis handoff report` is read the way the command reads it.** With no summary after
  `report`, only redirections, flags or a bare `--`, the call is a handoff into a workspace
  called `report`, and its brief is judged (#1471).
- **The guards read a little more of what a shell runs.** A heredoc fed to any shell the guards
  read a string for counts as commands, never as data. The project-root guard reads an `eval`
  under the shell's `set -a`. Each change only adds refusals.
- **The guards read busybox and `coproc` through to what they run.** A command busybox runs as
  an applet, or one `coproc` runs, named or not, is read as the command it is, so an ask or deny
  rule and a consent rule hold behind either, as they do behind `env`. A string handed to
  busybox's own shells, `ash -c` and `hush -c`, is read as `sh -c '…'` is (#1325).
- **A command that asks for your consent is refused when spelt so that nothing would ask.** A
  report filed with `--yes` and a todo promoted to a forge wait for your yes through rules spelt
  with the bare `charter` name. The guard now refuses either command when it is spelt so those
  rules don't match: through a path to the binary, in another case, behind a prefix or a
  wrapper, quoted, in a subshell, or inside a string or heredoc a shell runs. The refusal names
  the spelling that asks. The persona tool gate now reads a program's name in any case, as the
  other guards already did (#1279).
- **The guards read more shells' command strings, and the project-root guard reads them
  too.** A string handed to the ksh family, `rbash`, `yash`, `posh`, `csh`, `tcsh` or `fish`
  is read as `sh -c '…'` is, in each spelling those shells give their `-c`, so an ask or deny
  rule and a consent rule hold inside it. The guard that keeps the project root on its
  branch now reads a string a shell runs (`sh -c`, `eval`, a here-string) as a line of its
  own, from where that shell runs (#1325).
- **The guards read a few more shapes, and none fewer.** `watch`, `flock`, `script`,
  `parallel`, `caffeinate`, `arch` and `gtimeout` are read through to the program they run, and
  where one hands a shell a string instead (`watch 'a | b'`, `flock -c`, `script -c`), the
  string is read as `sh -c '…'` is. An ask or deny rule that opens with a wildcard and then
  names its program (`*kubectl delete*`) holds under every spelling of that program, and the
  rules in your own Claude Code settings (`~/.claude/settings.json`) are held as the project's
  are; purlis reads that file and never writes it. A heredoc whose substitution closes on a
  later line into a pipe to a shell is read as a script that shell runs. A handoff's brief fed
  by `xargs` or a duplicated descriptor (`<&3`), and a `report` that carries a handoff's own
  flags, are judged as briefs; a handoff that carries the hidden `--now` is asked about. A few
  more forge CLI commands that publish text (gh's `issue`/`pr` `close`/`reopen --comment`,
  `project item-create`/`item-edit`, `agent-task create`; glab's `incident note` and
  `work-items create`/`update`) refuse a live substitution as `gh issue create` does
  (#799, #1096, #1325, #1471).
- **The guards read more of a line's shell strings.** The guard that keeps the project root
  on its branch reads more of what a line hands a shell to run, and every guard that reads a
  script handed to `fish` reads it as fish does (#1325).
- **The project-root guard reads a directory the same command makes or re-points.** A link,
  a move or a copy made earlier on the line, or a file a redirection writes there, is made
  before git runs, and the guard reads directories before the line does. Git sent to such a
  directory is now refused as one the guard cannot name, as a directory held in a variable is
  (#1326).
- **A program word only the shell can name is read for your rules.** A variable, a command
  substitution or a glob where the program stands may be a program one of your ask or deny
  rules names, or the command line under a consent rule. Where the words after it match such a
  rule, the command is refused, naming the spelling the rule matches (#1325).
- **A chat cannot run `purlis doctor --fix rename-plane`.** The fix already refused a process
  that carries a chat's session; the Bash guard now refuses the command itself, under every
  spelling it reads, so taking the session variable away does not get past it (#1288).
- **The handoff guard reads a string that spans lines in a code span GNU bash 3.2 runs.** The
  consent and rule backstops already refused it (#1426).
- **The release floor's reading of one command is bounded.** It read each level of a nested
  command whole, so a long command nested deep was read once per level. Its whole reading is
  now held to a few times the command's length, and a command past that is refused as one the
  floor cannot read (#1409).
- **A vault's token is given to purlis itself and is kept in the system keyring alone.** A
  vault set up this way binds no environment variable, so there is no export for a chat's
  shell to read. The keyring record now also pins the item a vault keeps its secrets in.
  `vault add --token-stdin` refuses inside a chat before it reads anything (#1527, ADR 0047's
  2026-10-09 amendment).
- **A sandboxed chat can no longer approve a harness or a persona's servers for you.** In a
  project that runs chats sandboxed, no chat may write the records of what you approved to run
  (a local profile's command, a project's harness declaration, or a persona's credentialed MCP
  servers), nor the project's `harnesses/` folder, wherever it stands, the project root
  included. This holds for Claude Code, Codex and opencode chats alike. You still approve in
  the window or with `purlis persona approve-mcp` in your terminal, and a chat can still read
  the records. So "approved" now means you approved it. `purlis persona approve-mcp` no longer
  says "Recorded" when it could not write the approval: it exits with an error and says
  nothing was approved (#1458).
- **Kept browser logins are tightened further** (#2693). A kept login is opened under the same
  lock as its write-back, so a browser opened at that moment is never started fresh by mistake.
  A browser that outlived the removal of its profile never makes a store for that profile again.
  Only a browser that did nothing before its first login, or one opened from that login's store,
  is kept, and the chat is told to log in from a new browser otherwise. A build that does not
  say what of a browser's folder to leave out keeps no login.
- **A token kept in the keyring is held to the vault's provider and its file of references.**
  A commit that changes which provider reads a shared vault, or the file it reads references
  from, now stops the kept token being used, as a change to its variables or its 1Password
  vault already did. A record made before is held to them from the next time the token is
  stored (#1528).
- **A keyring read in a sandboxed chat is judged by where it runs too.** Besides its environment,
  purlis asks which chat a command runs below, and sends a keyring vault's read through the app
  unless that chat's record says it ran without the sandbox. Where this project's record or the
  command's own ancestry cannot be read, it reads nothing and says why. Your own terminal, an unsandboxed chat and a shell tab read as before.
- On macOS, the sandbox now keeps a link above a path it holds, and the folders above that link, in
  place. Writing through the link still works.
- **Holds more deleting commands from a sandboxed chat** (#1408). `purlis persona remove` and
  `purlis worktree remove` are refused there before anything is deleted, as `purlis workspace
  remove` is, with a sentence that asks the person to remove it from the window. A terminal
  removes as before.
- **A never is yours alone, and "any persona" is never an answer.** A never for a pair is kept
  on this machine in a file of its own, beats every grant including the project's and "any
  persona", and is lifted only by you. Nothing in the project's file lifts it. It holds down a
  chain of chats: a chat working below a chat of that persona does not dispatch to that
  persona either. If the file that keeps your nevers cannot be read, purlis does not treat that
  as "none": no grant counts until it reads, you are asked and told why, and a chat nobody is
  at is refused. For a chat nobody is at, "any persona" does not carry it into another
  workspace as another persona: only a grant that names the two does. No answer on a dispatch's
  Notice writes "any persona", and a chat cannot ask for it: its target must be a persona's
  name. A teammate's "any persona" in the project's file covers nothing on your machine until
  you allow it there in Settings. A record edited by hand grants no more than it names: a `*`
  written where a persona's name goes grants nothing. A grant from one persona to another
  allows nothing the other way. Saying never, lifting it, and granting or revoking "any
  persona" are each recorded in purlis's event log (#1503).
- **A Node package's `exports` and `module` are protected as its `main` is.** Where a project's
  hook loads a package from `node_modules` first (`node -r <package>`), the files its manifest
  maps through `exports`, under every condition, and its `module` are kept from a sandboxed chat
  as the file its `main` names already was (#1425).
- **A sandbox permission given to a session does not reach its tasks**, and one given to a task
  reaches neither its session nor its siblings. One answer to several tasks names the block
  shown for each task, and is refused whole unless purlis holds each task on exactly that block
  now and its own record puts each below that session (#1508).
- **A dispatch grant counts only while both personas exist, and a new persona under an old
  name is asked about once.** A grant that names a persona the project does not have now
  allows nothing: a chat still running as a removed persona dispatches to no one, and nothing
  is dispatched to a name that is no persona. Nothing is moved while a persona is away, so
  switching to a branch without it and back changes no grant. When a persona that purlis saw
  gone is there again with a different definition, or when you create a persona under a name
  your grants still hold, those grants are set aside: Settings shows them greyed, and one
  **Give back** for the name returns them. A never you said keeps holding for the name.
  **What this does not catch:** a persona removed and another made under its name, by hand or
  in one pull, with no dispatch and no look at Settings in between, is not noticed, and the
  new one has the old one's grants. Accepting a project grant, declining it and giving grants
  back are each recorded in purlis's event log, and each is a press in the window: no command
  and nothing a chat sends reaches them (#1504).
- **A persona's memory and the shared store follow no link.** Listing, reading, editing,
  archiving and restoring a persona's memory, or the shared store's, now reach the store the way a
  workspace's store is reached: one folder at a time, with no link on the way. A link at or below
  the store, its `archive/` included, is refused or left out even when it points somewhere else
  inside the project, and nothing outside the store changes (D-90c, #1194).
- **A persona's deny-list fails closed.** Where purlis cannot deny a chat the tools a persona's
  `disallowed-tools:` names, the chat is not started. And a persona's credentialed MCP server
  is never started without a person's approval on that machine, which a chat cannot give
  (#1451).
- **A chat cannot write Podman's folders.** Podman's settings, storage and run state are
  denied to every chat's writes (#2680).
- **Podman's run state is closed to chats in every session.** Where `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` is unset,
  as over ssh, Podman's run state in `/tmp` is denied to every chat's writes too (#2896).
- **An administrator's policy locks sandbox values, and the strictest wins.** purlis reads this
  machine's `/etc/purlis/policy.json`, only where root owns it and its folder and no one else can
  write either (never a link), and no chat may write its folder. It can fix the Internet access
  presets and the hosts any level may add (a project's forges included), and forbid your own
  hosts, a persona's own hosts, a person's opt-out, and folders granted to a chat. A policy that
  forbids the opt-out requires the sandbox in every project on that machine. Each locked value
  shows "Locked by policy" and who set it in Settings › Sandbox, with no control; the new-chat
  picker, a block's Notice and a held persona's Notice offer nothing policy forbids and still
  say why and who to ask. A policy file, or its folder, that purlis cannot trust or read locks
  everything it could lock but the presets (#1343).
- **A policy that forbids the opt-out now requires the sandbox.** With `"opt-out": false` in
  `/etc/purlis/policy.json`, every chat on that machine runs sandboxed. A project with no
  `[sandbox]`, or one that has not turned it on, is run as if it had, with the default presets
  and within the policy's own presets and hosts. Settings › Sandbox shows the mode as "On,
  required by policy" with who set it, and no control. On a system with no sandbox backend
  (Windows today) a harness chat is refused and never started unconfined, and the refusal names
  the policy and its owner (#1423).
- **A chat can no longer plant charter's settings or state under their coming purlis names.** The
  sandbox now denies a chat writing `purlis.toml`, `purlis.local.toml` and `.purlis/app` as it
  already denied `charter.toml`, `charter.local.toml` and `.charter/app`, and a chat may not
  create either state folder at the project root when it isn't already there. An extension may not
  declare either name as a write path, a chat's commit may not change `.purlis-scan-allow.toml`,
  and the vault guards cover `.purlis/vaults`. charter reads a project's files under either name,
  the purlis one first, and keeps writing the file the project already has (#1257).
- **Publishing a skill checks where it runs** (Skill studio preview). `purlis skill publish` now also uses the check the vault commands use for whether a process runs inside a chat, and takes any doubt as inside.
- **A chat removes a branch folder of its own workspace without a prompt** (#3879). Claude Code
  chats are now allowed `purlis worktree remove` and the `worktree_remove` tool unasked, alone
  in their call. The app never forces the removal, refuses a folder another live chat holds,
  and `--force` is refused for every chat, by the command and by purlis's hook.
- **A chat's push is scanned before it is sent.** git's `pre-push` in a chat now runs the commit
  scan over every commit the push would send that the remote does not have, so a secret in a
  commit that never passed the commit scan (made in your own terminal, or by a cherry-pick,
  rebase or `git am`) is refused before it is published. The refusal names the file and line,
  masks the value, and puts the chat in needs-you. A push that would publish a change to the
  scan's allowlist is refused too: you push those yourself. The repository's own `pre-push` still
  runs, and the guard refuses `git push --no-verify` and `git send-pack` (SQ-7, #586).
- **The folder that holds dispatch reports is never read, emptied or written through a link.**
  Its folders are opened one at a time without following a link, and every report is listed,
  read, written and removed relative to the folder that was opened. A file in it that does not
  read as a report is left where it is (#1463, #1457).
- **rustls is updated to 0.23.46**, which fixes RUSTSEC-2026-0346, RUSTSEC-2026-0347,
  RUSTSEC-2026-0348 and RUSTSEC-2026-0349 (qw390).
- **A sandboxed chat never writes your package caches.** A cached package is code a later
  build runs, so a chat's downloads go to caches only that project's sandboxed chats use. Each
  cache folder purlis makes is pinned, and a link planted in one is taken out, unfollowed,
  before the chat starts.
  In cargo's git cache, a chat writes inside each repository cargo made, never a new one, and
  never a repository's config or hooks.
- **A Claude Code profile's program is asked its version inside purlis's sandbox.** On macOS,
  the check that a profile's program answers as Claude Code runs it in a sandbox that lets it
  write nothing but a temp folder of its own and reach no network. A program that does not
  answer in time is told apart from one that answers wrong, so the chat can be started again.
- **A sandboxed chat still can't change its own sandbox through a manifest.** The project root's
  manifests, and those in each folder from the chat's folder up to the root, stay denied in
  every harness. A manifest kept as a link, such as a `purlis.local.toml` linked from a
  dotfiles repository, is held by the link itself as well as its target, so a chat can't
  remove it and put its own file in its place (#1336).
- **A sandboxed chat no longer writes what a program run later loads.** This holds for Claude
  Code, opencode and Codex chats in every sandboxed project. Such a chat can no longer write any of
  these, at any depth of any directory it may write:
  - git's config and hooks, in every clone, worktree and submodule;
  - `.husky/` and `.githooks/`, the directory a `core.hooksPath` names, and every script a
    harness's project config runs;
  - shell startup files;
  - `.mcp.json`;
  - Claude Code's, Codex's, opencode's and editors' project config.
  As a result, a sandboxed opencode chat can no longer create a git repository, or clone one,
  inside its directory. What Claude Code's own sandbox still lets through is listed in
  `SECURITY.md` (#1065).
- **No sandboxed chat starts in a linked folder.** If the chat's folder, or any folder between
  it and the project, is a link, the chat is refused with a sentence that says so.
- **A sandboxed chat starts only on the program it was compiled for.** Each of these is refused
  with a sentence that says so:
  - a Claude Code profile whose program does not answer as Claude Code;
  - a program named by a relative path;
  - a program that lies anywhere the chat could write, such as the project or a temp folder,
    whether by its path or through a link;
  - a command that names a file in such a place anywhere in a word, such as a script handed
    to an interpreter, a flag's value or a `file:` URL.
  The chat then runs the program's real path, the one that was checked. The Claude Code check
  takes the program's own answer, so it catches a profile that is not Claude Code by mistake,
  not one written to pass. Approving the profile is what vouches for its program. It also
  vouches for a path no word spells, in any encoding, and for a program that reads and runs
  such a file without being handed it. The check of a command's words catches mistakes; it is
  not the boundary. For opencode and Codex, the boundary is purlis's own wrap around the whole
  harness; Claude Code is not inside it yet (#1150). A command word over 4 KiB is refused.
- **A project whose `charter.toml` cannot be read starts no chat.** purlis cannot tell whether
  such a project runs chats sandboxed. So it says so and starts nothing, rather than starting
  the chat unsandboxed.
- **Codex runs inside purlis's own sandbox.** Codex's own sandbox could not be kept to the
  rules purlis compiles while it runs, so purlis now runs Codex inside its own sandbox, as it
  runs opencode (see *Codex chats run sandboxed on macOS*).
- **A sandboxed chat can no longer author or edit a project's skills at all.** In every
  harness, a sandboxed chat may never write `.claude/skills/`, `.agents/`, or opencode's
  `tui.json` and `tui.jsonc`, at any depth. These join the other harness config it already may
  not write. Each of them can make a later chat, run outside the sandbox, start code (#1057).
- **A project save reads a JSON or TOML file as the document it is, not only as its text.** A
  string in either can spell a character as an escape, so the secret check now also scans the
  parsed values of each staged `.json` and `.toml` file, the way the settings editors already
  do. A file that does not parse is scanned as text, as before (#1295).
- **The fetch after purlis merges a save's request goes only to the remote you saved to.** It
  was the one window fetch not held to the recorded remote; with another remote it now fetches
  nothing and the save stops (#1864).
- **A chat's screenshot paints over what you typed wherever the page draws it.** A screenshot
  the agent gets paints over what you typed or purlis filled wherever a page draws it, in text
  the page hides from its tree or draws through its style as well as in fields. On pages of the
  site where you typed, it also paints over every canvas, image and video, which purlis cannot
  read. When a page cannot be read at all, the screenshot is withheld and the agent is told why
  (#2303).
- **More of the code a project's hooks load is kept from a sandboxed chat's writes.** A bare
  name Node, tsx or bun is asked to load first (`-r`, `--import`, `--preload`) is now also
  protected in each `node_modules` from the folder the hook runs in up to the project, and in
  your home folder's, with the file a package's `main` names. Ruby's `RUBYLIB` is followed as its `-I` is, and Perl's `-M`
  and `-m` modules are protected where Perl looks them up, along `PERL5LIB` and `-I` (#1425).
- An administrator's policy can turn off asks for a secret a persona doesn't declare
  (`"undeclared-secret-asks": false`): the chat is told it was declined by policy and you aren't
  asked, and Settings shows the lock under Secret asks. Each step of a Secret ask is recorded
  in the event log as metadata only (no value, name or purpose), and the chat's stated purpose
  is masked wherever it's shown or kept.
- **What Add a grant can and cannot do.** It asks first and says what the grant reaches,
  including that a chat nobody is at may use it. It is held to every rule an Allow is: both
  names must be personas of the project, a pair an administrator's policy locks and a pair
  you said never to are refused, a grant for everyone is refused for a pair whose project
  grant you said Not on my machine to, no grant is kept for a workspace that is not there,
  and a persona's dispatch to itself needs none. Where the project has workspaces, the form
  starts with none chosen: any workspace is picked on purpose. A grant for everyone writes the project's
  committed file and is followed on this machine as it is written, bound to the project's
  history like any acceptance. Each one is recorded in purlis's event log as yours before it
  counts, and its command is the window's alone: nothing a chat sends can make one (#1465).
- **Each chat has a cap on the session records it asks purlis to write.** A chat may ask for a
  few records in ten minutes and a bounded number while it is open. Past the cap nothing is
  written and the chat is told why. Notices from a Smart close without a pass have their own
  per-chat cap, past which they go to the log only (#1361).
- **A spooled tool line keeps no digest of its arguments.** When the app does not take a hook's
  line in time, the line is kept in the chat's spool until the next drain. A tool line's
  arguments digest is now left out of it, so nothing on disk holds a digest that could be
  matched against a guess at the arguments. The event a drained line becomes has no `args`
  (#977).
- **Session credentials are written through the folder that was checked.** Each scope's
  credential file is made and renamed inside the directory purlis checked, through the
  descriptor it checked it on, so a folder put in its place afterwards is never written to
  (#992).
- **A runner's internal-address floor reads Teredo's pre-RFC prefix.** An address under
  `3ffe:831f::/32` is judged as the server and the client IPv4 addresses it carries, as one
  under `2001::/32` is, and a `sandbox.relayed-internal` range that takes it in is refused
  (#2741).
- **The docs say purlis needs no Full Disk Access.** macOS counts what a chat does as the
  app's doing, so a grant to the app reaches every chat it starts. *Updating* says to turn it
  off (#1654).
- **The browser skill's terminal flow keeps Playwright's traces out of the project.** It points
  `playwright-cli`'s output at a private folder outside the project before the session opens,
  and closes the session and removes the folder when the flow ends, so a trace of a logged-in
  run is never left where a save could commit it (#2686).
- **No secret is filled into a browser you have taken over.** The chat is told why, and can ask
  again once you hand the browser back.
- **A chat's commit and push are refused for an IBAN, eight more national ID numbers and 54
  more vendor tokens.** The scan before a chat commits or pushes now finds an IBAN (its country,
  length and mod-97 check), a UK National Insurance number, a Canadian SIN, an Aadhaar number, a
  German tax ID, a Spanish DNI or NIE, an Italian codice fiscale, a Brazilian CPF and a Dutch
  BSN, each only when its check holds, so a random number is not a hit. An ID written as bare
  digits is found when its name stands in front of it (`BSN: …`) or in its national grouping.
  It also finds every gitleaks default rule held by a fixed vendor marker that it did not find
  already, among them Stripe restricted keys, Vault, Sentry, PlanetScale, Fly.io, Twilio and
  Azure AD client secrets. A refusal names the kind and shows the value masked, as before, and
  personal data is let through by path only, never by fingerprint (#773).
- **The commit and push scan reads a change with the unchanged lines it joins.** A line that
  ends in a backslash joins the next, as a TOML `"""` string reads it. A chat's commit or push
  that completes a credential an unchanged line began, or begins one an unchanged line
  completes, is now refused as well (#1346).
- **A credential assignment or a signed token split by a line-ending backslash is caught in any
  file.** Where a `"""` string opens the value, the guards that read whole texts (a project
  save, a handoff or dispatch brief, the settings editors) now find it in a file of any name,
  not only one that parses as TOML (#1346).
- **Text from Docker and runners is shown safely in the window.** What Docker or a runner says
  about a pool, in Devices, the Pools settings, a project's mark and a pool's removal, is drawn
  on one line, capped, apart from purlis's own words, without characters a reader does not see
  and without the user or password of an address (#2052).
- **The app reads a branch's file lists in its bounded reader, and starts no git for them.**
  Opening a file, handing it to your editor, expanding a folder in the explorer, ⌘P and ⌘⇧F
  used to run git in the app's own process to list the files a branch offers, what it ignores
  and its submodules. They now ask the short-lived reader that already reads a branch's changes,
  with its time and memory limits, so a branch an agent built to hang or swell those reads costs
  the reader and not the app. A search you stop still stops at once. The folder watch and
  "Start a chat here" find a branch's folder the same way (#1189).
  A branch whose index the reader cannot read yet, such as one tracking a path of 4,095 bytes
  or more, is still listed as before: for that branch only, the app reads it with its hardened
  git, as it did until now (#1130).
- **The first secret check now answers the way the last one does.** These checks now read
  string escapes, as the project save does: the warning on a memory or ref write, a session
  record, a repo's instructions offered as memory, a harness profile's fields, a workspace's
  settings, the git identity form, a handoff brief, the summary of a permission ask, and the
  redaction of a bug report and of the app's log. Before, an earlier check could pass a spelling
  that the save then refused. A backslash at the end of a line now joins it to the next, as in a
  TOML `"""` string, so a token split across the break is found, the commit and push check
  included. A line read without the join is still read too, and a join never turns prose such
  as a Markdown line break into a credential assignment (#1315).
- **The handoff, consent and operator-rule checks read every level of a shell string.** A
  command a shell is handed as a string, and that string hands on to another shell, is now read
  at every level up to the nesting limit, and refused past it. That covers a `-c` string inside
  a `-c` string, a heredoc fed to a shell, a script piped or given as a here-string to a shell,
  and the command a `find -exec` runs. The handoff check also reads a `case` branch and a shell
  function the command defines. The three checks read one way, and they agree on a script a
  string writes to a file: each refuses it. A test runs every shape through bash and zsh to
  confirm which ones really run the command (#1426, #1419).
- **A helper's dispatch is seen in the same places.** The check that refuses a dispatch from a
  helper, and the one that refuses a dispatch's text beside a live substitution, read every
  level a shell is handed a text at, the same way (#1582).
- **More of what a project's hooks load is protected from a chat.** A colon list in a
  variable (`PYTHONPATH=./a:./b`) is read part by part. A bare name Node, gawk or Ruby looks up
  along `NODE_PATH`, `AWKPATH` or a `-I` folder is protected there too (#1425).
- **One process can no longer tie up the hook channel by opening connection after
  connection.** The app served every connection to its hook socket on a new thread, with no
  limit. It now serves them from a bounded pool: at most 32 at once from one process, and 128
  from all processes together. A connection past either limit is answered at once and closed.
  The hook spools its line for the next drain, and a `purlis` command that asked something says
  the app is busy. Hooks from many chats firing at once are still all served (#991).
- **A runner's internal-address floor reads every NAT64 layout and takes ranges.** An IPv6
  address under NAT64's local-use prefix is read at every length it may be used at, and one
  under the runner's own NAT64 prefix is read where that prefix puts it. The runner reads its
  prefix from its resolver. In either case the address is judged as the IPv4 address it
  carries. `sandbox.relayed-internal` takes ranges such as `10.96.0.0/12`. An entry that is
  not taken is named on its own and leaves the rest of the policy as written (#2530).
- **A runner's internal-address floor reads Teredo and ISATAP addresses.** A Teredo address is
  judged as the server and the client IPv4 addresses it carries, and an ISATAP address as the
  IPv4 address it carries and as itself. `sandbox.relayed-internal` has to list each internal
  one as that IPv4 address, and a range that takes in Teredo addresses is refused (#2678).
- **purlis no longer reads the keyring from inside a sandboxed chat.** A vault whose values come
  from the keyring (a `keyring` vault, or a 1Password vault whose token purlis keeps there) is
  read for a sandboxed chat only by the app, through `purlis secret exec`. When the app does not
  take the run, and for `purlis secret get`, `cp` and every other read in the chat, the command
  refuses with a sentence saying why and what to run instead, rather than reading the keyring
  itself and raising a Keychain question on the chat's behalf (#1638). On Linux this is new
  for `get`, `cp` and every other read of such a vault in a sandboxed chat, which used to
  read it; there the refusal names `secret exec` through the app.
- **The kill switch holds in the session host.** With chats running in the session host, Stop
  all on the title bar, and `purlis stop --all` once the app hears it, stop every chat the host
  runs; the stop holds when the host starts again, and nothing starts until you re-arm it from
  the title bar. Only the window re-arms; any other client of the host is refused (#2001).
- **The leak guard reads a command substitution wherever the shell runs one.** A read of a vault
  or a revealed secret inside a substitution is now refused when the substitution sits in double
  quotes, in a parameter's default, in backticks or in an expanding heredoc body, exactly as the
  same read is refused unquoted. The guard reads quotes, comments, heredoc bodies and `case`
  patterns inside a substitution the way the shell does. A substitution nested more deeply
  than purlis reads (the same limit as the rest of its checks), or one that would take too long
  to read, is refused as too big to check. A test runs every shape through bash and zsh to
  confirm which ones really read (#1412).
- **A chain of tasks still holds when a chat in the middle of it has closed.** A dispatch to a
  persona above the asking chat in its chain is refused, and the person's never for a chat
  above holds below it too. Both read the chain from the record purlis keeps of each task when
  it starts it, no longer from the chats that happen to be open, so a chat that finished,
  closed or was cleared is still counted. A finished task reopened as an ordinary chat starts a
  new chain. A chat whose chain began under an older version, which kept no record of it,
  and has a closed chat in it is refused any dispatch to another persona, and is told why; so
  is the person asking from its tab. A chat that closes while its own ask is being decided
  starts nothing (#1521).
- **Allow on Blocked lately allows only a connection the record refused.** A host the network
  record holds no refused connection to is not allowed from there (#1681).
- **A held ask is not dropped.** A burst of new hosts a chat's connections ask about no longer
  pushes out an ask whose connection still waits on your answer (#1709).
- **A granted folder's path is checked.** purlis refuses to grant a folder whose name it could
  not show as written (#1709).
- **A Docker pool's check holds rootless Podman to what it asked its runtime for.** The check is
  measured against the machine's IPC, host name, cgroups, folders and devices on every engine,
  and on rootless Podman it also reads the container's runtime config (#2895).
- **The project root's branch guard follows an alias after a program held in a variable.**
  `G=git; $G co -b x`, where `co` is an alias of `checkout` in the root's config or set on the
  line with `-c alias.co=checkout`, is now refused like `git co -b x`. The guard reads aliases
  there the way it already does after a substitution among git's options: one alias read per
  command line, and a line whose aliases git cannot be asked about is refused rather than
  allowed. A word that is no alias of a branch move, such as `$G status`, is still allowed
  (#1326).
- **The runner image carries build provenance and an SBOM.** Every runner image a release
  publishes has SLSA build provenance and a CycloneDX SBOM of each architecture's image (its
  packages and the `purlis` binary's crates), attached to the image in the registry and
  verified in the run that pushed it. docs/runner-image.md says how to check them (#2191).
- **The secret scan reads more of what a commit or a push publishes.** A chat's push is now
  read for what a merge's own resolution adds (including a merge made with `git commit-tree`),
  for each commit's and annotated tag's message (credentials only, so a `Co-Authored-By` line is
  never refused), and, at commit and at push, for a text file git only shows as "Binary files
  differ" because of an attribute or a lowered `core.bigFileThreshold`. `purlis save` now scans
  what its own push would send before pushing, so a commit made by hand in the project is no
  longer published unscanned. Real binary files, LFS pointers, submodules, deletions and merges
  that add nothing of their own are let through as before (#1133).
- **A secret purlis reads after a chat said it is masked in what that chat said, too.** The
  waiting strip, the Inbox card and the quiz no longer show it until the chat's next turn
  (#4843).
- **Text from Docker and runners hides the user and password of more address spellings.** An
  address written in percent escapes, and one a blank parts in two, now lose their user and
  password before the window shows them. Addresses with a host and a port, digests and image
  names still show as they are (#3592).
- **Hardens the hold on removing a workspace from a sandboxed chat** (#1408). A terminal removes
  a workspace as before.
- **The wrap also holds the hook socket's folder.** A chat purlis wraps (opencode, Codex) keeps
  the folder that holds its hook socket unwritten, as a Claude Code chat's settings do (#1408).
- **The update manifests carry build provenance, and the provenance is on the release page.**
  `latest.json`, `dev.json` and their weekly twins are now attested like every build file, so
  `gh attestation verify latest.json --repo purlis/purlis` checks them too. A job that holds
  no key and cannot write the release writes them. Each release also carries
  `purlis.intoto.jsonl`, the attestation's own bundle, for checking offline (#778, #1133).
- **A release build checks that the macOS app keeps the hardened runtime and carries no
  entitlement.** The check reads the signed app itself, on every macOS build, in both signing
  modes. A test also holds that no release build turns on the fence purlis's own tests run
  under (#1180, #1517).
- **A vault in the state folder is never reached through a link.** A plain-file or reference vault
  inside the project's state folder is now checked from the project down, as the vault registry
  is, so a state folder that is itself a link is refused for the vault in it: nothing is read
  from where it points and nothing is written there (#1321).
- **Vault values handed to a run are wiped from memory as they go**, on the runner and on your
  desktop: as the window reads them, as the run reads them, every copy a run is prepared with, and
  what the window measures before it sends them, on success and on every refusal (#3420).
- **More of a profile is filtered before it goes to a runner** (#3866). An agent's or a skill's
  frontmatter no longer carries environment or headers, a URL no longer carries a user or password,
  and a hook, status line or file suggester whose command shows a credential stays behind. What was
  removed is said in the log, by name and never by value.
- **A sandboxed Claude Code chat can no longer read or write what waits to be told to another
  chat.** A dispatched chat's report, and purlis's own word on a dispatch you were asked
  about, wait in the project's state folder until the chat they are for takes its next turn.
  That folder is now denied, for reading and writing, to a sandboxed chat of a harness whose
  hooks run outside its sandbox: a chat could have written a line there that another chat
  would have read in purlis's voice. purlis's hooks deliver, outside the sandbox.
- **On Codex and opencode that folder is still readable and writable by a chat.** Their
  sandbox is a wrap around the whole harness, so the hooks that deliver run inside it and
  must reach the folder. What holds there is the check each file gets as it is read. The
  denial reaches them once delivery moves onto the hook socket (#1457).
- **Who may dispatch to whom is answered and read in your own window only.** Every answer
  to a dispatch's question, Settings › Project › Dispatch, and the lists of a teammate's
  grants and of refusals kept while you were away are your window's alone.
- **Every yes is held to what it was shown.** An answer to a dispatch's question, to a
  teammate's grant, or to a refusal kept while you were away grants nothing where what it
  said has changed since, and you are shown it as it reads now.
- **A teammate's grant limited to one workspace is bound to the project's history** as every
  project grant is, and so is what Give back restores.
- **A chat nobody is at moves work into another workspace as another persona only under a
  grant that names the two**, by a handoff as by a task (#1483).
- **A link a chat leaves at a workspace's other files no longer carries your writes anywhere
  else.** `workspace.md` (its vision, its sections and its `## Sessions` line),
  `workspace.json`, the piece log and liveness records in `pieces/`, the work link log in `work/`
  and the project's own `sessions/` are now written the way the four stores are: with no link
  anywhere on the way, and through the folder purlis opened. A link at one of them, or at the
  folder above it, is refused and nothing is written, even when it points at another workspace or
  a persona inside the project (#1082). The piece and work link logs are read the same way.
- **The last readers that opened a store's entries by path read them through the store.** The
  briefing's persona memory digest and the change store's record check, landing log and pending
  landings never read another workspace's or a persona's files through a store swapped for a
  link (#1083).
- **A link a chat plants in its own workspace no longer carries your writes anywhere else.** Your
  `purlis` commands and the app now write a workspace's todos, memory, session records and
  changes the way purlis's MCP tools do: with no link anywhere on the way, and through the
  directory they opened. A store that is a link, or a link inside one, is never followed by a
  write, even when it points at another workspace or a persona inside the project: the write is
  refused and writes nothing. The readers that list and read those stores leave such a link out
  too, apart from a few that #1083 tracks (the doctor's memory rows, some counts, and the landing
  logs). A store whose lock a chat keeps is refused after a few seconds instead of hanging your
  command (#1064).
- **The floor guard refuses more ways an unattended agent could merge.** When nobody is
  watching (`bypassPermissions`), a forge API call to a merge endpoint, a setting that makes a
  pull or merge request merge on its own later (auto-merge, a merge queue or train), an alias
  that stands for a held command or the start of one, and the same commands inside a script a
  shell runs or a command substitution are refused, as `gh pr merge` already was. A forge API call whose effect on a merge
  purlis cannot read is refused too. Reads, opening a request and ordinary pushes are
  unchanged, and attended use is untouched (#866).
- **An unattended agent cannot print the forge token or read other stored secrets.** The CLIs'
  token commands, the auth-status and config reads that show the token, git's credential fill,
  and commands that read the OS keychain or a password store are refused when nobody is
  watching, since a run holding a secret could act where no guard sees it. Attended use is
  untouched (#866).
- **A guard that cannot answer refuses the call.** The tool-call guards run with a deep stack and
  a deadline inside the harness's own hook timeout, and the floor bounds how deep it reads a command inside a command, so a line
  built to exhaust them is refused instead of slipping through when the hook dies (#866).
- **The handoff guard finds a handoff in a shell's script past the shell's options**, including
  options that take a value (#866).
- **The hook channel reads only your own user's connections.** Besides each chat's token, the
  app now checks which user is on the other end of its hook socket, and closes a connection
  from any other user before reading it. The socket's private directory already kept other
  users out; this still holds if that directory's permissions are ever wrong (FD-6, #645).
- **The release runs only the code it pinned.** Every GitHub Action in purlis's workflows is
  pinned to a commit rather than a tag, and the release jobs that hold the signing keys restore
  no build cache (ADR 0042).
- **A chat starts from an allowlisted environment.** A chat is no longer given the app's whole
  environment minus a few names: it gets a keep-list (`PATH`, `HOME`, the locale, the proxies,
  `XDG_*`, `CHARTER_*` and the like), the variables its harness declares, and whatever the plane's
  `charter.local.toml` lists under `[chat_env] pass`. Cloud, forge and model-provider credentials
  pass only when listed by exact name.
- **A plane save scans every file it commits.** `purlis save` reads every staged file for
  secrets, not only memory and refs, and also catches a bare token by its forge's prefix. A hit
  names the path and line, never the value; a binary or over-10-MiB file outside memory and refs
  is named as not scanned.
- **Plane trust covers persona tool grants.** Each persona's `tools:`, with a digest of any
  `bin/` script a tool names, is part of the approval, and a grant that changed since asks again
  before it runs without a prompt. Old per-session tool ceilings are removed when a plane opens
  (ADR 0035).
- **Hook calls are authenticated per chat.** Each chat gets its own token when it starts, and the
  hook channel accepts a call only with that chat's token.
